Generative AI, Large Language Models, and Coding Agents Foundations, adaptation, evaluation, and practical Claude workflows Davut Ayan 2026-11-02 Introduction This book combines two formerly separate sets of study notes: foundations of generative AI and large language models, and practical workflows for working with Claude and AI coding agents. The goal is to connect model concepts with safe, reproducible practice for data science and software work. The book has four parts: LLM foundations — transformers and attention, pre-training and scaling laws, fine-tuning and PEFT, evaluation, alignment (RLHF, DPO), and building LLM applications (inference optimization, RAG, tools, responsible AI). Prompt engineering — prompt anatomy, techniques, use-case strategies, evaluation, and safety (in progress). Agentic AI — vendor-neutral design of agentic workflows: reflection, tool use and code execution, evaluation and error analysis, planning, and multi-agent systems. Applied agent workflows — prompting, code review, verification loops, Claude Code hooks and skills, reproducible notebooks, MCP, and supervisor agents on Databricks. An appendix summarizes the hands-on labs that accompanied the LLM foundations material. These are educational notes, not vendor certification material. Product features change quickly, so product-specific chapters link to primary vendor documentation and should be checked against the installed product version. How to use this book Read the LLM chapters in sequence when learning the underlying concepts. Read the Agentic AI part before building agents; the Claude chapters then serve as practical, tool-specific references. Run and inspect generated code; do not treat model output as validated merely because it is fluent. Protect secrets and private data, use least-privilege tool permissions, and keep a human reviewer responsible for consequential decisions.

These chapters began as study notes from the DeepLearning.AI / AWS course Generative AI with Large Language Models (Coursera). They have since been rewritten as a reference, checked against the primary papers cited in each chapter, and extended with later developments. 1.1 What generative AI is Generative models learn the statistical structure of their training data and produce new samples from it: text, images, audio, video, or code. This book focuses on large language models (LLMs): neural networks trained on very large text corpora to predict the next token. Chatbots, code assistants, and writing tools are applications built on top of that one capability. Key terms: Foundation model. A model trained broadly enough to be adapted to many downstream tasks. Examples include BERT, GPT, T5/FLAN-T5, BLOOM, and Llama. Its capabilities must be measured on each task; they cannot be assumed from its size. Parameters. The learned weights, currently up to hundreds of billions for large models. Parameters encode distributed statistical patterns, not a database of retrievable facts. More parameters add capacity, but data, training recipe, and adaptation matter as much. Prompt, completion, inference. The text you send is the prompt. Producing text is inference. The output is the completion. Context window. The maximum number of tokens the model can attend to at once: instructions, conversation, documents, tool results, and its own output. The limit varies by model; check current documentation. You interact with an LLM in natural language, not in a formal programming language. You can use it as is, or adapt it (Chapter 3) without training a new model. In short. An LLM is a neural network trained on huge text corpora to predict the next token; chatbots and assistants are applications built on that. Parameters store statistical patterns, not a fact database. The context window caps everything the model can see at once. 1.2 What LLMs are used for Many tasks reduce to next-token prediction under the right prompt: Generation: drafting essays, emails, or marketing copy. Summarization: condensing dialogues, documents, or reviews. Translation: between natural languages, or from natural language to code or SQL. Information extraction: pulling named entities (people, places, organizations), fields, or labels out of text. Augmented tasks: answering from documents or calling APIs. These are not abilities of the model alone; the surrounding application supplies the data and tools (Chapter 5). Larger models generally handle more tasks without examples. Smaller or specialized models can still be the better choice on cost, latency, privacy, or a narrow task. Choose by evaluating on your own use case. In short. Generation, summarization, translation, and extraction are all next-token prediction under the right prompt. Answering from documents or calling APIs needs an application around the model. Pick the model size by evaluation, not by default. 1.3 Before transformers: recurrent networks Earlier language models used recurrent neural networks (RNNs). An RNN reads tokens one at a time and carries a hidden state forward, so in principle it summarizes everything seen so far. In practice it has three problems: Long-range dependencies. Gradients shrink (or explode) as they flow back through many time steps, so plain RNNs struggle to learn from distant context (Bengio et al. 1994). LSTMs reduced but did not remove the problem (Hochreiter and Schmidhuber 1997). Sequential computation. Step \(t\) needs the result of step \(t-1\). Training cannot be parallelized across positions, which limits model and data scale. A fixed-size bottleneck. The whole history must be squeezed into one state vector. Language needs wide context. Words have several meanings: a bank can be a financial institution or a riverside. Sentences can be syntactically ambiguous: in “The teacher taught the students with the book”, whose book is it? Resolving such cases often requires the whole sentence or document. Attention was the fix. It was first added to RNN translation models: the decoder learned to look back at all encoder states and weight the most relevant ones (Bahdanau et al. 2015). The transformer took the next step and dropped recurrence entirely. In short. RNNs read one token at a time: weak on long-range context, impossible to parallelize across positions, and limited by one state vector. Attention lets the model look back at all earlier states directly. 1.4 The transformer “Attention Is All You Need” (Vaswani et al. 2017) introduced the transformer. It is built from attention and position-wise feed-forward layers, with no recurrence. Two properties explain its success: Parallelism. All positions in a sequence are processed at once. That makes training efficient on GPUs and allows much larger models and datasets. Direct context. Every token can attend to every other token in one step, however far apart they are. 1.4.1 From text to vectors Tokenization. Text is split into tokens from a fixed vocabulary. Tokens are usually subword units learned by algorithms such as byte-pair encoding (Sennrich et al. 2016), so rare words split into pieces. Each token maps to an integer ID. A model must always be used with the tokenizer it was trained with. For example, a tokenizer might split “unbelievably” into un + believ + ably, while “the” is a single token (the exact split depends on the tokenizer). For English, a common rule of thumb is about 0.75 words per token, so 1,000 tokens is roughly 750 words. Embedding. Each token ID is mapped to a learned vector of dimension \(d_{\text{model}}\) (512 in the original transformer). Tokens with related meanings end up close together in this space. Positional information. Attention by itself ignores order, so position must be added. The original paper added fixed sinusoidal positional encodings to the embeddings. Many modern LLMs instead use rotary position embeddings (RoPE), which encode relative position inside the attention computation (Su et al. 2024). 1.4.2 Self-attention Each token’s vector \(x_i\) is projected into three vectors with learned matrices. The query \(q_i = x_i W^Q\) says what the token is looking for. The key \(k_j = x_j W^K\) says what each token offers. The value \(v_j = x_j W^V\) is what gets passed along if the token is attended to. Stacking these vectors into matrices \(Q, K, V\) gives scaled dot-product attention: \[ \text{Attention}(Q, K, V) = \text{softmax}\!\left(\frac{Q K^\top}{\sqrt{d_k}}\right) V \] \(QK^\top\) scores how relevant every token is to every other token. The softmax turns each row of scores into weights that sum to one; plotted as a grid, these weights form an attention map. Each output is a weighted average of the value vectors. Why divide by \(\sqrt{d_k}\)? Dot products grow with the vector dimension \(d_k\). Large scores push the softmax towards a one-hot output, where gradients become very small. Scaling keeps training stable. Multi-head attention runs \(h\) attention operations in parallel, each with its own projections (the original used \(h = 8\) heads of size \(d_k = 64\)), and concatenates the results. Different heads learn different relations, for example syntactic agreement, coreference, or topic. Which relation a head learns is not chosen in advance. Cost. The score matrix is \(n \times n\) for a sequence of \(n\) tokens, so attention compute and memory grow quadratically with context length. That is why long contexts are expensive. At 4,096 tokens the matrix has about 16.8 million entries per head and layer; at 131,072 tokens (32 times longer) it has about 17.2 billion, 1,024 times more. Optimized kernels such as FlashAttention avoid storing the full matrix, but the compute still grows quadratically. Example: one attention step. In “The campaign missed its target because it launched late”, the token “it” should attend mostly to “campaign”. Suppose its scaled scores against “campaign”, “target”, and “late” are 2.0, 0.0, and 1.0. The softmax turns them into weights of about 0.67, 0.09, and 0.24. The output for “it” is then \(0.67\,v_{\text{campaign}} + 0.09\,v_{\text{target}} + 0.24\,v_{\text{late}}\): a vector that now carries mostly the meaning of “campaign”. (Real models attend over every token, and each head produces its own weights.) 1.4.3 The rest of a transformer block Each layer (block) wraps attention with: a position-wise feed-forward network: two linear layers with a nonlinearity, applied to each token separately (inner width 2,048 in the original); residual connections and layer normalization around both sub-layers, which make deep stacks trainable. The original model stacked six such layers in the encoder and six in the decoder. A final linear layer maps each output vector to one logit per vocabulary token, and a softmax turns the logits into a probability distribution over the next token. 1.4.4 Encoder, decoder, and the three model families The encoder reads the whole input with bidirectional self-attention. It produces a contextual representation of each input token. The decoder generates output one token at a time. Its self-attention is masked (causal): each position sees only earlier positions, so the model cannot peek at the token it is predicting. In an encoder–decoder model, the decoder also uses cross-attention, where its queries attend over the encoder’s outputs. Using one or both halves gives three families: encoder-only (BERT), decoder-only (GPT, Llama), and encoder–decoder (T5, BART). They differ in pre-training objective and in which tasks they suit. Chapter 2 compares them in detail. 1.4.5 Generating text, end to end Take translation with an encoder–decoder model, from “J’aime l’apprentissage automatique” to “I love machine learning”: Tokenize the French sentence with the model’s tokenizer. The encoder processes all input tokens in parallel into contextual representations. The decoder starts from a start-of-sequence token. Attending to its own previous outputs and (through cross-attention) to the encoder’s representations, it produces a distribution over the next token, and one token is chosen. The chosen token is appended and fed back in. Step 3 repeats until an end-of-sequence token is produced or a length limit is reached. Detokenize the output tokens into text. A decoder-only model works the same way without the encoder. The prompt and the tokens generated so far form one sequence, and the model extends it one token at a time. This loop is autoregressive generation. How the next token is chosen from the distribution is set by the generation configuration (Section 1.6). 1.4.6 Landmark models Model Year Family Size Why it matters BERT (Devlin et al. 2019) 2018 Encoder 110M (Base), 340M (Large) Bidirectional pre-training with masked language modelling; set the pattern of pre-train then fine-tune for understanding tasks T5 (Raffel et al. 2020) 2019 Encoder–decoder Up to 11B Framed every task as text-to-text; FLAN-T5 is its instruction-tuned version GPT-3 (Brown et al. 2020) 2020 Decoder 175B Showed strong few-shot in-context learning at scale BLOOM (BigScience Workshop 2022) 2022 Decoder 176B Open-science, multilingual (46 natural and 13 programming languages) LLaMA (Touvron et al. 2023) 2023 Decoder 7B–65B Smaller models trained on more tokens; led a wave of open-weight models Model families move quickly. Self-attention, \(\text{softmax}(QK^\top/\sqrt{d_k})V\), lets every token take a weighted average of every other token’s values; multi-head runs several in parallel; cost is quadratic in length. Encoder (bidirectional), decoder (causal), encoder–decoder (cross-attention); generation is autoregressive, one token at a time. 1.5 Prompting and in-context learning Prompt engineering is designing the input so the model produces the desired completion. Its most important effect, discovered at scale, is in-context learning (ICL): the model picks up a task from examples placed in the prompt, with no weight updates (Brown et al. 2020). Zero-shot: an instruction and the input, no examples. For example, “Classify this review: … Sentiment:”. One-shot: one solved example before the real input. Few-shot: several solved examples, ideally covering the label space (for example, both a positive and a negative review). A few-shot prompt for tagging customer comments: Tag each comment as PRICE, DELIVERY, or PRODUCT. Comment: "Arrived three days late and the box was crushed." Tag: DELIVERY Comment: "Great jacket, but $40 more than at the outlet." Tag: PRICE Comment: "The zipper broke after one week." Tag: The model continues with “PRODUCT”. The examples teach both the labels and the output format, without any training. What to know: ICL depends on scale. Large models often do well zero-shot. Small models may fail even with several examples. Examples cost context. They use up the context window and add tokens to every call. There is a ceiling. If a handful of examples does not get the performance you need, more examples rarely help. That is the signal to fine-tune (Chapter 3). The Prompt Engineering part of this book (starting with Chapter 6) covers prompt structure, techniques, and evaluation in depth. In short. In-context learning: the model picks up a task from examples in the prompt, with no weight updates. Zero-, one-, and few-shot differ only in the number of solved examples. It depends on scale and costs context; if a few examples do not work, fine-tune. 1.6 Configuring generation At each step the model outputs a probability distribution over the vocabulary. Inference-time settings (as opposed to training parameters) decide how the next token is picked from it, and when to stop. Max new tokens. A cap on the number of generated tokens. Generation can stop earlier at an end-of-sequence token. Greedy decoding. Always pick the most probable token. It is deterministic and fine for short factual outputs, but prone to repetitive loops in longer text. (Beam search, which keeps the best few partial sequences, is a deterministic alternative common in translation.) Random sampling. Draw the next token in proportion to its probability. This adds variety but can wander into low-probability, incoherent tokens. In Hugging Face Transformers, sampling is enabled with do_sample=True. Top-k sampling. Sample only from the \(k\) most probable tokens, renormalized. Top-p (nucleus) sampling. Sample from the smallest set of tokens whose cumulative probability reaches \(p\). The candidate set adapts to how confident the model is (Holtzman et al. 2020). Temperature. Rescale the logits before the softmax: \(p_i \propto \exp(z_i / T)\). \(T < 1\) sharpens the distribution (more predictable). \(T > 1\) flattens it (more varied). \(T = 1\) leaves it unchanged. Worked example. Suppose the next-token logits are apple \(= -1.0\), banana \(= 0.5\), cake \(= 2.0\), and donut \(= 1.2\). Next token \(T = 0.5\) \(T = 1.0\) \(T = 2.0\) apple 0.002 0.029 0.094 banana 0.040 0.130 0.200 cake 0.797 0.581 0.423 donut 0.161 0.261 0.283 At \(T = 1\): Top-k with \(k = 3\) keeps cake, donut, and banana and renormalizes them to 0.598, 0.269, and 0.133. Top-p with \(p = 0.8\) keeps cake and donut, the smallest set whose cumulative probability (0.842) reaches 0.8, and renormalizes them to 0.690 and 0.310. Apple can never be sampled under either filter. In practice, use low temperature or greedy decoding for extraction, classification, and code. Use moderate temperature with top-p for open-ended writing. Hosted APIs may expose only some of these settings, and reasoning models may fix them. In short. Generation settings choose the next token from the model’s distribution. Greedy is deterministic; sampling adds variety; top-k and top-p cut off unlikely tokens; temperature sharpens (\(T<1\)) or flattens (\(T>1\)). Low temperature for extraction and code, moderate with top-p for writing. 1.7 The generative AI project lifecycle An LLM project moves through four stages, and later results often send you back to an earlier one: Stage Key decisions Covered in Scope Define the use case narrowly: which tasks, which inputs, what counts as success This section Select Use an existing foundation model (the usual choice) or pre-train your own Chapter 2 Adapt and align Prompting first, then fine-tuning or PEFT, then alignment with human feedback; evaluate at every step Chapters 3 and 4 Integrate Optimize for inference; add retrieval and tools to overcome model limits; deploy, monitor, and manage risks Chapter 5 Scoping matters most. A model that must do many things needs to be larger and more general than one that only extracts named entities from invoices. A narrow scope makes model choice, evaluation, and risk assessment easier and cheaper. The inner loop is adapt → evaluate → adapt. Start with prompt engineering and in-context learning. Measure against a held-out evaluation set. Fine-tune only if prompting falls short. Then return to prompting with the tuned model. 1.7.1 What each lever costs The levers differ sharply in what they change, how long they take, and the skill they demand. That is why the usual order is cheapest first: Pre-training Prompting Fine-tuning / PEFT Alignment (RLHF, DPO) Compression What changes All weights, plus the architecture, tokenizer, and context length Nothing in the model; only the input All weights, or small adapter weights (Section 3.5) Weights or adapters, steered by preference data Model size or precision: pruning, quantization, distillation Data needed A very large general or domain corpus None, or a few examples in the prompt Hundreds to many thousands of labeled task examples Preference comparisons from humans or AI, often with a reward model Little: a calibration set, or teacher outputs for distillation Training time Weeks to months on large clusters None Minutes to days Similar to fine-tuning or longer None to hours; distillation is a full training run Objective Next-token prediction on broad text Better task performance Better task performance on a specific task or domain Match human preferences (helpful, honest, harmless) Cheaper, faster inference Expertise High Low Medium Medium to high Medium Read the table across, not down. Moving right from prompting adds data requirements, training cost, and the risk of degrading general abilities (catastrophic forgetting). A lever is worth its cost only when the cheaper ones have been measured and fall short. Current practice (October 2026). The time ranges are rough orders of magnitude; they depend on model size, data size, and hardware. Few teams pre-train their own LLM: they start from an open-weight or API model. Most alignment beyond the vendor’s own now uses DPO or similar offline methods (Chapter 4) rather than a full RLHF loop, which moves its expertise closer to that of fine-tuning. Even a well-adapted model invents information when unsure and is unreliable at exact computation. It also knows nothing after its training cut-off. Production systems therefore add retrieval, tools, and verification around the model; see Chapter 5. In short. Scope, select, adapt and align, integrate, with evaluation throughout. A narrow scope makes every later step easier. Use the levers cheapest first: prompting, then fine-tuning, then alignment; pre-train only in rare cases. 1.8 Key takeaways The section summaries above hold the details. The chapter in five lines: What: an LLM predicts the next token; most text tasks reduce to that. How: transformers replaced recurrence with attention, which is parallel, direct, and quadratic in length. Shapes: encoder, decoder, and encoder–decoder models suit different tasks. Steering: prompts and in-context examples shape what it does; generation settings shape how it samples. Process: scope narrowly, start from an existing model, adapt cheapest first, and evaluate throughout. 1.9 Interview checkpoints Why did transformers replace RNNs? Parallel training across positions, and direct attention between any two tokens instead of a long chain of recurrent steps. Write the attention formula. Why the \(\sqrt{d_k}\)? \(\text{softmax}(QK^\top/\sqrt{d_k})V\). Without scaling, large dot products saturate the softmax and shrink the gradients. What are Q, K, and V? Learned projections of each token: what it is looking for (query), what it offers to be matched on (key), and the content it passes on when attended to (value). Why multi-head attention? Several heads can capture different relations in parallel at the same total cost. Why does attention need positional information? Attention treats its inputs as an unordered set; positional encodings or RoPE inject word order. What does causal masking do? It stops each decoder position from seeing future tokens, so training matches left-to-right generation. What is the complexity of self-attention in sequence length? Quadratic, \(O(n^2)\). Top-k vs. top-p? Top-k keeps a fixed number of tokens. Top-p keeps a variable number whose cumulative probability reaches \(p\). What does temperature do? It divides the logits before the softmax. Lower values sharpen the distribution; higher values flatten it. Zero-shot vs. few-shot? When do you move to fine-tuning? Few-shot includes solved examples in the prompt. Move on when a handful of examples does not reach the target performance, or when context or cost limits bite. References

Chapter 2 Pre-training and Scaling Large Language Models After scoping a use case, the next lifecycle decision (Section 1.7) is which model to build on. Almost always the answer is an existing pre-trained model. This chapter explains why, covering: how pre-training works; why training large models strains GPU memory, and the techniques that make it feasible (number formats and distributed training); the scaling laws that link model size, data, and compute; and the narrow case where pre-training your own domain model can be worth it. 2.1 Choosing a starting model Open models are distributed through model hubs such as Hugging Face. Each model ships with a model card (Mitchell et al. 2019). The card records the intended uses, training data and procedure, evaluation results, and known limitations. Read it before anything else. It tells you whether the model’s architecture, licence, languages, and context length fit your task. In short. Start from an existing model on a hub, and read its model card first: intended use, data, evaluations, limits, licence. 2.2 Pre-training objectives and architecture families Pre-training is self-supervised learning on a very large text corpus. The labels come from the text itself, so no human annotation is needed. What the model learns to do depends on its training objective, and the objective is tied to its architecture: Family Pre-training objective What the model sees Good at Examples Encoder-only (autoencoding) Masked language modelling: predict randomly masked tokens Both sides of each token (bidirectional) Classification, named-entity recognition, embeddings BERT (Devlin et al. 2019), RoBERTa (Liu et al. 2019) Decoder-only (autoregressive) Causal language modelling: predict the next token Only earlier tokens (left-to-right) Text generation; at scale, zero-shot and few-shot on many tasks GPT (Brown et al. 2020), BLOOM, Llama Encoder–decoder (sequence-to-sequence) Varies. T5 uses span corruption: masked spans are replaced by sentinel tokens, and the decoder reconstructs them Encoder: whole input; decoder: earlier outputs Translation, summarization, input-to-output tasks T5 (Raffel et al. 2020), BART The two main losses, for a token sequence \(x_1, \dots, x_T\): \[ \mathcal{L}_{\text{causal}} = -\sum_{t=1}^{T} \log p_\theta(x_t \mid x_{<t}), \qquad \mathcal{L}_{\text{masked}} = -\sum_{t \in \mathcal{M}} \log p_\theta(x_t \mid x_{\setminus \mathcal{M}}) \] Here \(\mathcal{M}\) is the set of masked positions. BERT masks about 15% of tokens (Devlin et al. 2019). Example: one sentence, three objectives. Take “The spring campaign lifted online sales by twelve percent.” Objective Input the model sees What it must predict Masked LM (BERT) The spring campaign [MASK] online sales by twelve [MASK]. “lifted” and “percent”, using words on both sides Causal LM (GPT) The spring campaign lifted online “sales”, then each later word in turn, seeing only what came before Span corruption (T5) The spring campaign <X> by twelve percent. <X> lifted online sales The data are identical; the objective decides whether the model learns to fill gaps from both sides, to continue text, or to rebuild missing spans. Today’s general-purpose LLMs are almost all decoder-only. Encoder models remain the workhorses for classification and embeddings. Data. Pre-training corpora contain trillions of tokens drawn from web crawls, books, code, and curated collections. Raw web text needs heavy processing: language identification, quality filtering, deduplication, removal of personal data, and toxicity filtering. This usually discards a large share of the raw crawl. If you ever plan to pre-train, budget data collection for that loss. Filtering reduces some risks but does not guarantee unbiased or safe data. In short. Pre-training is self-supervised: the text supplies its own labels. Masked LM (encoders) for understanding and embeddings; causal LM (decoders) for generation; span corruption (encoder–decoders) for input-to-output tasks. Corpora have trillions of tokens, after heavy filtering and deduplication. 2.3 Why training does not fit on one GPU Storing a model is cheap compared with training it. At 32-bit precision each parameter takes 4 bytes, so 1 billion parameters need 4 GB just for the weights. Training also needs, for every parameter: Component FP32 training (bytes/param) Mixed-precision training (bytes/param) Weights used in forward/backward 4 2 (16-bit copy) Gradients 4 2 Adam optimizer: momentum + variance 8 8 (kept in FP32) FP32 master copy of weights — 4 Total, before activations 16 16 Activations come on top. These are the intermediate outputs saved for the backward pass, and they grow with batch size and sequence length. Activation checkpointing saves memory by storing only some activations and recomputing the rest during the backward pass (Chen et al. 2016). Rules of thumb: Training needs roughly 4–6× the memory of the FP32 weights. That is about 16 GB for a 1B-parameter model before activations, and around 24 GB with a typical allowance for activations. A 175B-parameter model needs about 2.8 TB for weights, gradients, and optimizer states alone. No single GPU comes close. Fine-tuning has the same profile when all weights are updated. That is the main motivation for PEFT (Section 3.5). Two levers reduce the problem: smaller number formats (next section) and splitting the work across GPUs (the section after). In short. Training needs about 16 bytes per parameter before activations: weights, gradients, and Adam states. A 7B model therefore needs about 112 GB, more than one 80 GB GPU, and a 175B model about 2.8 TB. Full fine-tuning has the same profile, which is why PEFT exists. 2.4 Number formats and quantization A floating-point number has three parts: a sign bit, exponent bits that set the range, and fraction (mantissa) bits that set the precision. Format Sign / exponent / fraction bits Bytes Largest value \(\pi\) stored as FP32 1 / 8 / 23 4 \(\approx 3.4 \times 10^{38}\) 3.1415927 FP16 1 / 5 / 10 2 65,504 3.140625 BF16 1 / 8 / 7 2 \(\approx 3.4 \times 10^{38}\) 3.140625 INT8 8-bit integer, \(-128\) to \(127\) 1 Set by a scale factor Depends on the scale (see below) FP16 vs. BF16. Both use 2 bytes and, for \(\pi\), give the same rounded value. The difference is range. FP16 overflows above 65,504, so FP16 training needs loss scaling to keep small gradients from underflowing to zero (Micikevicius et al. 2018). BF16 (brain floating point, from Google Brain) keeps FP32’s 8 exponent bits. It trades precision for the full FP32 range, which makes training more stable. That is why it became the default 16-bit training format on hardware that supports it. Mixed-precision training runs the forward and backward passes in 16-bit but keeps an FP32 master copy of the weights for the optimizer update (Micikevicius et al. 2018). This gives most of the speed and activation-memory benefit of 16-bit arithmetic while preserving update accuracy. Integer quantization maps real values to integers through a scale factor \(s\). With symmetric quantization, \(q = \text{round}(x / s)\) and \(s = \max|x| / 127\). Precision therefore depends on the range of the values being quantized. For example, if the largest weight magnitude in a tensor is 4.0, then \(s = 4/127 \approx 0.0315\). \(\pi\) is stored as \(q = 100\) and recovered as \(100 \times 0.0315 \approx 3.150\). Choosing \(s\) well is the central problem. Quantization-aware training learns the scale factors during training. Post-training quantization estimates them afterwards (Section 5.1.2). Current practice (October 2026). BF16 mixed precision is the baseline for training. Recent accelerators also support 8-bit floating-point (FP8) formats. Large models have been trained with FP8 mixed precision, for example DeepSeek-V3 (DeepSeek-AI 2024). For inference, 8-bit and 4-bit weight quantization are routine. In short. Exponent bits set range; fraction bits set precision. BF16 keeps FP32’s range at half the size, so it trains stably; FP16 needs loss scaling. Mixed precision computes in 16-bit but updates an FP32 master copy; integer quantization depends on a well-chosen scale factor. 2.5 Distributed training Multiple GPUs serve two purposes: speed (process more data in parallel) and capacity (fit a model that one GPU cannot hold). 2.5.1 Data parallelism (DDP) Distributed data parallel (PyTorch DDP) puts a full copy of the model on every GPU and gives each GPU a different slice of every batch. After the backward pass, gradients are averaged across GPUs (an all-reduce), so every copy applies the same update and stays identical. DDP speeds up training almost linearly, but each GPU must hold the full model, its gradients, and its optimizer states. It adds speed, not capacity. 2.5.2 Sharding: ZeRO and FSDP Under DDP, every GPU stores identical copies of the same states, which is pure redundancy. ZeRO (Zero Redundancy Optimizer) (Rajbhandari et al. 2020) shards these states across the \(N_d\) data-parallel GPUs instead, in three progressive stages. With \(\Psi\) parameters and mixed-precision Adam (2 + 2 + 12 bytes per parameter), the memory per GPU is: Stage What is sharded Memory per GPU 7.5B params, 64 GPUs Baseline (DDP) Nothing \(16\Psi\) 120 GB ZeRO-1 Optimizer states \(4\Psi + 12\Psi / N_d\) 31.4 GB ZeRO-2 + gradients \(2\Psi + 14\Psi / N_d\) 16.6 GB ZeRO-3 + parameters \(16\Psi / N_d\) 1.9 GB Stages 1 and 2 cut memory by up to about 4× and 8×. Stage 3 cuts it in proportion to the number of GPUs. The example column is the paper’s own illustration. Fully Sharded Data Parallel (PyTorch FSDP) (Zhao et al. 2023) implements the same idea natively in PyTorch: Before computing a layer, each GPU gathers that layer’s full parameters from the other GPUs (all-gather). It runs the forward or backward computation, then frees the gathered copy. After the backward pass, gradients are reduced and re-sharded (reduce-scatter), so each GPU updates only its own shard. The cost is extra communication. FSDP exposes this trade-off as a sharding strategy: Full sharding: most memory saved, most communication. No sharding: equivalent to DDP. Hybrid sharding: shard within a machine and replicate across machines, keeping heavy traffic on fast local links. CPU offload: parameters or optimizer states can be moved to CPU memory, at a further speed cost. 2.5.3 Model parallelism Sharding still runs each layer whole on one GPU at a time. The largest models also split the computation itself: Tensor parallelism splits individual weight matrices across GPUs. This is the Megatron-LM approach (Shoeybi et al. 2019). It needs very fast interconnects, so it is usually kept within one machine. Pipeline parallelism places different layers on different GPUs and streams micro-batches through them to keep all stages busy (Huang et al. 2019). Frontier training combines data, tensor, and pipeline parallelism (“3D parallelism”) with sharding. As GPU count grows, communication overhead lowers the throughput per GPU. That is a real cost when planning a training run. Which strategy when: Situation Usual choice The model, gradients, and optimizer states fit on one GPU; you want speed DDP They do not fit on one GPU, but each layer does FSDP or ZeRO (stage 2 or 3) A single layer’s computation is too large, or the model is very large Add tensor parallelism within a machine and pipeline parallelism across machines Fine-tuning a large model on few GPUs PEFT (LoRA or QLoRA) first; shard only if still needed In short. DDP copies the model to every GPU: more speed, no more capacity. ZeRO and FSDP shard optimizer states, gradients, and parameters: capacity at a communication cost. Tensor and pipeline parallelism split the computation itself; frontier runs combine all three. 2.6 Scaling laws Pre-training minimizes next-token loss. Three quantities determine how low the loss goes: model size \(N\) (parameters), dataset size \(D\) (training tokens), and compute \(C\). For dense transformers, training compute is approximately \[ C \approx 6ND \quad \text{FLOPs.} \] Large budgets are often quoted in petaFLOP/s-days. One petaFLOP/s-day is \(10^{15}\) operations per second sustained for a day, which is \(8.64 \times 10^{19}\) FLOPs. GPT-3 175B, trained on 300B tokens, used about \(3.14 \times 10^{23}\) FLOPs, or roughly 3,640 petaFLOP/s-days (Brown et al. 2020). That matches \(6 \times 175\text{B} \times 300\text{B}\). 2.6.1 Kaplan et al.: loss follows power laws Kaplan et al. (2020) found that test loss falls as a power law in each of \(N\), \(D\), and \(C\), provided the other two are not the bottleneck. For example, \(L(N) \approx (N_c / N)^{\alpha_N}\) with \(\alpha_N \approx 0.076\). On log–log axes these are straight lines over many orders of magnitude. That makes loss predictable: small, cheap runs forecast the loss of large ones. In practice compute is the hard constraint (hardware, time, money). The practical question is therefore: for a fixed compute budget, how should it be split between a bigger model and more data? Kaplan et al. recommended putting most extra compute into model size. That reasoning shaped the very large models of 2020–21. 2.6.2 Chinchilla: scale data and parameters together Hoffmann et al. (2022) revisited the question with more careful experiments, including learning-rate schedules matched to each run’s length. They fitted the loss as \[ L(N, D) = E + \frac{A}{N^{\alpha}} + \frac{B}{D^{\beta}}. \] Here \(E\) is the irreducible loss of the data, and the two other terms are the penalties for finite model size and finite data. Minimizing this subject to \(C \approx 6ND\) gives the main result: \(N\) and \(D\) should grow in roughly equal proportion, which works out to about 20 training tokens per parameter. This is a historical empirical estimate for their model family and setup, not a universal constant. Example: sizing a model for a budget. With \(C = 6ND\) and \(D = 20N\), compute is \(C = 120N^2\), so \(N = \sqrt{C / 120}\). For a budget of \(10^{23}\) FLOPs, \(N \approx 2.9 \times 10^{10}\) (about 29B parameters) and \(D \approx 580\)B tokens. A team with that budget that instead trained a 175B model would get only about 95B tokens, far short of the roughly 3.5T that size would need. The test: Chinchilla (70B parameters, 1.4T tokens) used the same compute as Gopher (280B parameters, 300B tokens). It outperformed Gopher, GPT-3, and other much larger models on a wide range of downstream tasks. Measured against the 20× rule, many earlier models were over-parameterized and under-trained: Model Parameters Chinchilla-optimal tokens (~20×) Actual training tokens GPT-3 (Brown et al. 2020) 175B ~3.5T 300B BLOOM 176B ~3.5T ~366B Chinchilla (Hoffmann et al. 2022) 70B ~1.4T 1.4T LLaMA-65B 65B ~1.3T 1.4T Interpreting scaling laws: They predict pre-training loss, not specific downstream abilities. Individual skills can improve unevenly. They hold for the architecture, data mixture, and recipe they were fitted on. Change those and you must re-fit. “Compute-optimal” optimizes training compute only. It ignores the cost of serving the model afterwards. Current practice (October 2026). The last point changed practice. A model that will serve billions of requests is cheaper overall if it is smaller and trained on far more than 20 tokens per parameter (Sardana et al. 2024). Llama 3’s 8B model, for example, was trained on about 15T tokens, close to 1,900 tokens per parameter (Llama Team, AI @ Meta 2024). “Over-training” small models is now normal. Chinchilla remains the reference point for the training-compute trade-off. In short. Training compute is about \(6ND\) FLOPs; loss falls as a power law in parameters, data, and compute. Chinchilla: for a fixed training budget, grow parameters and tokens together, about 20 tokens per parameter. Serving costs now favour smaller models trained on far more tokens. 2.7 Domain adaptation and pre-training your own model You rarely need to pre-train. The exception is a domain whose language is poorly represented in general corpora: Rare terms: legal terms such as mens rea and res judicata. Everyday words with special meanings: consideration in contract law means the value exchanged that makes an agreement binding, not kindness. Shorthand: a prescription note like “1 tab po qid pc & hs” means one tablet by mouth four times a day, after meals and at bedtime. A model learns its vocabulary and representations in pre-training. Later stages build on those, so a domain the model barely saw may be handled poorly. Before committing to from-scratch training, climb this ladder of options, from cheapest to most expensive: Prompting and retrieval (Chapter 5). Fine-tuning or PEFT on domain tasks (Chapter 3). Continued (domain-adaptive) pre-training. Keep pre-training an existing model on unlabelled domain text. Gururangan et al. (2020) showed consistent downstream gains from this across biomedical, computer-science, news, and review domains. Pre-training from scratch on a mixed domain and general corpus. 2.7.1 Case study: BloombergGPT BloombergGPT (S. Wu et al. 2023) is the best-known from-scratch domain model: Model and data. A 50.6B-parameter decoder trained on a corpus of about 51% financial text (Bloomberg’s own and public financial data) and 49% general public text. The general data preserved broad language ability. Compute. About 1.3 million A100 GPU-hours. Scaling choices. The authors used Chinchilla scaling laws to size the model for their budget, and the parameter count landed close to compute-optimal. The training tokens (569B) fell short of the compute-optimal amount, because there was not enough high-quality financial text. Real data limits forced a trade-off. Result. The paper reports that BloombergGPT outperformed similarly sized open models on financial tasks by clear margins while staying competitive on general-purpose benchmarks. The lesson is that from-scratch domain pre-training is justified only when the domain language is distinctive, high-quality domain data exists at scale, and the compute budget is large. Current practice (October 2026). Given how capable general models now are, combined with continued pre-training, fine-tuning, and retrieval, from-scratch domain pre-training is a rare choice. Justify it with an evaluation showing that the cheaper options fall short. In short. Pre-train only when the domain’s language is distinctive, high-quality domain data exist at scale, and the budget is large. First climb the cheaper ladder: prompting and retrieval, fine-tuning, continued pre-training. BloombergGPT shows the trade-offs: Chinchilla-sized, but data-limited. 2.8 Key takeaways The section summaries above hold the details. The chapter in five lines: Start: from an existing model; the objective (masked, causal, span) matches the architecture and the task. Memory: about 16 bytes per parameter to train, so large models need BF16, mixed precision, and sharding. Distribution: DDP for speed; ZeRO/FSDP for capacity; tensor and pipeline parallelism for the largest models. Scaling: loss follows power laws; Chinchilla’s ~20 tokens per parameter for training compute, more when serving costs count. Domain models: the expensive end of a ladder; justify them with evidence that cheaper options fall short. 2.9 Interview checkpoints Masked vs. causal language modelling? Masked LM predicts hidden tokens using both sides of the context. Causal LM predicts the next token using only earlier ones. How much GPU memory does training a 7B-parameter model need? With mixed precision and Adam, about 16 bytes × 7B ≈ 112 GB before activations. That calls for sharding, or PEFT for fine-tuning. Why BF16 over FP16? The same 8-bit exponent as FP32 gives the full range, so there is less overflow or underflow and no need for loss scaling. The cost is lower precision. DDP vs. FSDP? DDP replicates everything and adds speed only. FSDP shards parameters, gradients, and optimizer states, which adds capacity at a communication cost. The three ZeRO stages? Shard optimizer states; then also gradients; then also parameters. What is \(C \approx 6ND\)? The approximate training FLOPs for a dense transformer with \(N\) parameters trained on \(D\) tokens. The Chinchilla result in one line? For a fixed training-compute budget, scale parameters and tokens together, at about 20 tokens per parameter. Many earlier models were under-trained. Why train beyond Chinchilla-optimal? Serving costs dominate over a model’s life. A smaller model trained on more data is cheaper to run at the same quality. When would you pre-train a domain model? When the domain language is distinctive, domain data is plentiful, the budget is large, and prompting, RAG, fine-tuning, and continued pre-training have been shown to fall short. References

Chapter 3 Fine-Tuning and Evaluation There are three ways to make a pre-trained model better at your task. Each one changes something different: Lever What changes Covered in Prompting and in-context learning Only the input; the weights stay fixed Section 1.5 and the Prompt Engineering part Fine-tuning The weights, using labelled examples This chapter Alignment with human feedback The weights, using preference signals Next chapter This chapter covers supervised fine-tuning: full instruction fine-tuning first, then parameter-efficient methods. It ends with how to measure whether the adapted model actually improved. 3.1 Why fine-tune instead of prompting In-context learning puts worked examples in the prompt (Section 1.5). It needs no training, so it should be tried first. It has four limits: Small models may not pick up the task, even from several examples. Examples use up the context window, leaving less room for the actual input, retrieved documents, or tool results. Examples are paid for on every call, in tokens and in latency. Prompts are not great at fixing a style or format across thousands of calls. Training on examples usually makes the output more consistent. Fine-tuning moves the task knowledge from the prompt into the weights. A practical rule of thumb: fine-tuning is good at teaching behaviour (a task, format, style, or domain vocabulary). It is a poor way to add facts that change. Fresh or private facts are better supplied at inference time through retrieval, which a later chapter covers. Example: one marketing assistant, three needs. Need Best lever Why Always write in the brand’s voice and house format Fine-tuning Stable behaviour, needed on every call Quote this week’s promotions and prices Retrieval Facts that change weekly Handle an unusual one-off request Prompting No training data, and it may never recur In short. Try prompting first; fine-tune when examples don’t work, eat the context window, cost too much per call, or give inconsistent output. Fine-tuning teaches behaviour; retrieval supplies changing facts. 3.2 Instruction fine-tuning Instruction fine-tuning (also called supervised fine-tuning, SFT) continues training a pre-trained model on pairs. Each pair is a prompt containing an instruction plus the desired completion: Prompt: Classify this review: "I loved this book, could not put it down." Completion: Sentiment: positive It differs from pre-training in two ways. Pre-training is self-supervised on unlabelled text. Instruction fine-tuning is supervised on labelled pairs, and the dataset is many orders of magnitude smaller. When every weight is updated, the procedure is called full fine-tuning. Its output is a new copy of the model, often called an instruct model. 3.2.1 Building the dataset Most existing NLP datasets (reviews, Q&A pairs, dialogues) are not written as instructions. Prompt template libraries such as PromptSource (Bach et al. 2022) solve this. A template wraps each record in an instruction. For example, an Amazon review can become a rating-prediction prompt, a review-generation prompt, or a summarization prompt. Using several phrasings of the same instruction (“Summarize the dialogue”, “What was this conversation about?”, …) helps the model generalize beyond one wording. The original FLAN work wrote ten templates per dataset for this reason (Wei, Bosma, et al. 2022). Split the data into training, validation, and test sets, as in any supervised problem. The test set must stay untouched until the final evaluation. 3.2.2 Training objective The model is trained with the same next-token cross-entropy loss used in pre-training, applied to the completion. For a prompt \(x\) and target completion \(y = (y_1, \dots, y_T)\): \[ \mathcal{L}(\theta) = -\sum_{t=1}^{T} \log p_\theta\left(y_t \mid x, y_{<t}\right) \] The loss is commonly computed only on the completion tokens. The prompt tokens are masked out, so the model is not trained to reproduce the instruction. For the review example above: Tokens: Classify this review: "I loved this book ..." Sentiment: positive In loss: no no no no no no no ... yes yes The model still reads the whole sequence, but only the completion tokens produce gradients. Gradients from batches of examples update the weights over one or more epochs. The validation loss or metric is tracked to choose when to stop. Full fine-tuning has the same memory profile as training. Weights, gradients, and optimizer states must all fit in memory (Section 2.3). That cost motivates the parameter-efficient methods in Section 3.5. In short. Instruction fine-tuning is supervised next-token training on prompt–completion pairs, with the loss usually on the completion only. Templates turn existing datasets into instructions; several phrasings per task help generalization. Full fine-tuning updates every weight and needs training-level memory. 3.3 Single-task fine-tuning and catastrophic forgetting If an application needs only one task, such as summarizing support chats, you can fine-tune on that task alone. Single-task fine-tuning often works with hundreds to a few thousand high-quality examples. That is tiny compared with pre-training corpora. LIMA, for example, reported strong instruction following after tuning on 1,000 curated examples (C. Zhou et al. 2023). Treat any number as a starting point to validate, not a requirement. Label quality and representativeness matter more than volume. The risk is catastrophic forgetting: updating the weights for one task can degrade abilities learned earlier (McCloskey and Cohen 1989). For example, a model tuned only for sentiment classification may stop doing named-entity recognition correctly, or may answer every prompt with a sentiment label. Ways to handle it, roughly in order of cost: Check whether it matters. If the deployed model only ever performs the tuned task, losing other skills may be acceptable. Mix in general data. Add a sample of general instruction data (or the earlier tasks) to the fine-tuning set. This is sometimes called replay. Regularize the update. Penalize movement of weights that mattered for earlier tasks, for example with elastic weight consolidation (Kirkpatrick et al. 2017). Use parameter-efficient fine-tuning. Freeze the original weights and train a small add-on (Section 3.5). Fine-tune on many tasks at once (next section). Whatever you choose, evaluate both the target task and a fixed set of capabilities you need to keep. Without the second set, forgetting goes unnoticed. In short. One task often needs only hundreds to a few thousand good examples. The risk is catastrophic forgetting of other skills. Mitigate with replay, regularization, PEFT, or multi-task training, and always measure retained capabilities. 3.4 Multi-task instruction fine-tuning and FLAN Multi-task instruction fine-tuning trains on a mixture of tasks (summarization, classification, translation, question answering, code, …) at the same time. Because no single task dominates, the model improves across many tasks instead of trading them off. The cost is data: you need diverse, high-quality examples for every task in the mixture. The FLAN models are the reference example (FLAN stands for Fine-tuned LAnguage Net): Wei, Bosma, et al. (2022) fine-tuned a 137B-parameter model on more than 60 datasets phrased as instructions. Its zero-shot performance improved on task types that were held out of training. This was the key evidence that instruction tuning teaches the general skill of following instructions, not just the training tasks. Chung et al. (2022) scaled the approach to 1,836 tasks (drawn from 473 datasets in 146 task categories) and released Flan-T5 and Flan-PaLM. Two findings matter: performance kept improving as both the number of tasks and the model size grew, and including chain-of-thought examples in the mixture preserved the models’ step-by-step reasoning ability. Instruction tuning was also cheap: for Flan-PaLM 540B it used about 0.2% of the pre-training compute. The Flan 2022 paper uses three terms precisely (Chung et al. 2022): a dataset is an original data source, such as SQuAD; a task category is a kind of task setup, such as extractive question answering or question generation (one dataset can serve several); a task is one (dataset, task category) pair, such as question generation on SQuAD, with any number of instruction templates. The fine-tuning mixture combined four collections, and evaluation used benchmarks kept out of training: Collection Datasets Task categories Tasks What it adds Muffin 69 27 80 The original FLAN tasks plus dialogue and program synthesis T0-SF 55 14 193 Tasks from T0 that do not overlap with Muffin (“sans Flan”) Natural Instructions v2 372 108 1,554 A large crowd-sourced task collection (MMLU-related tasks removed) CoT 9 1 9 Reasoning tasks with human-written chains of thought Total 473 146 1,836 Some datasets appear in more than one collection Held-out benchmark What it tests Size MMLU Exam-style knowledge across subjects 57 tasks BBH (BIG-Bench Hard) Hard reasoning tasks where models trailed average human raters 23 tasks (27 subtasks) TyDiQA Information-seeking question answering 8 languages MGSM Grade-school math word problems 10 languages The point of the split is the claim being tested. A gain on tasks the model never saw during fine-tuning is evidence that it learned to follow instructions in general, not just the training tasks. The authors removed 44 MMLU-related tasks from the training mixture for exactly this reason. One dataset in the FLAN mixture is SAMSum: about 16,000 messenger-style dialogues with summaries, written by linguists (Gliwa et al. 2019). It explains both the strength and the limit of a general instruct model. Flan-T5 can summarize casual chats between friends. However, a customer-support dialogue has a different structure (a customer request, staff actions, a resolution). A general model may miss key actions or invent details there. The fix is a further round of fine-tuning on data close to the deployment setting. DialogSum is a public example: about 13,000 dialogues from real-life scenarios such as hotel check-ins and service desks, each with a summary (Y. Chen et al. 2021). In production, permissioned internal data (your own support transcripts and the summaries your team wants) is usually the better choice. Even then, evaluate hallucination, privacy, and distribution shift separately. In short. Training on many tasks at once improves many tasks instead of trading them off. FLAN’s evidence: gains on benchmarks held out of training, so the model learned to follow instructions in general. A general instruct model may still need a further round of tuning on data close to your deployment. 3.5 Parameter-efficient fine-tuning (PEFT) Full fine-tuning has three practical costs: Training memory. Gradients and optimizer states are needed for every parameter. With Adam, that is several times the memory of the weights themselves. Storage. Each task produces a complete copy of the model. Forgetting. Every weight can move, which risks catastrophic forgetting. Parameter-efficient fine-tuning methods freeze most or all of the pre-trained weights and train a small number of parameters. That reduces the gradient and optimizer memory. The task-specific artefact can be a few megabytes instead of a full model. The frozen base also makes forgetting less likely. Note what PEFT does not remove: the frozen weights must still sit in memory for the forward and backward passes. QLoRA (below) attacks that remaining cost. 3.5.1 Three families of methods Lialin et al. (2023) group PEFT methods into three families: Family Idea Examples Selective Train only a chosen subset of the existing parameters BitFit trains only the bias terms (Ben Zaken et al. 2022); training only the top layers Reparameterization Learn the weight update in a compact, low-rank form LoRA (Hu et al. 2022) Additive Keep the original weights frozen and add new trainable parameters Adapter layers inserted inside each block (Houlsby et al. 2019); soft prompts (Lester et al. 2021; Li and Liang 2021) Selective methods are simple. They are less common for large generative models because their quality and memory savings vary a lot. The two methods most used in practice are LoRA and soft prompts. Both are explained below. 3.5.2 LoRA: low-rank adaptation Idea. Full fine-tuning learns an update \(\Delta W\) for each weight matrix \(W_0\). Hu et al. (2022) hypothesized that this update has low intrinsic rank. If so, it can be written as the product of two thin matrices. LoRA freezes \(W_0\) and trains only those two matrices: \[ h = W_0 x + \Delta W x = W_0 x + \frac{\alpha}{r} B A x, \qquad B \in \mathbb{R}^{d \times r},\; A \in \mathbb{R}^{r \times k},\; r \ll \min(d, k) \] \(r\) is the rank, the main hyperparameter. \(\alpha\) is a scaling constant. \(A\) starts random and \(B\) starts at zero. At step 0, \(\Delta W = 0\), so training begins exactly at the pre-trained model. Only \(A\) and \(B\) get gradients and optimizer states. Parameter count. A \(d \times k\) matrix has \(dk\) parameters. Its LoRA update has \(r(d + k)\). Matrix Full update \(dk\) LoRA, \(r = 8\): \(r(d+k)\) Share trained One attention head projection in the original Transformer, \(512 \times 64\) (Vaswani et al. 2017) 32,768 4,608 14% A \(4096 \times 4096\) projection, typical of a 7B-parameter model 16,777,216 65,536 0.39% The savings grow with the matrix size. On GPT-3 175B, Hu et al. (2022) reported about 10,000× fewer trainable parameters and about 3× lower GPU memory than full fine-tuning. Quality was on par with or better than full fine-tuning on the tasks they evaluated. Inference. After training, the update can be merged into the base weights, \(W = W_0 + \frac{\alpha}{r} BA\). The merged model has exactly the original shape, so it adds no inference latency. Alternatively, keep the adapters separate and load a different \((A, B)\) pair per task on one shared base model. That is how one deployment can serve many tasks. Which matrices to adapt. The LoRA paper adapted the attention projections (mainly the query and value matrices). It found that adapting more matrix types at a small rank beat adapting one type at a larger rank (Hu et al. 2022). Despite a common claim, attention does not hold most of a transformer’s parameters. With the usual feed-forward width of \(4d\), the feed-forward layers hold about two-thirds of each block’s weights. The QLoRA authors found that applying LoRA to all linear layers was needed to match full fine-tuning (Dettmers et al. 2023). Choosing the rank. In Hu et al. (2022), very small ranks (even single digits) were competitive on the tasks studied. Raising the rank did not reliably help. Values from 4 to 64 are common in practice. Treat \(r\) (and \(\alpha\)) as hyperparameters to tune on the validation set. A larger rank means more capacity and more memory, not automatically better results. 3.5.3 QLoRA: LoRA on a quantized base LoRA shrinks the trainable part, but the frozen base model still has to fit in memory. QLoRA stores the frozen base in 4-bit precision and trains LoRA adapters in 16-bit on top of it (Dettmers et al. 2023). Three techniques make this work: 4-bit NormalFloat (NF4), a 4-bit data type designed for weights that are roughly normally distributed. Double quantization, which also quantizes the quantization constants to save more memory. Paged optimizers, which move optimizer state to CPU memory during memory spikes. The paper fine-tuned a 65B-parameter model on a single 48 GB GPU while preserving the task performance of 16-bit fine-tuning. Section 2.4 explains the data types involved. 3.5.4 Prompt tuning with soft prompts Prompt tuning is not prompt engineering. Prompt engineering edits the words of a prompt by hand. Prompt tuning learns a short sequence of continuous vectors, a soft prompt, that is prepended to the input embeddings (Lester et al. 2021): Ordinary (“hard”) tokens map to fixed rows of the embedding table. A soft prompt is \(p\) virtual tokens: free vectors \(P \in \mathbb{R}^{p \times d}\) in the same embedding space, not tied to any word. The model is completely frozen. Backpropagation updates only \(P\), using the same supervised loss as fine-tuning. The trainable count is tiny. Twenty virtual tokens with \(d = 4096\) is 81,920 parameters. One soft prompt per task can be stored and swapped at inference, and a single batch can even mix tasks. Evidence. On SuperGLUE, prompt tuning trailed full fine-tuning for small T5 models. The gap closed as model size grew, and at about 11B parameters it matched full fine-tuning. It also outperformed GPT-3’s few-shot prompting by a large margin. In the same experiments, about 20 virtual tokens captured most of the gain; longer prompts added little (Lester et al. 2021). Interpretability. The learned vectors do not correspond to vocabulary tokens. Their nearest vocabulary neighbours tend to form semantically related clusters, often connected to the task. Even so, a soft prompt cannot be read like a sentence. Related method. Prefix tuning learns trainable vectors at every layer, not only at the input, giving it more capacity per virtual token (Li and Liang 2021). 3.5.5 Choosing an adaptation method Method Trainable parameters Training memory Inference overhead Typical use Prompting / in-context learning None None Longer prompts First attempt; fast iteration Full fine-tuning All Highest None Large shift in behaviour, enough data and compute LoRA Well under 1% for large models (depends on rank and layers) Low (base still in memory) None if merged Default PEFT choice; many tasks on one base QLoRA Same as LoRA Lowest (4-bit base) None if merged; quantized base otherwise Large models on limited GPUs Prompt tuning Tiny (\(p \times d\)) Low A few extra input positions Very large frozen models; many tasks Current practice (October 2026). LoRA and QLoRA remain the standard PEFT methods in common open-source tooling, such as the Hugging Face peft library. Many hosted model APIs offer fine-tuning without exposing the method. Supervised fine-tuning is now usually one stage in a pipeline that also includes preference-based alignment (next chapter). In short. PEFT freezes most weights and trains a small add-on: less memory, tiny task files, less forgetting. LoRA learns a low-rank update \(BA\), mergeable with no inference cost; apply it to all linear layers. QLoRA adds a 4-bit frozen base; prompt tuning learns input vectors and catches up with full fine-tuning at large scale. 3.6 Evaluating fine-tuned models Classifier accuracy is easy to compute because there is one right label. Generated text is harder to score. Two sentences can mean the same thing with almost no shared words (“Mike really loves drinking tea” vs. “Mike adores sipping tea”). Two others can differ by one word and mean the opposite (“Mike does drink coffee” vs. “Mike does not drink coffee”). Automatic metrics approximate quality through overlap with a human reference. That makes them cheap and repeatable, but blind to meaning. Terminology: a unigram is one word, a bigram is two consecutive words, and an n-gram is \(n\) consecutive words. 3.6.1 ROUGE ROUGE (Lin 2004) scores summaries by their overlap with reference summaries. For n-gram matches between a candidate and a reference: \[ \text{Recall} = \frac{\text{matched n-grams}}{\text{n-grams in reference}}, \qquad \text{Precision} = \frac{\text{matched n-grams}}{\text{n-grams in candidate}}, \qquad F_1 = \frac{2PR}{P + R} \] ROUGE-1 uses unigrams, ROUGE-2 uses bigrams (which are slightly sensitive to word order). ROUGE-L uses the length of the longest common subsequence (LCS) as the match count. A subsequence keeps word order but does not have to be contiguous. Mixing this up with the longest contiguous match is a common error. Worked example. Reference: “It is cold outside” (4 words). Candidate: “It is very cold outside” (5 words). Metric Matches Recall Precision F1 ROUGE-1 it, is, cold, outside = 4 4/4 = 1.00 4/5 = 0.80 0.89 ROUGE-2 “it is”, “cold outside” = 2 2/3 = 0.67 2/4 = 0.50 0.57 ROUGE-L LCS “it is cold outside” = 4 4/4 = 1.00 4/5 = 0.80 0.89 Failure modes: Meaning reversal. “It is not cold outside” gets exactly the same ROUGE-1 scores as the candidate above. Overlap does not check meaning. Repetition. “cold cold cold cold” has a ROUGE-1 precision of 4/4 = 1.00 if every repeat counts. Clipping caps each n-gram’s matches at its count in the reference. The idea comes from BLEU’s modified precision (Papineni et al. 2002). With clipping, precision becomes 1/4 = 0.25. Reordering. “outside cold it is” still scores 1.00 on clipped ROUGE-1. Order-sensitive variants catch it: ROUGE-2 F1 = 1/3 = 0.33 (only “it is” matches) and ROUGE-L F1 = 0.50 (LCS = 2). ROUGE scores are comparable only within the same task, dataset, reference set, and implementation settings (tokenization, stemming). Use them to track progress on summarization while you iterate, never as the final verdict. 3.6.2 BLEU BLEU (Papineni et al. 2002) was designed for machine translation. It is precision-oriented and combines several n-gram sizes: \[ \text{BLEU} = \text{BP} \cdot \exp\left(\sum_{n=1}^{N} w_n \log p_n\right), \qquad \text{BP} = \begin{cases} 1 & \text{if } c > r \\ e^{\,1 - r/c} & \text{if } c \le r \end{cases} \] \(p_n\) is the clipped n-gram precision. Usually \(N = 4\) with equal weights \(w_n = 1/4\), so the exponential term is the geometric mean of the four precisions (not a simple average). The brevity penalty BP penalizes candidates shorter than the reference (\(c\) = candidate length, \(r\) = reference length). Without it, a very short output with only safe words would score high precision. BLEU was defined at the corpus level. Sentence-level BLEU is noisy and needs smoothing, because a single missing 4-gram makes the geometric mean zero. For example, a 4-word translation against a 5-word reference gets \(\text{BP} = e^{1 - 5/4} \approx 0.78\). Even with perfect n-gram precision, its BLEU cannot exceed 0.78. 3.6.3 Beyond overlap metrics ROUGE and BLEU are cheap diagnostics. They cannot judge factual correctness, faithfulness to the source, safety, or usefulness. A defensible evaluation combines: a representative held-out set drawn from the deployment setting; task-appropriate automatic metrics (overlap, exact match, schema validity, executable tests); structured human review with a written rubric where judgment is needed; error analysis by category and subgroup; retained-capability checks to detect catastrophic forgetting; and latency and cost. LLM-as-a-judge (using a strong model to grade outputs against a rubric) scales human-like judgments cheaply. Zheng et al. (2023) found that strong judges agree with human preferences about as often as humans agree with each other. They also documented systematic biases: position bias, a preference for longer answers, and a tendency to favour the judge’s own outputs. Calibrate a judge against human labels before trusting it. Chapter 10 shows how to do this, and how to build rubric-based evals for multi-step systems. In short. ROUGE (recall-leaning, summaries) and BLEU (precision plus brevity penalty, translation) measure surface overlap with references. They miss meaning, so use them for iteration, not as the final verdict. Combine held-out data, task metrics, human or calibrated-judge review, error analysis, and retained-capability checks. 3.7 Benchmarks Benchmarks are fixed, public task suites used to compare models across many skills: Benchmark Year What it measures GLUE (Wang, Singh, et al. 2019) 2018 Nine sentence- and sentence-pair understanding tasks (sentiment, entailment, paraphrase, …) SuperGLUE (Wang, Pruksachatkun, et al. 2019) 2019 Eight harder tasks (multi-sentence reasoning, reading comprehension, coreference), created as models saturated GLUE MMLU (Hendrycks et al. 2021) 2020 Multiple-choice knowledge and problem-solving across 57 subjects (elementary mathematics, US history, law, computer science, …) BIG-bench (Srivastava et al. 2023) 2022 204 community-contributed tasks (linguistics, common sense, mathematics, social bias, software, …); a smaller “Lite” subset keeps evaluation cost manageable HELM (Liang et al. 2023) 2022 A framework scoring models on seven metrics (accuracy, calibration, robustness, fairness, bias, toxicity, efficiency) across 16 core scenarios, so trade-offs are visible rather than hidden in one number How to read benchmark results: Saturation. Top systems surpassed the SuperGLUE human-baseline estimate within about two years. A model matching humans on a benchmark is not human level at the general skill. This “arms race” is why benchmarks keep being replaced. Contamination. If test items appeared in the pre-training data, scores overstate ability. Prefer held-out or recently created items. Fit. A leaderboard rank says little about your task. A small evaluation set drawn from your own data is usually more informative. Holistic view. Accuracy alone hides calibration, robustness, and safety trade-offs, which is the point HELM was built to make. Current practice (October 2026). GLUE and SuperGLUE are of historical interest for frontier models, and MMLU is close to saturated. Harder successors such as MMLU-Pro (Y. Wang et al. 2024) and the expert-written GPQA (Rein et al. 2023) took their place, along with agentic and coding benchmarks and arena-style human-preference rankings. Leaderboards change quickly; check current sources before quoting a score. In short. Benchmarks compare models on fixed public tasks: GLUE, SuperGLUE, MMLU, BIG-bench, HELM. Read them with care: saturation, contamination, and poor fit to your task. Your own small eval set usually tells you more. 3.8 Key takeaways The section summaries above hold the details. The chapter in five lines: When: prompt first; fine-tune for behaviour, retrieve for facts. How: supervised next-token training on instruction pairs; many tasks at once (FLAN) generalize to held-out tasks. Risk: catastrophic forgetting; always test the skills you need to keep. Cheaply: PEFT, usually LoRA or QLoRA, trains under 1% of the parameters with no inference cost once merged. Measured: overlap metrics for iteration; held-out data, human or judge review, and error analysis for the verdict. 3.9 Interview checkpoints Fine-tuning vs. RAG? Fine-tuning changes behaviour, format, and style. Retrieval supplies current or private facts at inference. They are often combined. Why does LoRA add no inference latency? The update \(BA\) can be merged into \(W_0\), so the deployed model has the original shape. LoRA parameter count for a \(d \times k\) matrix? \(r(d + k)\) instead of \(dk\). Why is \(B\) initialized to zero? So that \(\Delta W = 0\) and training starts exactly at the pre-trained model. What does QLoRA add? A 4-bit NF4 frozen base, double quantization, and paged optimizers, so large models fit on one GPU. Prompt tuning vs. prompt engineering? Learned continuous vectors vs. hand-written discrete text. Prompt tuning needs training data and gradients. What is catastrophic forgetting, and how do you detect it? Loss of earlier skills after fine-tuning. Detect it with a fixed retained-capability evaluation set. ROUGE-L vs. ROUGE-2? ROUGE-L uses the longest common subsequence (order-preserving, not contiguous). ROUGE-2 counts matching bigrams. Why does BLEU need a brevity penalty? Precision alone rewards very short outputs. Why distrust a high benchmark score? Saturation, contamination, and mismatch with the deployment task. In FLAN, what is the difference between a dataset, a task category, and a task? A dataset is a data source (SQuAD); a task category is a task setup (question generation); a task is one dataset–category pair. How did Flan 2022 show that instruction tuning generalizes? By evaluating on benchmarks held out of training (MMLU, BBH, TyDiQA, MGSM), after removing overlapping tasks from the mixture. References
