Chapter 4 Aligning LLMs with Human Feedback Instruction fine-tuning (Chapter 3) teaches a model what tasks look like. It does not teach the model which of many plausible answers people actually prefer. A model trained to imitate internet text and demonstration data can still be unhelpful (it misreads the request), dishonest (it states falsehoods confidently), or harmful (it gives dangerous instructions or toxic language). Those behaviours exist in its training data. Alignment is the further training that moves a model towards human preferences. A common shorthand for the target is HHH: helpful, honest, and harmless (Askell et al. 2021). This chapter explains the classic method, reinforcement learning from human feedback (RLHF), and the methods that simplified or replaced parts of it. 4.1 Why preferences instead of demonstrations Supervised fine-tuning needs a correct completion for every prompt. For many qualities (tone, helpfulness, safety, a good summary) writing the ideal answer is hard. Recognising the better of two answers is much easier. Preference data is therefore cheaper to collect and often more informative. The evidence that this works: Christiano et al. (2017) trained RL agents from human comparisons of behaviour clips, with no hand-written reward function. Stiennon et al. (2020) applied the idea to summarization. Policies trained with human feedback produced summaries that people preferred over those of much larger supervised models, and even over the human reference summaries in the dataset. Ouyang et al. (2022) (InstructGPT) used the same recipe for general instruction following. Labelers preferred outputs of the 1.3B-parameter InstructGPT model to those of the 175B-parameter GPT-3. This was the template for the first wave of chat assistants. Example: one preference record. For the prompt “Explain our refund policy to a customer who missed the 30-day window”, a labeler sees two drafts. Draft A apologizes, restates the policy, and offers store credit as an exception. Draft B quotes the policy and stops. The labeler marks A as preferred. That record, (prompt, A preferred, B rejected), is all the training signal needs; nobody had to write the perfect reply. In short. Alignment trains towards preferred behaviour: helpful, honest, harmless. Judging which of two answers is better is easier than writing the ideal answer, so preference data is cheaper and often more informative. 4.2 Reinforcement learning, mapped to language models In reinforcement learning, an agent follows a policy to choose actions in an environment. It observes the resulting states and receives rewards. It learns a policy that maximizes the expected cumulative reward. For an LLM the mapping is: RL concept In RLHF Policy \(\pi_\theta\) The LLM being trained State \(s_t\) The prompt plus the tokens generated so far Action \(a_t\) The next token; the action space is the vocabulary Episode / rollout One full completion of a prompt Reward A score for the finished completion from a reward model, usually given once at the end Humans cannot score millions of rollouts during training. RLHF therefore first trains a reward model to imitate human judgments, then optimizes the policy against that model. RLHF changes only the values of the policy’s weights. The architecture, the number of parameters, and the vocabulary stay the same. The aligned model is the same network with different numbers in it. In short. The LLM is the policy, the next token is the action, and a full completion is one episode. A reward model stands in for human judges, because humans cannot score millions of rollouts. RLHF updates weight values only; the architecture is unchanged. 4.3 The RLHF pipeline The InstructGPT recipe (Ouyang et al. 2022) has three stages: Supervised fine-tuning (SFT). Start from an instruction-tuned model, so that sampled completions are already reasonable. Reward modelling. Collect human comparisons of completions and train a model that scores a (prompt, completion) pair. RL optimization. Optimize the SFT model against the reward model with PPO, while penalizing drift from the SFT model. 4.3.1 Collecting human feedback For each prompt in a prompt dataset, the SFT model generates several completions. Labelers rank them against a defined criterion, such as helpfulness, correctness, or harmlessness. The labeling instructions matter as much as the labelers. Good instructions state the criterion, say how to fact-check, define how to treat ties (allowed but rare), and provide a flag for nonsensical answers so they can be removed. Each item usually goes to several labelers, which shows agreement and exposes labelers who misread the task. For scale: InstructGPT used about 40 contractors and ranked between 4 and 9 completions per prompt (Ouyang et al. 2022). Ranking produces pairs. A ranking of \(K\) completions yields \(\binom{K}{2}\) pairwise comparisons; three completions give three pairs. Each pair becomes a training example (prompt, preferred \(y_w\), rejected \(y_l\)). Ranking yields more training signal per prompt than a thumbs-up/down label. 4.3.2 Training the reward model The reward model \(r_\phi(x, y)\) is usually a language model (often initialized from the SFT model) with a head that outputs one scalar. It is trained with the Bradley–Terry model of pairwise preference (Bradley and Terry 1952). Under that model, the probability that \(y_w\) beats \(y_l\) is \(\sigma\big(r_\phi(x, y_w) - r_\phi(x, y_l)\big)\). The loss is the negative log-likelihood of the human choices: \[ \mathcal{L}(\phi) = -\,\mathbb{E}_{(x,\,y_w,\,y_l)} \Big[\log \sigma\big(r_\phi(x, y_w) - r_\phi(x, y_l)\big)\Big] \] Only reward differences are identified, so the absolute scale is arbitrary. Rewards are often normalized before RL. For example, if the reward model scores the preferred answer 2.0 and the rejected one 0.5, it predicts the human choice with probability \(\sigma(1.5) \approx 0.82\), and that pair contributes a loss of \(-\log 0.82 \approx 0.20\). If it scored them the other way round, the loss would be large, and training would push the two scores apart in the right direction. Adding 10 to both scores changes nothing, which is why only differences matter. A classifier can also act as the reward. For a narrow goal such as detoxification, an existing classifier (for example, a hate-speech detector) can supply the reward. A common choice is its logit or probability for the desired class (“not hate”). This skips preference collection, but the policy is then optimized towards whatever that classifier happens to measure. 4.3.3 The RL objective and the KL penalty The policy is trained to earn high reward without drifting far from the SFT model, which is kept frozen as the reference policy \(\pi_{\text{ref}}\): \[ \max_\theta \; \mathbb{E}_{x \sim \mathcal{D},\, y \sim \pi_\theta(\cdot \mid x)} \big[r_\phi(x, y)\big] \;-\; \beta\, D_{\text{KL}}\!\big(\pi_\theta(\cdot \mid x) \,\big\|\, \pi_{\text{ref}}(\cdot \mid x)\big) \] What KL divergence measures, in plain words. At every position, both the policy and the frozen reference assign a probability to each possible next token. The Kullback–Leibler divergence measures how different those two distributions are. It is zero when they are identical and grows as the policy puts probability where the reference does not. It is not symmetric: \(D_{\text{KL}}(\pi_\theta \,\|\, \pi_{\text{ref}})\) generally differs from \(D_{\text{KL}}(\pi_{\text{ref}} \,\|\, \pi_\theta)\), so the order is part of the definition. A small example over three candidate next tokens: Next token Reference \(\pi_{\text{ref}}\) Policy \(\pi_\theta\) “great” 0.60 0.70 “good” 0.30 0.25 “fine” 0.10 0.05 \[ D_{\text{KL}}(\pi_\theta \,\|\, \pi_{\text{ref}}) = 0.70 \ln\tfrac{0.70}{0.60} + 0.25 \ln\tfrac{0.25}{0.30} + 0.05 \ln\tfrac{0.05}{0.10} \approx 0.028 \text{ nats} \] The reverse direction gives about 0.032: close here, but not equal. A small shift costs little; a policy that moves most of the probability to a token the reference considers unlikely pays a large penalty. Four facts are often confused: The KL is computed against the frozen reference model (the SFT model), not against the previous PPO iteration. It is not part of reward-model training. The reward model is trained first, on preference pairs alone; the KL term appears only in the RL objective. It always discourages moving away from the reference. It never rewards change; the reward model provides the pull, the KL the restraint. It is different from PPO’s clipping. Clipping limits how far one update moves from the previous iteration; the KL penalty limits how far the policy drifts from the SFT model over the whole run. In practice the KL term is estimated from the sampled tokens. Each generated token is charged \(\beta \log \frac{\pi_\theta(y_t \mid x, y_{<t})}{\pi_{\text{ref}}(y_t \mid x, y_{<t})}\), and the reward-model score is added at the final token. In the table above, if the policy samples “great”, that token is charged \(\beta \ln(0.70/0.60) \approx 0.15\beta\). The penalty does two things: It limits reward hacking. The reward model is accurate only near the kind of text it was trained on, so the policy should not wander into unfamiliar text. It preserves fluency and general ability learned in pre-training and SFT. \(\beta\) sets the trade-off. Too small and the policy exploits the reward model; too large and it barely moves. 4.3.4 PPO in the LLM setting Proximal Policy Optimization (Schulman et al. 2017) is the RL algorithm used in the original RLHF work. One iteration, showing which models are trained and which are frozen: prompts │ ▼ ┌───────────────────────┐ │ Policy π_θ (TRAINED) │──► completions └───────────────────────┘ │ ▲ ├──► Reward model r_φ (FROZEN) ──► score at last token │ ├──► Reference π_ref (FROZEN) ───► per-token KL penalty │ └──► Value model V_ψ (TRAINED) ──► baseline per token │ │ │ reward = score − β·KL │ │ advantages from reward and V ▼ └──────── PPO update (clipped) ◄─────┘ Two of the four models learn (the policy and the value model). The reward model and the reference stay fixed throughout. Each PPO iteration has two phases: Phase 1: rollouts. Sample completions for a batch of prompts from the current policy. Score them (reward model minus KL penalty), and record the token log-probabilities under the policy that generated them. Call that policy \(\pi_{\theta_\text{old}}\). Phase 2: updates. Take a few gradient steps on that batch, using three terms: Value loss. A value function \(V_\psi(s_t)\) predicts the future reward from a partial completion. It is usually a separate head or model, often initialized from the reward model. It is trained by regression, \(\big(V_\psi(s_t) - \hat{R}_t\big)^2\), towards the observed return \(\hat{R}_t\). Clipped policy loss. The advantage \(\hat{A}_t\) measures how much better token \(a_t\) turned out than the value function expected. Generalized advantage estimation combines the one-step errors \(\delta_t = r_t + \gamma V(s_{t+1}) - V(s_t)\) into \(\hat{A}_t = \sum_{l \ge 0} (\gamma\lambda)^l \delta_{t+l}\) (Schulman et al. 2016). With the probability ratio \(\rho_t(\theta) = \pi_\theta(a_t \mid s_t) / \pi_{\theta_\text{old}}(a_t \mid s_t)\): \[ L^{\text{CLIP}}(\theta) = \mathbb{E}_t\Big[\min\big(\rho_t \hat{A}_t,\; \text{clip}(\rho_t,\, 1-\epsilon,\, 1+\epsilon)\, \hat{A}_t\big)\Big] \] Maximizing \(\rho_t \hat{A}_t\) raises the probability of tokens with positive advantage and lowers it for tokens with negative advantage. The advantage estimates are reliable only while the new policy stays close to the one that generated the data. The clip (typically \(\epsilon \approx 0.2\)) and the \(\min\) remove any incentive to move the ratio outside \([1-\epsilon, 1+\epsilon]\). That gives an approximate trust region, which is the “proximal” in PPO. For example, with \(\epsilon = 0.2\), suppose a token had a positive advantage and an update has already raised its probability by 50% (\(\rho_t = 1.5\)). The objective uses \(\min(1.5\hat{A}_t, 1.2\hat{A}_t) = 1.2\hat{A}_t\), so pushing the ratio past 1.2 earns nothing more, and the gradient for that token is zero. The update stops pushing in that direction until fresh rollouts are collected. Entropy bonus. Adding the policy’s entropy \(S[\pi_\theta]\) discourages the policy from collapsing to one fixed answer. It acts during training, whereas temperature acts at inference. The combined objective, maximized by gradient ascent, is \(L^{\text{CLIP}} - c_1 L^{\text{VF}} + c_2 S\). Here \(c_1\) and \(c_2\) are weighting hyperparameters. After the updates, the new policy becomes \(\pi_{\theta_\text{old}}\) for the next round of rollouts. Two “old” models. \(\pi_{\theta_\text{old}}\) in the ratio is the previous iteration’s policy, and it changes every iteration. \(\pi_{\text{ref}}\) in the KL penalty is the frozen SFT model and never changes. Confusing the two is a common mistake. Cost. PPO-based RLHF keeps four models in play: the policy, the reference policy, the reward model, and the value model. It is also sensitive to hyperparameters. One way to cut memory is to train the policy as a LoRA adapter (Section 3.5). The reference policy is then the same base weights with the adapter switched off, so there is no second full copy. Hugging Face’s TRL library is a common open-source starting point. It provides trainers for supervised fine-tuning, reward modelling, DPO, GRPO, and other methods, and works with LoRA adapters; check its documentation for the current list. In short. Three stages: SFT, a reward model trained on ranked comparisons with the Bradley–Terry loss, then RL against that reward. The RL objective is reward minus a KL penalty to the frozen SFT model; KL measures how far the policy’s next-token distributions have moved. PPO limits each update with a clipped ratio, uses a value model for advantages, and adds an entropy bonus. Four models: policy and value are trained; reward model and reference are frozen. 4.4 Reward hacking Reward hacking happens when the policy finds outputs that score highly under the reward model but fail the real objective. It is Goodhart’s law applied to a learned proxy. Typical symptoms: A detoxification run learns to fill every answer with effusive phrases (“most awesome, most incredible”) because the toxicity classifier rewards them. Answers get longer or more hedged because the reward model learned that length correlates with preference. The text degrades into odd or ungrammatical strings that happen to score well. Leo Gao et al. (2023) measured this systematically. As optimization pushes the policy further from its starting point, the proxy reward keeps rising. The true quality (measured by a larger “gold” reward model) rises, peaks, and then declines. Defences: the KL penalty against the reference policy; early stopping on held-out human or gold-model evaluation, not on proxy reward; larger and better reward models, refreshed with new comparisons from the current policy; and reading samples. Hacked outputs are often obvious to a person long before the metrics show anything. In short. Reward hacking: the proxy reward rises while true quality peaks and falls. Defend with the KL penalty, early stopping on held-out evaluation, better and refreshed reward models, and reading samples. 4.5 Evaluating an aligned model Evaluate the aligned model with the same measure on the same held-out prompts, before and after. In the detoxification example, run the SFT model and the aligned model over the same evaluation prompts. Score each completion with a toxicity classifier, then compare the mean probability of the toxic class. It should go down. Also check for collateral damage: Capability regressions (“alignment tax”). InstructGPT showed drops on some standard NLP benchmarks. It reduced them by mixing pre-training gradients into the PPO updates (Ouyang et al. 2022). Over-refusal, where the model declines harmless requests. Sycophancy. RLHF-trained assistants tend to agree with the user’s stated views even when the user is wrong, partly because human raters reward agreement (Sharma et al. 2024). Human preference evaluation on held-out prompts remains the reference standard. In short. Compare the same measure on the same held-out prompts before and after alignment. Check for collateral damage: capability loss, over-refusal, sycophancy. 4.6 Scaling feedback: Constitutional AI and RLAIF Human labeling is slow and expensive, and labelers must read harmful content. There is also a tension between helpfulness and harmlessness, documented by Bai, Jones, et al. (2022). A model optimized mainly for helpfulness may comply with a harmful request, such as explaining how to break into a neighbour’s Wi-Fi. Constitutional AI (Bai, Kadavath, et al. 2022) replaces most of the human harmlessness labels with feedback from the model itself, guided by a short written list of principles called the constitution. An example principle: choose the response that is least likely to encourage illegal or unethical activity. It has two phases: Supervised phase (critique and revise). Prompt a helpful model with red-team prompts designed to elicit harmful answers. Ask it to critique its own answer against a principle, then to rewrite the answer to remove the problem. Fine-tune on the (red-team prompt, revised answer) pairs. RL phase (RLAIF). Sample pairs of responses from the fine-tuned model. Ask a model which response better satisfies the constitution. Train a preference model on these AI-generated comparisons (combined with human helpfulness labels in the paper), then run RL as in RLHF. This is reinforcement learning from AI feedback (RLAIF). The principles are explicit and editable, so the target behaviour is easier to inspect and adapt to a domain than thousands of individual labels. The quality of the result still depends on the principles and on the model’s ability to apply them. In short. Constitutional AI replaces most human harmlessness labels with model feedback guided by written principles. Supervised phase: critique and revise. RL phase: AI-labelled preferences (RLAIF). 4.7 Beyond PPO: current alignment methods Current practice (October 2026). PPO-based RLHF is the conceptual foundation, but it is no longer the only or default recipe. Two simpler or more targeted families are widely used. Check recent technical reports before treating any one pipeline as standard. 4.7.1 Direct Preference Optimization (DPO) Rafailov et al. (2023) showed that the KL-regularized objective above has a closed-form optimal policy, \(\pi^*(y \mid x) \propto \pi_{\text{ref}}(y \mid x) \exp\big(r(x, y)/\beta\big)\). Inverting this expresses the reward through the policy itself. Substituting into the Bradley–Terry loss gives a classification loss on preference pairs, with no reward model and no sampling during training: \[ \mathcal{L}_{\text{DPO}}(\theta) = -\,\mathbb{E}_{(x,\,y_w,\,y_l)} \left[\log \sigma\!\left( \beta \log \frac{\pi_\theta(y_w \mid x)}{\pi_{\text{ref}}(y_w \mid x)} - \beta \log \frac{\pi_\theta(y_l \mid x)}{\pi_{\text{ref}}(y_l \mid x)} \right)\right] \] DPO raises the likelihood of preferred answers relative to rejected ones, measured against the reference model. It needs only the policy and a frozen reference, trains like supervised fine-tuning, and has few hyperparameters. The trade-off: it learns from a fixed, offline preference dataset, not from fresh samples of the current policy. Online RL methods can keep collecting feedback as the policy changes. 4.7.2 RL with verifiable rewards and GRPO For tasks with checkable answers (mathematics, code that must pass tests, strict formats), the reward can be a program instead of a learned model. The reward is “1 if the final answer is correct or the tests pass, else 0”. This is reinforcement learning with verifiable rewards (RLVR) (Lambert et al. 2024). A rule-based reward is much harder to hack than a learned reward model. GRPO (Group Relative Policy Optimization) (Shao et al. 2024) is a PPO variant built for this setting. For each prompt it samples a group of \(G\) completions and uses each completion’s reward relative to the group as its advantage: \[ \hat{A}_i = \frac{r_i - \operatorname{mean}(r_1, \dots, r_G)}{\operatorname{std}(r_1, \dots, r_G)} \] For example, with \(G = 4\) attempts at a math problem and rewards \((1, 0, 0, 1)\), the mean is 0.5 and the standard deviation 0.5, so the two correct attempts get advantage \(+1\) and the two wrong ones \(-1\). If only one of four is correct, \((1, 0, 0, 0)\), the correct one gets about \(+1.73\) and each wrong one about \(-0.58\). A rare success is reinforced strongly. If all four are correct (or all wrong), every advantage is zero and the prompt teaches nothing. This is why practitioners often filter training prompts towards problems the model solves only some of the time. This removes the value model. GRPO keeps PPO’s clipped ratio and adds a KL term to the reference policy. DeepSeek-R1 showed that large-scale RL with rule-based rewards can teach a model long, self-checking chains of thought (DeepSeek-AI 2025). RLVR-style training is now a common ingredient of reasoning models. 4.7.3 Method comparison Method Feedback source Reward model? Models in memory during training Main strength Main risk RLHF with PPO Human rankings Yes, learned Policy, reference, reward, value Online; general preferences Cost, instability, reward hacking Constitutional AI / RLAIF Model judgments guided by principles Yes, learned from AI labels As PPO Scales feedback; explicit principles Inherits the judge’s blind spots DPO Human or AI preference pairs No (implicit) Policy, reference Simple, stable, cheap Offline; limited to its dataset RLVR with GRPO Programmatic checks No (rule-based) Policy, reference Hard to hack; drives reasoning gains Only for verifiable tasks In short. DPO turns preference learning into a classification loss: no reward model, no sampling, but offline. RLVR uses programs as rewards for checkable tasks; GRPO replaces the value model with group-relative advantages. These, not PPO alone, are common in current pipelines and in reasoning models. 4.8 Key takeaways The section summaries above hold the details. The chapter in five lines: Why: people judge better-of-two more easily than they write ideal answers, so alignment learns from preferences. Classic RLHF: SFT, a Bradley–Terry reward model, then PPO against it with a KL penalty to the frozen SFT model. The two restraints: PPO clipping limits each step; the KL penalty limits total drift. Neither is part of reward-model training. The main failure: reward hacking; catch it with held-out evaluation and by reading samples. Current methods: Constitutional AI/RLAIF for scale, DPO for simplicity, RLVR with GRPO for verifiable tasks and reasoning. 4.9 Interview checkpoints Why train a reward model instead of using humans directly? RL needs rewards for a huge number of samples. The reward model is a cheap, always-available stand-in for human judgment. Reward-model loss? Bradley–Terry: \(-\log \sigma\big(r(x, y_w) - r(x, y_l)\big)\). Only reward differences are learned. What does the KL penalty do? It keeps the policy close to the SFT model, where the reward model is trustworthy. That limits reward hacking and preserves fluency. Is the KL divergence used to train the reward model? No. The reward model is trained first, on preference pairs only. The KL term appears only in the RL objective, computed against the frozen reference. Does RLHF change the model’s architecture or size? No. Only the weight values change. What does PPO’s clipping do? It caps how far one update can move the probability ratio, giving an approximate trust region and stable training. \(\pi_{\theta_\text{old}}\) vs. \(\pi_{\text{ref}}\)? The previous iteration’s policy (in the PPO ratio) vs. the frozen SFT model (in the KL penalty). Which models does PPO-based RLHF need? The policy, reference, reward model, and value model. What is reward hacking, and how do you detect it? The proxy reward rises while true quality falls. Detect it with held-out human or gold-model evaluation and by reading samples. DPO vs. PPO? DPO is an offline classification loss on preference pairs with no reward model or sampling. PPO is online RL against a learned reward. What does GRPO remove? The value model. Advantages come from rewards relative to a group of samples for the same prompt. What is the alignment tax? Capability lost on other tasks after alignment. Mixing in pre-training data during RL reduces it. References

Chapter 5 From Model to Application The earlier chapters cover how to choose, adapt, and align a model. This chapter covers what happens after that: making the model cheap and fast enough to serve, and connecting it to data and tools so that it can do useful work reliably. It closes with the risks specific to generative applications. Three questions shape this stage of the project lifecycle (Section 1.7): Serving constraints. How fast must completions be, what compute budget is available, and how much quality can be traded for speed or cost? External resources. Does the model need data it was not trained on, or actions in other systems? Consumption. Who calls the model (people through a UI, or other systems through an API), and what must be logged, checked, or secured on the way? 5.1 Optimizing models for inference Inference cost scales with model size. Smaller or lower-precision models load faster, need less GPU memory, and generate tokens with lower latency. The challenge is to shrink the model without losing the quality that matters for the task. Three techniques work on the model itself. 5.1.1 Knowledge distillation Distillation trains a small student model to imitate a large, frozen teacher (Hinton et al. 2015). The teacher’s full output distribution carries more information than a single correct label. It shows which wrong answers are nearly right. A temperature \(T > 1\) in the softmax, \(p_i = \exp(z_i / T) / \sum_j \exp(z_j / T)\), flattens both distributions so that this information is visible (Section 1.6 explains temperature). For example, teacher logits \((4, 2, 1)\) for “cat”, “dog”, “car” give probabilities of about \((0.84, 0.11, 0.04)\) at \(T = 1\): nearly a hard label. At \(T = 4\) they become about \((0.48, 0.29, 0.23)\), and the student can now see that “dog” is a more plausible mistake than “car”. The student minimizes a weighted sum of two losses: \[ \mathcal{L} = \alpha \, T^2 \, D_{\text{KL}}\!\big(p^{\,T}_{\text{teacher}} \,\big\|\, p^{\,T}_{\text{student}}\big) + (1 - \alpha)\, \text{CE}\big(y,\; p^{\,T=1}_{\text{student}}\big) \] The first term (the distillation loss) matches the teacher’s softened distribution, the soft labels. The \(T^2\) factor keeps its gradient scale comparable as \(T\) changes. The second term (the student loss) is ordinary cross-entropy against the ground-truth hard labels at \(T = 1\). Distillation does not shrink the teacher. It produces a separate, smaller model that replaces the teacher at inference. DistilBERT is the classic encoder example: about 40% smaller and 60% faster than BERT, while keeping about 97% of its language-understanding performance (Sanh et al. 2019). Distillation is also standard for generative models. Two forms are common: Token-level, as above, matching the teacher’s next-token distribution. Gemma 2’s smaller models were trained this way (Gemma Team 2024). Sequence-level, where the student is fine-tuned on complete outputs generated by the teacher (Kim and Rush 2016). The small DeepSeek-R1 models were made by fine-tuning open models on reasoning traces generated by DeepSeek-R1 (DeepSeek-AI 2025). A practical pattern follows: launch with a large, capable model, collect real traffic and approved outputs, then distill or fine-tune a smaller model for that specific workload. 5.1.2 Post-training quantization Quantization stores numbers in fewer bits (Section 2.4). Quantization-aware training simulates low precision during training. Post-training quantization (PTQ) converts a model that has already been trained, so it is the usual route at deployment: Weights only or weights and activations. Quantizing activations as well saves more compute but usually costs more accuracy. Large LLMs have rare activation outliers with very large magnitude, which break naive 8-bit schemes. LLM.int8() handles them by keeping those dimensions in 16-bit (Dettmers et al. 2022). Calibration. PTQ runs a small sample of data through the model to estimate the range of values to be quantized. Error-aware methods. GPTQ quantizes weights to 3–4 bits layer by layer. It adjusts the remaining weights to compensate for each rounding error, which keeps accuracy close to the 16-bit model (Frantar et al. 2023). The result is a smaller memory footprint and often faster inference, usually with a small, measurable drop in quality. Measure that drop on your own evaluation set before deploying. For scale, the weights of a 7B-parameter model take about 14 GB in 16-bit precision (2 bytes per parameter), about 7 GB in 8-bit, and about 3.5 GB in 4-bit, plus a little for quantization constants. That is often the difference between needing a data-centre GPU and fitting on a laptop. 5.1.3 Pruning Pruning removes weights that contribute little. The simplest criterion is weights near zero (magnitude pruning). Methods differ in when they prune (during training, during fine-tuning, or after training) and in what they remove: Unstructured pruning zeroes individual weights. SparseGPT pruned 175B-parameter models to 50% sparsity in one shot with little loss in quality (Frantar and Alistarh 2023). Wanda reached similar results with a simpler score: weight magnitude times the norm of its input activation (Sun et al. 2024). Structured pruning removes whole neurons, attention heads, or layers. Zeros only save memory and time if the storage format and hardware can exploit them. Unstructured sparsity often gives little real speed-up. Structured or hardware-supported patterns (such as 2:4 sparsity on recent NVIDIA GPUs) are needed for actual gains. 5.1.4 Serving-side optimizations These leave the weights unchanged and optimize how tokens are generated: KV caching stores the attention keys and values of earlier tokens, so each new token is not recomputed from scratch. Memory for the cache, not compute, often limits how many requests fit on a GPU. Per token, the cache holds 2 (keys and values) × layers × KV heads × head dimension × bytes. For a 7B-class configuration (32 layers, 32 heads of dimension 128, 16-bit), that is about 0.5 MB per token, so one 4,096-token request needs about 2 GB of cache. Grouped-query attention, which shares keys and values across heads, cuts this several-fold. Batching and paged KV memory. Serving systems such as vLLM manage the cache in pages to pack many concurrent requests efficiently (Kwon et al. 2023). Speculative decoding. A small draft model proposes several tokens, and the large model verifies them in one pass. The output distribution is unchanged, and latency drops when the draft is usually right (Leviathan et al. 2023). 5.1.5 Effort across the lifecycle Stage Typical effort Needs training? Main expertise Pre-training Weeks to months, very large compute Yes Architecture, data, distributed training Prompt engineering Hours to days No Task knowledge, evaluation Fine-tuning / PEFT Hours to days once the data exist Yes Data preparation, evaluation Alignment (RLHF, DPO) Fast if a reward model or preference data exist; slow if human feedback must be collected Yes Labeling design, RL or preference tuning Optimization for deployment Hours to days Sometimes (distillation) Quality-versus-cost trade-off Most applications start from an existing model and spend their effort on the bottom four rows. In short. Shrink the model: distillation (a smaller student), quantization (fewer bits), pruning (fewer weights, fast only with structured sparsity). Serve it better: KV caching, paged batching, speculative decoding. Measure the quality cost of every optimization on your own eval set. 5.2 Problems that training alone does not solve Even a well-adapted model has structural limits: Knowledge cut-off. The weights reflect the training data at a point in time. A model trained before a change of government will name the old prime minister with full confidence. Arithmetic and exact computation. The model predicts likely tokens; it does not calculate. Long multiplication or a tax calculation can come out close but wrong. Hallucination. Models produce fluent, specific text even when the content is unsupported. Examples include invented citations, products, or facts (Ji et al. 2023). No access to private or real-time systems. The model cannot see your order database or call your shipping API unless the application connects them. The fix is to augment the model at inference time. An orchestration layer (application code or a framework) passes user input to the model, calls external data sources and tools based on the model’s output, and returns results to the model and the user. What orchestration frameworks are for. Every LLM application needs the same plumbing: prompt templates, calls to one or more models, retrieval, tool calls, conversation memory, and parsing of the model’s output. Frameworks such as LangChain and LlamaIndex package these pieces as reusable components and let you chain them into a pipeline or an agent loop, so you do not rewrite them for every project. They also make it easy to swap a model or a vector store. The trade-off is an extra layer of abstraction between you and the model call, which can make debugging harder. Many teams now write the orchestration directly against the provider’s API or use a vendor agent SDK, especially since native tool calling made the hardest part, parsing actions out of text, unnecessary (see the Current practice note under ReAct below). In short. Training cannot fix knowledge cut-offs, exact computation, hallucination, or access to private and live systems. An orchestration layer connects the model to data and tools at inference time; frameworks package that plumbing. 5.3 Retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) Retrieval-augmented generation gives the model relevant external text at inference time. It does not try to store that knowledge in the weights. Retraining for every update would be slow and expensive. Retrieval keeps knowledge current, supports private data, and lets answers cite their sources. 5.3.1 The original formulation Lewis et al. (2020) paired a retriever with a generator. The retriever was a dense passage retriever (DPR) (Karpukhin et al. 2020). A query encoder embeds the question, and the closest passages are found in a pre-built index of Wikipedia passage embeddings. The generator (BART) conditions on the question plus the retrieved passages. The query encoder and generator were fine-tuned jointly, with the document index held fixed. RAG improved results on open-domain question answering over models that relied on their parameters alone. 5.3.2 A typical RAG pipeline today Most applications use the same idea without joint training: off-the-shelf embedding models, a vector index, and a general LLM. Indexing (offline): Load and clean the sources: documents, wikis, tickets, web pages. Chunk them into passages small enough to retrieve precisely, often a few hundred tokens with some overlap. Keep metadata such as source, date, and access rights. Embed each chunk into a vector with an embedding model. Store vectors and metadata in a vector store. A vector database adds keys, filtering, and updates, so each chunk can be traced back to its source document. Answering (online): Embed the query with the same embedding model. Retrieve the top-\(k\) most similar chunks, usually by cosine similarity, \(\cos(\mathbf{q}, \mathbf{d}) = \frac{\mathbf{q} \cdot \mathbf{d}}{\lVert \mathbf{q} \rVert \lVert \mathbf{d} \rVert}\). Augment the prompt with those chunks, clearly delimited, along with an instruction to answer only from them and to cite them. Generate the answer, with citations back to the chunk sources. The augmented prompt in step 7 might look like this (illustrative): Answer the question using only the sources below. Cite each claim as [n]. If the sources do not contain the answer, say "I don't know." <source id="1" doc="returns_policy_2026.pdf" updated="2026-09-01"> Unworn items can be returned within 30 days with a receipt ... </source> <source id="2" doc="faq_shipping.html" updated="2026-07-14"> Return shipping is free for loyalty members ... </source> Question: Can I return shoes I bought 5 weeks ago? The instruction to say “I don’t know” matters: without it, the model tends to fill gaps from memory. The dates let the model, and the reader, see how current each source is. Retrieval is not limited to vectors. The “retriever” can be a keyword search engine, a SQL query against a database, or a web search API. 5.3.3 What makes RAG work or fail Retrieval quality caps answer quality. If the right chunk is not retrieved, the model cannot use it. Evaluate retrieval separately, for example with recall@\(k\) on labelled question–passage pairs. Chunking is a design decision. Chunks that are too large dilute relevance. Chunks that are too small lose context. Hybrid search and reranking usually help. Combine keyword search (exact names, codes, IDs) with dense search (paraphrases), then re-score the candidates with a more accurate cross-encoder or LLM reranker. Position matters in long contexts. Models use information at the beginning and end of a long context more reliably than information in the middle (Liu et al. 2024). Retrieving fewer, better chunks beats stuffing the context. Grounding reduces but does not remove hallucination. The model can still ignore, misread, or over-generalize from retrieved text. Evaluate faithfulness (is every claim supported by the cited chunks?) separately from retrieval. Access control. Retrieval must respect the user’s permissions. Otherwise RAG becomes a data-leak channel. Current practice (October 2026). Context windows are now far larger than the few thousand tokens of 2022–23 models. Check current model documentation. Long context reduces the need for aggressive chunking but does not replace retrieval. Cost, latency, position effects, and access control still favour sending only relevant material. Chapter 22 treats context selection as an engineering discipline. In short. RAG retrieves relevant, permitted text at inference time and grounds the answer in it, with citations. Pipeline: chunk, embed, store; then embed the query, retrieve top-\(k\), augment the prompt, generate. Retrieval quality caps answer quality; evaluate retrieval and faithfulness separately. RAG reduces hallucination but does not remove it. 5.4 Helping models reason 5.4.1 Chain-of-thought prompting Multi-step problems are a classic weakness of models that answer in one step. Chain-of-thought (CoT) prompting (Wei, Wang, et al. 2022) includes worked intermediate steps in the few-shot examples. The model then produces its own steps before the answer. The paper’s standard example: Q: Roger has 5 tennis balls. He buys 2 more cans of tennis balls. Each can has 3 tennis balls. How many tennis balls does he have now? A: Roger started with 5 balls. 2 cans of 3 tennis balls each is 6 tennis balls. 5 + 6 = 11. The answer is 11. Q: The cafeteria had 23 apples. If they used 20 to make lunch and bought 6 more, how many apples do they have? A: With a bare answer in the example (“The answer is 11.”), the model in the paper answered 27. With the worked steps, it reasoned 23 − 20 = 3, 3 + 6 = 9 and answered correctly. What the evidence says: CoT gains appeared mainly in large models (about 100B parameters in the original experiments). Smaller models produced fluent but illogical chains (Wei, Wang, et al. 2022). Zero-shot CoT: just adding “Let’s think step by step” also helps (Kojima et al. 2022). Self-consistency: sample several reasoning paths and take the majority answer. This improves accuracy over a single chain (X. Wang et al. 2023). The written chain is not guaranteed to be the real reason. Models can produce plausible explanations that hide the actual influence on their answer (Turpin et al. 2023). Treat CoT as a performance technique, not as a faithful explanation. Current practice (October 2026). Reasoning models are trained with RL to produce long internal chains of thought before answering (Chapter 4). With these models, hand-written CoT examples matter less. Reasoning effort is often a setting (a “thinking” budget) instead. The Prompt Engineering part covers prompting for reasoning in detail. 5.4.2 Program-aided language models (PAL) CoT fixes the plan but not the arithmetic: a correct chain can still contain a wrong multiplication. PAL (Luyu Gao et al. 2023) has the model write its reasoning as a program. Each reasoning step is a code comment, followed by the code that computes it: # Roger started with 5 tennis balls. tennis_balls = 5 # 2 cans of 3 tennis balls each is bought_balls = 2 * 3 # tennis balls. The answer is answer = tennis_balls + bought_balls The orchestrator runs the generated code in an interpreter and returns the result. The model decides what to compute; the interpreter guarantees the computation. PAL outperformed CoT on several mathematical and symbolic reasoning benchmarks in the original paper. Today the same idea is offered as a built-in code-execution tool by model providers. Run generated code only in a sandbox (Section 9.4.1). 5.4.3 ReAct: reasoning plus acting Many applications need several steps that involve external systems: look up an order, check a policy, request a shipping label, confirm an email address. ReAct (Yao et al. 2023) interleaves three kinds of output in a loop: Thought: reasoning about what to do next. Action: a call to one of a fixed set of allowed actions. In the paper’s Wikipedia question-answering tasks these were search[entity], lookup[keyword], and finish[answer]. Observation: the result of the action, which the orchestrator appends to the context before the next thought. The loop repeats until the model chooses finish. Few-shot examples teach the format, and an instruction block defines the allowed actions. Restricting the action space is essential: a model will otherwise “plan” steps the application cannot execute. In the paper, ReAct beat acting-only prompting throughout. On fact verification (FEVER) it also beat chain-of-thought. On multi-hop question answering (HotpotQA), the best results came from combining ReAct with chain-of-thought and self-consistency. The largest gains were on interactive decision-making tasks (ALFWorld, WebShop). For an LLM to drive actions reliably, its output must: name a valid action from the allowed set; be machine-parseable (a fixed syntax, JSON, a SQL statement, a script); and include the information needed to validate the action, such as the customer’s email address before a return label is sent. Current practice (October 2026). ReAct’s text-parsing loop has largely been replaced by native tool calling. The application declares tools with JSON schemas, the model emits structured tool calls, and the application executes them and returns results (Chapter 9). The Model Context Protocol standardizes how tools and data sources connect to models (Chapter 21). Orchestration frameworks (LangChain was the early example, offering prompt templates, memory, tools, chains, and agents) are joined by vendor agent SDKs. The Thought → Action → Observation loop remains the core mental model for agents. Chapter 11 extends it to planning and multi-agent systems, and Chapter 25 applies it on Databricks. In short. CoT: worked steps improve multi-step reasoning in large models, but the chain is not a faithful explanation. PAL: the model writes code and an interpreter computes. ReAct: Thought → Action → Observation over a fixed action set; today implemented with native tool calling (Chapter 9). 5.5 The application stack A production LLM application has several layers, and the model is only one of them: Layer Contents Infrastructure Compute, storage, and networking, on-premises or cloud; sized for real-time or batch inference Models Foundation models and adapted models (fine-tuned, LoRA adapters, distilled students) Data and retrieval Document stores, vector indexes, databases, and their access controls Orchestration and tools Prompt templates, tool definitions, agent loops, code execution, external APIs Output handling and feedback Validation of outputs, logging, conversation memory, user feedback for later evaluation and fine-tuning Interface and security UI or REST API, authentication, rate limits, guardrails Logged prompts, completions, and feedback are a valuable asset. They become the evaluation sets and training data for the next iteration, provided users have consented and private data is handled correctly. In short. The model is one of six layers: infrastructure, models, data, orchestration, output handling, and interface. Logged prompts, outputs, and feedback become the next round’s evals and training data. 5.6 Responsible generative AI Generative models add specific risks to the usual ML concerns: Risk What goes wrong Mitigations Toxicity and bias Harmful, offensive, or discriminatory output, including about protected groups Curate training and fine-tuning data; alignment (Chapter 4); guardrail classifiers on inputs and outputs; diverse annotators and red-teaming Hallucination Confident, false content: invented facts, sources, or numbers Grounding with RAG and citations; tools for exact computation; faithfulness evaluation; user education and disclaimers; restrict use to suitable tasks Intellectual property and privacy Reproducing copyrighted or personal data from training or retrieval sources Data governance and licensing; filtering and blocking of protected content; policy and legal controls; machine “unlearning” is an active research area, not a solved tool Prompt injection Instructions hidden in retrieved documents, web pages, or tool outputs hijack the model, for example to leak data or trigger actions (Greshake et al. 2023) Treat retrieved and tool content as untrusted data; least-privilege tools; human confirmation for consequential actions; output validation A workable process for each application: Define the use case narrowly. The narrower the task, the easier the risks are to assess and test. Assess the risks for that use case: who is affected, and what a failure costs. Evaluate on representative data, including adversarial and subgroup cases, against explicit acceptance criteria. Monitor and iterate across the whole lifecycle. Models, data, and misuse patterns change after launch. The NIST AI Risk Management Framework (National Institute of Standards and Technology 2023) and its generative-AI profile (National Institute of Standards and Technology 2024) are widely used, vendor-neutral references for organizing this work. Regulatory obligations (for example the EU AI Act) depend on jurisdiction and use case; check current requirements for a real deployment. In short. Four generative risks: toxicity and bias, hallucination, IP and privacy, prompt injection. Process: narrow use case, risk assessment, evaluation against explicit criteria, monitoring after launch. 5.7 Key takeaways The section summaries above hold the details. The chapter in five lines: Make it affordable: distil, quantize, prune, and optimize serving; measure the quality cost each time. Fill the gaps training leaves: an orchestration layer adds data and tools at inference time. Ground it: RAG supplies current, permitted, citable text; evaluate retrieval and faithfulness separately. Help it reason and act: CoT, PAL, and ReAct, the ancestors of today’s reasoning models and tool-calling agents. Deploy it responsibly: the model is one layer; narrow the use case, assess risks, evaluate, and monitor. 5.8 Interview checkpoints Why use a temperature above 1 in distillation? It softens the teacher’s distribution so that the relative probabilities of wrong answers (the “dark knowledge”) carry training signal. PTQ vs. QAT? PTQ converts a trained model and needs calibration data. QAT simulates quantization during training and usually loses less accuracy, at extra training cost. Why might pruning not speed up inference? Unstructured zeros need sparse formats and kernel or hardware support to save time. RAG vs. fine-tuning for company knowledge? RAG for facts that change or must be cited and permission-filtered. Fine-tuning for behaviour, format, and style. They are often combined. Main RAG failure points? Missed retrieval, poor chunking, lost-in-the- middle effects, unfaithful generation, and permission leaks. What is cosine similarity, and why use it for embeddings? The normalized dot product. It compares direction (meaning) independently of vector length. CoT vs. PAL? CoT writes reasoning in text and computes in the model. PAL writes code and computes in an interpreter. What are the three parts of a ReAct step? Thought, Action (from a fixed set), Observation. What is indirect prompt injection? Malicious instructions placed in content the model reads (documents, web pages, tool outputs) rather than typed by the user. What is LangChain for? It is an orchestration framework: reusable components for prompts, model calls, retrieval, tools, memory, and output parsing, chained into pipelines or agents. The trade-off is an extra abstraction layer; many teams now use provider SDKs and native tool calling directly. References

Chapter 7 Agentic Workflows The earlier parts of this book treat an LLM call as a single step: a prompt goes in, a completion comes out. This part is about systems that call models many times. They decide what to do next, use tools, check their own work, and iterate until a task is done. Chapter Question it answers This chapter What is an agentic workflow, when is it worth building, and how do you break a task into steps? Reflection (Chapter 8) How can a model critique and improve its own output, and when does that actually help? Tool use (Chapter 9) How do models call functions, run code, and connect to external systems? Evaluation and error analysis (Chapter 10) How do you measure an agentic system and decide what to improve next? Planning and multi-agent systems (Chapter 11) How can a model choose its own steps, and when should several agents work together? These chapters began as study notes from the DeepLearning.AI course Agentic AI (Andrew Ng). They have been rewritten as a reference and checked against primary sources. 7.1 From direct generation to agentic workflows The usual way to use an LLM is direct generation: a single prompt, such as “write an essay on topic X”, answered in one pass. That is like asking a person to write an essay from the first word to the last without stopping to think, look anything up, or revise. Models do surprisingly well under that constraint, but it is not how good work gets done. An agentic workflow is a process in which an LLM-based application carries out multiple steps to complete a task. For the essay, it might: write an outline; decide what to search for, and call a web search API; fetch and read the most relevant pages; write a first draft; critique the draft and identify gaps or weak sections; optionally ask a human to check key facts; and revise the draft. Each step is either an LLM call (with its own prompt) or ordinary software, such as a search API, a database query, or a script. The workflow takes longer and costs more than one call, but for many tasks it produces much better work. Classic background. In AI, an agent is anything that perceives its environment and acts on it to achieve goals (Russell and Norvig 2021). An LLM agent’s “perception” is its context (prompts, documents, tool results), and its “actions” are generated text and tool calls. In short. Direct generation is one prompt and one pass. An agentic workflow is several steps, each an LLM call or ordinary software. The extra steps cost time and money, and buy quality on tasks that need research, checking, or revision. 7.2 Degrees of autonomy There has been a lot of debate about which systems deserve to be called “agents”. A more useful view treats agentic as an adjective. Systems can be agentic to different degrees, depending on how many decisions the model makes rather than the developer. Level Steps Tools Typical example Control and predictability Less autonomous All predetermined by the developer Every tool call is hard-coded; the model’s autonomy is only in the text it generates Generate search queries → always run web search → fetch pages → write essay High Semi-autonomous The model makes some decisions The developer predefines the tools; the model chooses which to use and when The model decides whether to search the web, search news, or search papers, and how many pages to fetch Medium Highly autonomous The model decides the sequence itself The model can write code or create new tools on the fly The model drafts a plan, executes it, reflects, and loops back for more research as needed Low Schluntz and Zhang (2024) draw a similar line between workflows, where LLMs and tools are orchestrated through predefined code paths, and agents, where the LLM dynamically directs its own process and tool use. Their advice matches long experience: use the simplest design that works, and add autonomy only when the task needs flexibility that fixed steps cannot provide. Many valuable business applications sit at the less autonomous end. They are easier to test, debug, and trust. Highly autonomous systems handle a wider range of requests but are harder to control and predict. Example: a weekly campaign report at two levels. The difference shows up clearly in code. In a fixed workflow, the developer writes the sequence. In an agent, the model picks the next step inside a loop. Both sketches below are illustrative, not a specific library. # Workflow: the developer fixes every step. def weekly_report(week): spend = query_db("SELECT channel, spend, conversions FROM ads WHERE week = ?", week) notes = llm("Summarize what changed versus last week:\n" + spend) return llm("Write a one-page report for the CMO:\n" + notes) # Agent: the model decides which tool to call next, and when to stop. def weekly_report_agent(week, tools, max_steps=10): history = [f"Write the weekly campaign report for {week}."] for _ in range(max_steps): action = llm_choose_action(history, tools) # e.g. query_db, web_search, finish if action.name == "finish": return action.text history.append(tools[action.name](**action.args)) return "Stopped: step limit reached." The workflow always runs the same three steps, so it is easy to test. The agent can look up a competitor’s promotion when conversions drop, but you cannot know in advance which steps it will take. Note the step limit: an agent loop always needs a stopping rule. In short. “Agentic” is a spectrum: the more decisions the model makes, the more flexible and the less predictable the system. Workflows fix the code paths; agents choose them at run time. Start with the least autonomy that solves the task. 7.3 Why agentic workflows help 1. Better output quality. Breaking a task into steps, and letting the model check and revise its work, often gains more than switching to a stronger model. On the HumanEval coding benchmark (M. Chen et al. 2021), zero-shot pass@1 rose from 48.1% for GPT-3.5 to 67.0% for GPT-4 (OpenAI 2023). Ng (2024) reported that wrapping GPT-3.5 in an iterative agentic loop (generate, test, reflect, revise) reached up to 95.1%. In other words, the workflow improvement exceeded a full model generation. That figure comes from a newsletter summarizing published agentic coding methods, not from a peer-reviewed comparison, so treat it as indicative. The direction is well supported, though: later chapters cite controlled studies for reflection and tool use. 2. Parallelism. Independent steps can run at the same time. A research agent can run several searches and fetch nine web pages simultaneously, where a person would read them one after another. The overall workflow is slower than one LLM call, but it can be much faster than a human doing the same task. 3. Modularity. Each step is a component with a defined input and output, so it can be swapped without changing the rest of the workflow. For example, you can replace one web search engine with another, swap a general search for a news search, change the retrieval system, or use a different LLM for a single step. Modularity is what makes systematic improvement possible: you change one component, measure, and keep the change only if it helps (Chapter 10). In short. Quality: iterating with feedback can gain more than a model upgrade. Parallelism: independent steps run at once. Modularity: swap one component, measure, keep it only if it helps. 7.4 Which applications are easy or hard Easier to build reliably Harder to build reliably A clear, known sequence of steps, ideally an existing standard operating procedure Steps not known in advance; the agent must plan as it goes Text-only inputs (emails, documents, records) Rich multimodal inputs (images, audio, video) Narrow, well-defined outputs (fields, labels, a drafted reply) Open-ended goals with many acceptable outcomes Actions are reversible or reviewed by a human Actions with real consequences taken without review Some examples along that spectrum: Invoice processing (easy). Convert the PDF to text, check that the document is an invoice, extract the biller, address, amount due, and due date, then write them to a database. The steps are fixed. Order-status replies (moderate). Extract the order details from a customer email, query the order database, and draft a reply. A human reviews the reply before it is sent. General customer service (hard). “Do you have black or blue jeans?” needs two inventory queries. “I want to return the beach towel” needs a purchase check, a policy check, a return slip, and a database update. The agent must work out the sequence for each request. Computer use (among the hardest). The agent operates a web browser, reading pages, clicking, and typing to complete a task such as checking flight availability. Slow pages, unusual layouts, and dynamic content often derail it. It has improved quickly, but it is still slower and less reliable than calling an API, so prefer an API whenever one exists. 7.4.1 When you do not need an agentic workflow Not every LLM task benefits from multiple steps. If the model already has everything it needs in the prompt, and one pass produces acceptable output, a single well-written prompt is simpler, cheaper, and faster. Writing a product description from a supplied list of specifications is an example: nothing needs to be looked up, checked against a policy, or acted on. Signals that a workflow is worth it: the task needs information the model does not have, such as current market data, a customer’s order, or internal documents; it needs actions, such as updating a database, sending an email, or running code; it has verifiable intermediate results, such as tests, policies, or word limits, that a check-and-revise loop can exploit; or one-pass output is measurably not good enough. When one of these holds, ask which steps need a tool. In a competitor analysis, for example, collecting current competitor and market information needs web search. Comparing offers, writing a SWOT, and recommending a positioning can work from the collected material with the LLM alone. In short. Easiest: known steps, text inputs, narrow outputs, reversible or reviewed actions. Hardest: steps planned on the fly, rich media, open goals. Skip the workflow when one well-written prompt already does the job. Use one when the task needs outside information, actions, checkable intermediate results, or better quality than one pass gives. 7.5 Task decomposition The central design skill is turning a task into steps that each component can do well. A practical procedure: Ask how a skilled person would do the task. List the steps they would take. For each step, ask: can an LLM, a short piece of code, or an available tool do this reliably? If not, decompose that step further until each piece passes the test in step 2. Build it, look at the outputs, and refine the decomposition where the results fall short. Worked example: the essay. Version 1, direct generation: one step. The result is shallow and covers only obvious points. Version 2, three steps: outline → web search → write the essay. The result is deeper but reads as disjointed; the start, middle, and end do not quite fit together. Version 3, five steps: outline → web search → first draft → critique the draft → revise. The writing step is itself decomposed, the way a person would draft and then edit. Each refinement came from looking at the output and asking what a person would do differently. Decomposition is iterative, not designed once. Other examples: Customer email: extract the key fields (LLM) → query the order database (LLM writes the query; a tool runs it) → draft and send the reply (LLM plus an email tool). Invoice: extract the fields (LLM) → validate them and update the database (LLM plus a database tool). Worked example: a paid-media anomaly alert. Task: every morning, flag campaigns whose cost per acquisition (CPA) jumped and suggest a likely cause. Applying the procedure gives: Step Done by Why that component Pull yesterday’s spend and conversions per campaign Code (SQL query) Exact and repeatable; no LLM needed Compute CPA and flag rises above a threshold Code Arithmetic and rules are more reliable in code Gather context for flagged campaigns (budget changes, creative swaps, competitor news) Tools: change log, web search Facts the model does not have Explain the likely cause in two sentences LLM Reasoning over the gathered context Send the alert to the channel owner Action tool (email or chat) Changes the outside world; easy to review Only one of the five steps needs an LLM. That is typical: good decomposition gives deterministic work to code and keeps the model for judgment and language. In short. Ask how an expert would do the task, then check that each step can be done reliably by an LLM, code, or a tool. Split any step that cannot. Decomposition is iterative: refine it after reading real outputs. Give exact work to code and keep the LLM for judgment and language. 7.6 Building blocks Block Examples Good for LLMs and multimodal models General chat models, reasoning models, vision-language models Generating text, deciding what to do, extracting information, critiquing Specialized AI models PDF-to-text, speech-to-text, text-to-speech, image analysis Converting inputs the LLM cannot handle directly Information tools Web search, retrieval over documents (RAG, Section 5.3), database queries Bringing in facts the model does not have Action tools Email, calendar, ticketing, payment, or file APIs Changing the state of the world Code execution A sandboxed Python interpreter Exact computation and flexible data processing Humans A review queue or an approval step Checking high-stakes outputs before they take effect Knowing what blocks are available, and what each does well, is what lets you see how a business process could become an agentic workflow. In short. Six kinds of blocks: LLMs, specialized models, information tools, action tools, code execution, and humans. Designing a workflow means matching each step to the block that does it best. 7.7 Evaluate from the start What goes wrong in an agentic system is hard to predict in advance. The recommended practice is to build a quick, safe first version, then look at its outputs. Suppose a support agent turns out to mention competitors by name (“unlike RivalCo, we make returns easy”). That is a problem nobody anticipated, and it is easy to track once found. Objective criteria can be checked with code. For example, scan replies for a list of competitor names and report the error rate (see the sketch below). Subjective criteria, such as essay quality, need human judgment or an LLM-as-a-judge with a clear rubric. End-to-end evals measure the final output. Component-level evals measure one step. Traces (the intermediate outputs of every step) show where things go wrong. Systematically reading them is error analysis. A code-based check for the competitor problem takes a few lines: COMPETITORS = ["rivalco", "shopmart", "dealzone"] def mentions_competitor(reply: str) -> bool: text = reply.lower() return any(name in text for name in COMPETITORS) replies = [run_agent(email) for email in test_emails] # 20-50 real emails error_rate = sum(mentions_competitor(r) for r in replies) / len(replies) print(f"Replies naming a competitor: {error_rate:.0%}") Run it after every change to the prompt or model. If the rate goes up, the change made things worse, whatever else improved. Chapter 10 develops all of this. It is the most important practical skill for building agentic systems. In short. Build a quick, safe prototype and read its outputs; the real problems are rarely the ones you predicted. Check objective criteria with code and subjective ones with humans or an LLM judge. Traces show where a failure happens; reading them is error analysis. 7.8 The four design patterns Most agentic systems combine four recurring patterns (Ng 2024): Pattern Idea Example Trade-off Reflection The model (or a second “critic” model) reviews an output and revises it, ideally using external feedback such as test results Write code → run it → feed the errors back → fix Cheap to add; gains vary by task Tool use The model requests function calls to fetch information or take actions Web search, database query, code execution, calendar Greatly extends capability; needs safe tool design Planning The model decides the sequence of steps or tool calls itself HuggingGPT chains vision, image-generation, and speech models to fulfil a multi-part request (Shen et al. 2023) Flexible, but harder to control and predict Multi-agent collaboration Several role-specialized agents work together ChatDev simulates a software company with CEO, programmer, and tester agents (Qian et al. 2024) Helps decompose complex work; adds coordination cost and unpredictability Reflection and tool use are mature and widely used. Planning and multi-agent systems are powerful but less predictable. As of 2026, agentic coding tools are their clearest success story. In short. Four patterns: reflection, tool use, planning, and multi-agent collaboration. The first two are mature and predictable; the last two are more flexible and harder to control. 7.9 Costs and risks Agentic workflows trade cost and latency for quality, and they add failure modes of their own: Latency and cost. Every step is another model call or API call. Optimize them once the outputs are good (Section 10.7). Compounding errors. If failures are independent, step reliabilities multiply. A ten-step workflow whose steps each succeed 95% of the time succeeds end to end only about \(0.95^{10} \approx 60\%\) of the time. Shorter workflows, validation between steps, and recovery logic matter (see the table below). Control. The more the model decides, the less predictable the system, and the harder it is to test. Security. Agents read untrusted content and can take actions, which exposes them to prompt injection (Section 5.6). Use least-privilege tools, sandboxed code execution, and human approval for consequential actions. End-to-end success rate, \(p^n\), for \(n\) steps that each succeed with probability \(p\) (independent failures assumed): Per-step success \(p\) 3 steps 5 steps 10 steps 20 steps 99% 97% 95% 90% 82% 95% 86% 77% 60% 36% 90% 73% 59% 35% 12% Real failures are often correlated (one bad search result spoils several later steps), so treat the table as a rough guide. The lesson holds either way: long chains need checks between steps, not only at the end. In short. Every step adds cost and latency; optimize only after the output is good. Errors compound across steps, so validate between steps and keep chains short. Agents read untrusted content and take actions: use least privilege, sandboxes, and human approval. 7.10 Key takeaways The section summaries above hold the details. The chapter in five lines: Why: multi-step workflows trade cost and latency for quality, and often beat a model upgrade. How much autonomy: as little as the task allows; fixed workflows are easier to test and trust than agents. How to design: decompose like an expert would, give exact work to code and tools, and keep the LLM for judgment. What to build with: six building blocks combined through four patterns (reflection, tool use, planning, multi-agent). How to stay in control: evaluate from the first prototype, check between steps, and guard actions that matter. 7.11 Interview checkpoints What makes a workflow “agentic”? It takes multiple steps (model calls, tools, iteration) rather than a single prompt-and-response. Workflow vs. agent? In a workflow, the developer fixes the code paths. In an agent, the model decides its next steps and tool calls at run time. Why can GPT-3.5 in an agentic loop beat GPT-4 used directly on coding tasks? Iteration with feedback (tests, error messages, critique) corrects mistakes that one pass cannot, and that gain can exceed a model-generation upgrade. What does modularity buy you? The ability to replace one component, such as a search engine, retriever, or model, without changing the rest, then measure the effect. What makes an agentic application hard? Unknown steps that need dynamic planning, multimodal inputs, irreversible actions, and open-ended goals. How do you decompose a task? Mirror how an expert works. Check that each step can be done by an LLM, code, or a tool. Split any step that cannot. If each of 8 steps is 90% reliable, what is end-to-end reliability? About \(0.9^8 \approx 43\%\), assuming independent errors. That is why validation and shorter chains matter. Name the four agentic design patterns. Reflection, tool use, planning, and multi-agent collaboration. Generate code → run it → feed the error messages back → fix, repeated until it runs. Which pattern is this? Primarily reflection, with external feedback. Running the code is a tool, but the defining loop is examine-and-revise. When is an agentic workflow unnecessary? When the prompt already holds everything needed and one pass is good enough. For example, writing a product description from given specifications. In a multi-step task, which steps need tools? Those that need information the model lacks (current data, private records) or actions in other systems. Reasoning over material already gathered usually does not. References
