Chapter 9 Tool Use and Code Execution A trained model is frozen at its training cut-off. It does not know today’s date, cannot see your company’s sales table, and cannot send an email. Ask it “what time is it?” and the best it can honestly say is that it does not know. Tool use removes these limits. The developer provides a set of functions (tools) and describes them to the model. The model can then request that one be called. The application runs the function and returns the result, and the model uses it to continue. This chapter explains how that works, how to design tools a model can use well, why code execution is a special tool, and how to run tools safely. 9.1 What a tool is A tool is ordinary code with a name, a description, and typed inputs: Need Tool Example request Current information get_current_time(timezone), web_search(query) “What time is it in Auckland?” Private data query_sales_db(sql) “Which customers bought white sunglasses last month?” Exact computation compound_interest(principal, rate, years) or a code interpreter “What will $500 be worth after 10 years at 5%?” Actions check_calendar(date), create_event(...), delete_event(id) “Find a free slot on Thursday and book a meeting with Alice” The key word is may. Given a set of tools, the model decides whether to use any of them. Asked how much caffeine is in green tea, a model with only a clock tool should answer directly and not call it. This is the difference from the fixed workflows in Chapter 7, where the developer hard-codes “always run a web search here”. With tools, the model makes that decision at run time. A model can chain calls. For the calendar request above: The model calls check_calendar("Thursday"). The application returns the free slots. The model picks 3 pm and calls create_event(...) with Alice as attendee. The application returns a confirmation. The model replies: “Your meeting with Alice is booked for 3 pm Thursday.” Each tool result is appended to the conversation, so the model sees everything that has happened so far when it chooses the next step. In short. A tool is ordinary code with a name, a description, and typed inputs. Tools give the model current information, private data, exact computation, and actions. The model decides at run time whether to call a tool, and can chain calls using earlier results. 9.2 How tool calling works An LLM only generates text. It never executes anything. “The model calls a tool” is shorthand for “the model writes a structured request, and the application calls the tool”. Keeping that distinction in mind explains most of the design and security issues later in this chapter. 9.2.1 The manual protocol Before models were trained for tool use, developers built it with prompting alone. The idea is still the core of every implementation: Describe the tool and an output convention in the system prompt: You can use a tool called get_current_time(timezone), which returns the current time in an IANA timezone such as "America/New_York". To use it, reply with exactly one line: FUNCTION: get_current_time("<timezone>") Otherwise, answer the user directly. Parse the model’s output. If it contains the convention (for example FUNCTION: get_current_time("Pacific/Auckland")), extract the function name and arguments. Execute the function in application code. Append the result to the conversation (“Tool result: 04:12”) and call the model again. Repeat until the model answers instead of requesting a tool. ReAct (Section 5.4.3) is a well-known prompted version of this loop, with interleaved thoughts, actions, and observations. Toolformer (Schick et al. 2023) went a step further and trained a model, in a self-supervised way, to insert API calls (a calculator, a question-answering system, search engines, a translator, a calendar) into its own text where they helped predict what came next. The manual protocol works, but it is fragile. The model may vary the syntax, the parser must handle every variation, and arguments arrive as free text. 9.2.2 Native tool calling Current models are trained to emit tool requests in a structured format, and model APIs accept tool definitions as a separate request parameter. A tool definition is a name, a description, and a JSON Schema for the inputs: { "name": "get_campaign_metrics", "description": "Return daily spend, impressions, clicks, and conversions for one campaign over a date range. Use when the user asks how a specific campaign performed.", "input_schema": { "type": "object", "properties": { "campaign_id": {"type": "string", "description": "Campaign ID, e.g. 'CMP-2041'"}, "start_date": {"type": "string", "format": "date"}, "end_date": {"type": "string", "format": "date"}, "metrics": { "type": "array", "items": {"enum": ["spend", "impressions", "clicks", "conversions"]} } }, "required": ["campaign_id", "start_date", "end_date"] } } The loop is the same as before, but each step is structured: # Illustrative agent loop; the client and message shapes vary by vendor. messages = [{"role": "user", "content": user_question}] for _ in range(MAX_TURNS): # always cap the loop response = client.create(model=MODEL, tools=TOOLS, messages=messages) messages.append(response.message) calls = response.tool_calls # empty if the model answered if not calls: break results = [] for call in calls: # may be several in parallel try: args = validate(call.arguments, TOOLS[call.name]) output = REGISTRY[call.name](**args) results.append(tool_result(call.id, output)) except Exception as err: results.append(tool_result(call.id, str(err), is_error=True)) messages.append(results) # all results in one message final_answer = response.text Points worth noticing: Each call has an ID, and each result refers to it. This is how the model matches results to requests when it makes several calls at once. Errors are returned as results, not swallowed. “Unknown campaign ID CMP-2401; did you mean CMP-2041?” lets the model correct itself. This is reflection with external feedback (Chapter 8). The application validates arguments before running anything. The model produced them, so treat them as untrusted input. The loop has a ceiling (MAX_TURNS) to stop runaway sequences of calls. Well-behaved tasks rarely reach a modest limit such as 5 to 10 turns. Reaching it is a signal worth logging. 9.2.3 Vendor formats The concepts are the same across providers; the field names differ. Concept Anthropic Messages API OpenAI Chat Completions API Tool definition name, description, input_schema type: "function" with function.name, description, parameters Model requests a call tool_use content block (id, name, input); stop_reason: "tool_use" tool_calls list (id, function.name, function.arguments as a JSON string); finish_reason: "tool_calls" Application returns a result tool_result block with tool_use_id, in a user message Message with role: "tool" and tool_call_id Failed tool tool_result with is_error: true Return the error text as the tool message content Common options across vendors: Tool choice. Let the model decide (the usual default), forbid tools for one turn, or require a tool call. Some recent models reject forced tool choice, so check the documentation. Parallel calls. The model may request several independent calls in one turn, such as metrics for three campaigns. Run them concurrently and return all results together. Strict schemas. A strict mode constrains the model’s arguments to validate against the schema exactly. Hosted tools. Some tools, such as web search and code execution, can run on the provider’s infrastructure, so the application does not execute them. Helper libraries hide much of this. SDK “tool runners” and multi-provider wrappers such as the open-source aisuite package build the JSON schema from a Python function’s signature and docstring, and run the loop for you. They are convenient, but it pays to know what they do underneath when something goes wrong. Here is what such a library does with a plain Python function. Every part of the schema comes from something you wrote: def get_campaign_metrics(campaign_id: str, start_date: str, end_date: str, metrics: list[str] | None = None) -> dict: """Return daily metrics for one campaign over a date range. Use when the user asks how a specific campaign performed. Args: campaign_id: Campaign ID, e.g. 'CMP-2041'. start_date: First day, ISO format (YYYY-MM-DD). end_date: Last day, ISO format (YYYY-MM-DD). metrics: Which metrics to return; all if omitted. """ ... { "name": "get_campaign_metrics", // the function name "description": "Return daily metrics for one campaign over a date range. Use when the user asks how a specific campaign performed.", // the docstring summary "input_schema": { "type": "object", "properties": { "campaign_id": {"type": "string", "description": "Campaign ID, e.g. 'CMP-2041'."}, // type hint + Args line "start_date": {"type": "string", "description": "First day, ISO format (YYYY-MM-DD)."}, "end_date": {"type": "string", "description": "Last day, ISO format (YYYY-MM-DD)."}, "metrics": {"type": "array", "items": {"type": "string"}, "description": "Which metrics to return; all if omitted."} }, "required": ["campaign_id", "start_date", "end_date"] // parameters without a default } } (The // comments are annotations for the reader; real JSON has no comments.) Two consequences follow. The docstring is the tool description the model reads, so write it for the model. And anything the type hints cannot express, such as the allowed metric names, is lost unless you add it, for example with an enum in a hand-written schema or a Literal type hint. Current practice (October 2026). Native tool calling is supported by all major model providers. Raw text-parsing protocols survive mainly in teaching and in very small open models. OpenAI’s newer Responses API (2025) represents calls and results as separate items (function_call and function_call_output, linked by a call_id) rather than chat messages; the concepts in the table are unchanged. Field names and options still change between API versions, so check the vendor documentation before relying on a specific parameter. In short. The model only writes a structured request; the application validates and runs the tool, then returns the result. Native tool calling uses a JSON Schema per tool, call IDs, and results tied to those IDs. Errors go back as results. Libraries build the schema from a function’s signature and docstring, so the docstring is effectively a prompt. Always cap the loop. 9.3 Designing tools a model can use well The model sees only a tool’s name, description, and schema. These are effectively a prompt, and they deserve the same care. Schluntz and Zhang (2024) call this designing the agent–computer interface, and they recommend investing in it as much as in a human–computer interface. Say what the tool does and when to use it. “Use when the user asks how a specific campaign performed” helps the model choose between similar tools. Use clear, distinct names. get_campaign_metrics and get_account_metrics are clear. fetch_data and get_data are not. Narrow the inputs. Prefer enums, IDs, and dates to free text. A query_sales_db(sql) tool is flexible but risky; top_products(month, metric, n) is safer and easier for the model to use correctly. Make mistakes hard. Require absolute rather than relative file paths. Validate dates. Reject impossible combinations with a helpful message. Return concise, readable results. Return the 20 rows that matter with column names, not a 50,000-row dump that floods the context window. Summarize or paginate large outputs. Write useful error messages. Say what was wrong and how to fix it. Separate reading from writing. Read-only tools can run freely. Tools that change state (send, delete, pay, update) should be distinct, narrowly scoped, and often gated by human approval. Prefer a few well-scoped tools to many overlapping ones. Each extra tool is one more choice the model can get wrong, and one more description in the context. Example: the same tool, before and after. Before After Name get_data top_products Description “Gets data from the database.” “Return the top N products for one month, ranked by revenue or units. Use for ‘best-selling’ or ‘top products’ questions. For a single product’s history, use product_sales instead.” Inputs sql: string month: string (YYYY-MM), metric: enum [revenue, units], n: integer, 1–50, default 10 Output All matching rows, raw Up to n rows with product name, metric value, and rank Error Database stack trace “Month ‘2026-13’ is invalid; use YYYY-MM, e.g. ‘2026-03’.” The “after” version tells the model when to use it, points to the alternative, cannot run arbitrary SQL, and fails with a message the model can act on. Test tools the way a user would: give the model realistic requests and read which tools it calls, with what arguments, and where it gets confused. In short. The name, description, and schema are all the model sees: treat them as a prompt. Say when to use each tool, narrow the inputs, return concise results, and write errors the model can act on. Keep read and write tools separate, and prefer a few clear tools to many overlapping ones. 9.4 Code execution: the general-purpose tool Suppose a math assistant has tools for add, subtract, multiply, and divide. Then a user asks for a square root, then a logarithm, then a loan amortization schedule. Writing one tool per button of a scientific calculator does not scale. The alternative is a single tool: let the model write code, and run it. Code can do arithmetic, statistics, data manipulation, date handling, string processing, and file conversion. One tool covers an open-ended range of tasks. A manual version looks like this: Prompt: “Write Python code that answers the user’s question. Put it between <execute_python> and </execute_python> tags and print the result.” Extract the code between the tags (for example with a regular expression). Run it and capture standard output and errors. Return the output to the model, which writes the final answer. For the question “What will $500 be worth after 10 years at 5%, compounded monthly?”, the model’s reply and the application’s extraction step look like this: <execute_python> principal, rate, years = 500, 0.05, 10 value = principal * (1 + rate / 12) ** (12 * years) print(round(value, 2)) </execute_python> import re match = re.search(r"<execute_python>(.*?)</execute_python>", reply, re.DOTALL) code = match.group(1) if match else None output = run_in_sandbox(code, timeout_seconds=10) # see the next section # output == "823.5"; the model then writes: "About $823.50." The model never does the arithmetic itself, so it cannot get it slightly wrong. Its only job is to write a correct formula. If the code fails, return the error message and let the model fix it, with a cap on attempts. This is reflection with external feedback again. This idea has a research lineage. PAL (Section 5.4.2) had the model express its reasoning as a program so that an interpreter, not the model, did the arithmetic. Section 11.1.5 takes it further, with code as the plan itself. In practice, model providers now offer a hosted code-execution tool, and coding agents run code as a matter of course. Model developers put considerable effort into making code generation and execution work well, because it is so useful. 9.4.1 Running generated code safely Running code that a model wrote means running code that nobody reviewed. Most generated code is harmless, and many developers run it without much checking. The failures are rare but costly: Destructive actions. A coding agent asked to “clean up” can delete files that matter. With version control the damage is recoverable; without it, it may not be. Data leakage. Code can read environment variables, credentials, or private files and send them over the network. Resource exhaustion. Infinite loops, huge allocations, or fork bombs. Injected instructions. If the model has read untrusted content, such as a web page or an email, an attacker’s text can steer the code it writes (Greshake et al. 2023). Python’s built-in exec() runs code inside your own process, with all of your permissions. It is acceptable for a quick local experiment and nothing more. The best practice is a sandbox: Control Purpose Isolated environment (a container such as Docker, a micro-VM sandbox, or a provider-hosted execution tool) Code cannot touch the host system No network, or an allowlist Prevents data exfiltration and unexpected downloads No secrets in the environment Nothing valuable to steal Read-only or temporary file mounts Limits what can be changed or deleted CPU, memory, and time limits Stops runaway code Fresh environment per task No state leaks between users or tasks Human approval for destructive operations Final check on actions that cannot be undone Hosted sandbox services (E2B is one example) provide lightweight isolated environments built for this purpose. On your own machine, a container with the controls from the table takes one command (illustrative): docker run --rm --network none --memory 512m --cpus 1 \ --read-only --tmpfs /tmp -v "$PWD/task:/work:ro" \ python:3.12-slim timeout 30 python /work/generated.py That gives no network, capped memory and CPU, a read-only file system with scratch space in /tmp, the task folder mounted read-only, a 30-second time limit, and a fresh container that is deleted afterwards (--rm). No secrets are passed in. In short. Code execution is the most general tool: one tool covers an open-ended range of computation. The model writes the code; an interpreter does the exact work. Errors go back to the model to fix. Model-written code is unreviewed code: run it in a sandbox with no network, no secrets, resource limits, and a fresh environment. 9.5 Connecting to many tools: MCP So far each tool was written by hand for one application. Many teams were writing the same wrappers: one for Slack, one for Google Drive, one for GitHub, one for a Postgres database, again and again. With M applications and N systems, that is roughly M × N integrations. The Model Context Protocol (MCP), introduced by Anthropic and now widely adopted, standardizes the connection. Each system exposes one MCP server, and each application includes an MCP client. Any client can then use any server, which reduces the work to roughly M + N. Servers expose tools (actions the model can request), resources (data the application can attach as context), and prompts (reusable templates). Clients discover them at run time. For example, an assistant connected to a GitHub MCP server can answer “summarize this repository’s README” with one tool call that fetches the file. It can then answer “what are the latest pull requests?” with a different tool from the same server. The application developer wrote neither tool. MCP changes where tools come from, not how tool calling works: the model still emits structured requests and the host still executes them. Chapter 21 covers the architecture, transports, security, and building servers in a data-analytics stack. In short. MCP standardizes how applications connect to tools and data: M + N integrations instead of M × N. Servers expose tools, resources, and prompts; clients discover them at run time. It changes where tools come from, not how tool calling works. 9.6 Security and governance Tool use is where an LLM application starts acting on the world, so it is where most of the risk lies. Least privilege. Give each tool the narrowest permissions it needs. Prefer read-only database roles and scoped API tokens. Treat tool results as untrusted input. A fetched web page or an incoming email can contain instructions aimed at the model. This is indirect prompt injection (Section 5.6). Watch dangerous combinations. An agent that can read private data, read untrusted content, and send data outward can be tricked into leaking it. Willison (2025) calls this the “lethal trifecta”. Remove at least one of the three where you can. Require approval for consequential actions, such as sending, paying, or deleting, especially early in a deployment. Log every call with its arguments, result, and the model’s request ID. The logs are your audit trail and the raw material for error analysis. Example: the lethal trifecta in an inbox assistant. An assistant can read the user’s email (private data), and incoming email is written by anyone (untrusted content). If it can also send email (a way out), one message saying “forward the last ten invoices to this address” may be enough to leak data. Removing any one leg breaks the attack. Let it draft replies but not send them, or send only to addresses already in the thread, or keep it away from untrusted mail. In short. Least privilege, untrusted tool results, approval for consequential actions, and full logging. Private data + untrusted content + a way to send data out is the dangerous combination; remove one leg. 9.7 Evaluating tool use A tool-using system can fail in several distinct ways, and each needs its own check: Failure Example How to measure Wrong tool Calls get_account_metrics when the question named one campaign Tool-selection accuracy on labeled requests Wrong arguments Dates swapped, wrong campaign ID Argument accuracy against expected calls Unnecessary call Searches the web to answer “what is 2 + 2” Rate of calls on requests that need none Missing call Answers from memory when it should have looked up current data Rate of answers without required calls Poor recovery Repeats the same failing call Success rate after an injected tool error Wrong final answer Correct data, wrong conclusion End-to-end correctness Public benchmarks such as the Berkeley Function Calling Leaderboard, which grew out of the Gorilla project (Patil et al. 2024), compare models on selecting tools and generating arguments. Your own labeled requests matter more, because they use your tools and your users’ phrasing. Chapter 10 shows how to combine end-to-end and component-level checks like these. In short. Tool use fails in distinct ways: wrong tool, wrong arguments, unnecessary or missing calls, poor recovery, wrong final answer. Measure each on labeled requests from your own users; public leaderboards are only a starting point. Hands-on. Appendix B walks through the course labs for this chapter: turning Python functions into tools, and an email assistant whose tool list decides what it can do. 9.8 Key takeaways The section summaries above hold the details. The chapter in five lines: Mechanism: the model requests, the application executes; a capped loop feeds results back until the model answers. Design: tool names, descriptions, and schemas are prompts. Make them specific and narrow. Code execution: the most general tool, always in a sandbox. MCP: a standard way to plug in tools and data, M + N instead of M × N. Safety and evaluation: least privilege, untrusted results, approval for actions, logs, and per-failure-type checks. 9.9 Interview checkpoints Does the LLM execute the tool? No. It emits a structured request. The application validates the arguments, executes the function, and returns the result. How did tool use work before native function calling? The prompt described the tools and an output convention. The application parsed the text, ran the function, and appended the result. ReAct is the best-known example. What goes into a tool definition? A name, a description of what it does and when to use it, and a JSON Schema for the inputs. Why return tool errors to the model instead of raising them? The model can read a clear error message and correct its call. This is reflection with external feedback. The model requests three tool calls in one turn. What do you do? Run them, concurrently if they are independent, and return all three results, each tied to its call ID, in the next message. Why give a model code execution instead of many small tools? Code covers an open-ended range of computations with one tool. Writing a separate tool for every operation does not scale. What are the risks of executing model-written code, and how do you reduce them? Destructive actions, data leakage, runaway resource use, and injected instructions. Use a sandbox with no secrets, a network allowlist, resource limits, and a fresh environment per task. Require approval for destructive steps. What problem does MCP solve? It replaces M × N custom integrations with M + N: servers expose tools, resources, and prompts once, and any compliant client can use them. What makes a good tool description? It says what the tool does and when to use it, distinguishes it from similar tools, and documents each parameter with formats and examples. How do you evaluate a tool-using agent? Check tool selection, argument accuracy, unnecessary and missing calls, error recovery, and end-to-end correctness, each on labeled examples. References

Chapter 10 Evaluating and Improving Agentic Systems An agentic system has many parts: prompts, models, retrievers, tools, and the code that connects them. When it does not work well enough, which is most of the time during development, almost any part could be to blame. Teams that improve quickly differ from teams that stall mainly in how they decide what to work on next. In Andrew Ng’s experience, a disciplined process of evaluation and error analysis is one of the strongest predictors of how effective a team will be. This chapter covers that process: build a quick prototype and look at its outputs; turn recurring problems into end-to-end evals; read traces and run error analysis to find the component responsible; build component-level evals to improve that component efficiently; and once quality is good enough, optimize cost and latency. The reflection chapter (Section 8.7) used a small version of this process to decide whether a reflection step was worth keeping. Here it becomes a general method. 10.1 Build first, then look It is hard to predict where an agentic system will fail. Weeks of up-front design often guess wrong. The more productive approach is to build a quick, safe prototype, one that does not leak data or take irreversible actions, and then read its outputs. Take 10 to 20 realistic inputs, run them, and note what is wrong with each output in a spreadsheet. Patterns appear quickly: An invoice-processing workflow keeps extracting the issue date when the task needs the due date. An ad-copy assistant writes good headlines, but many exceed the 30-character headline limit of Google search ads. A campaign-insights agent writes fluent summaries but sometimes misses the point a senior analyst would lead with, such as a budget overspend. Each observation leads to one of two actions. If the fix is obvious, such as a missing instruction, just fix it. If improving it will take sustained iteration, build an eval for that problem so you can measure progress. Looking at outputs also tells you what to evaluate. You cannot write a good rubric before seeing how the system fails. Shankar et al. (2024) call this criteria drift: people need criteria to grade outputs, but grading outputs is how they discover their criteria. Expect your evals to change as you learn. In short. You cannot predict the failures; build a safe prototype and read 10–20 outputs. Fix obvious problems directly; build an eval for anything that needs sustained work. Criteria come from reading outputs, so expect them to change. 10.2 End-to-end evals An end-to-end eval measures the final output for a given input, treating the whole system as one unit. End-to-end evals differ along two axes: Who grades: code (objective checks) or an LLM judge (subjective judgments). What the output is compared with: a per-example reference (each input has its own correct answer or key points) or a shared criterion (the same rule applies to every example). Per-example reference Shared criterion Code grades Invoice due date matches the labeled date Headline is at most 30 characters; output is valid JSON; no competitor names LLM judge grades Report mentions the 3–5 key points an expert listed for this question Chart passes a rubric (title, axis labels, chart type); reply has a professional tone 10.2.1 Code-graded evals Prefer code whenever the criterion is objective. It is cheap, fast, and deterministic. Make outputs easy to check: if the prompt tells the model to write dates as YYYY-MM-DD, a few lines of code can grade them. import re def due_date_correct(output: str, label: str) -> bool: """Compare the first ISO date in the model output with the labeled due date.""" match = re.search(r"\d{4}-\d{2}-\d{2}", output) return bool(match) and match.group() == label accuracy = sum(due_date_correct(o, y) for o, y in zip(outputs, labels)) / len(labels) For the ad-copy example there is no per-example label; the check is simply len(headline) <= 30 for every output. 10.2.2 LLM-judged evals When the criterion needs reading comprehension, use an LLM judge. Suppose that for each question in the campaign-insights eval set, an analyst has written the three to five points a good answer must cover. Key points can be phrased in many ways, so string matching fails, but a judge can count them: You are grading a campaign-performance summary. <question>{question}</question> <key_points>{expert_key_points}</key_points> <summary>{agent_output}</summary> For each key point, decide whether the summary states it clearly (paraphrase is fine). Return JSON: {"explanation": "<one line per key point>", "points_covered": <integer>} Asking for the explanation before the score makes the judge commit to its reasoning first, and the explanation is what you read when the score looks wrong. 10.2.3 Making LLM judges trustworthy LLM judges have known biases, including position bias, a preference for longer answers, and a preference for their own outputs (Zheng et al. 2023). The fine-tuning chapter introduced them (Section 3.6.3), and the reflection chapter showed how position bias can reverse direction. Practical defenses: Grade one output at a time against a rubric of specific yes/no criteria, instead of asking which of two outputs is better. Give the judge references (key points, a correct answer, the source document) whenever you have them. If you must compare pairs, evaluate both orders and count only consistent verdicts. Use a different model family as judge from the one that generated the outputs, to reduce self-preference. Validate the judge against human labels. Have a person grade 50 to 100 examples and measure agreement with the judge. Raw agreement can look high when most outputs pass, so also report Cohen’s kappa, which corrects for agreement expected by chance (Cohen 1960). Re-check whenever the judge prompt or model changes. Example: why raw agreement misleads. A person and a judge each grade 100 replies. Each passes 90 of them, and they agree on 90 (85 both pass, 5 both fail). Raw agreement is 90%, which sounds excellent. But two graders who pass 90% of replies at random would agree \(0.9 \times 0.9 + 0.1 \times 0.1 = 82\%\) of the time. Kappa measures agreement beyond that baseline: \[ \kappa = \frac{p_o - p_e}{1 - p_e} = \frac{0.90 - 0.82}{1 - 0.82} \approx 0.44 \] That is only moderate agreement. The judge agrees with the person mostly because almost everything passes. It catches only half of the 10 failures the person found, and those failures are what the eval exists to find. 10.2.4 Start small, then grow the set Teams sometimes delay evals because they imagine a multi-week project. A first eval with 10 to 20 examples and a simple metric is far better than none. Use it alongside reading outputs, not instead of it. As the eval grows and proves reliable, you can trust the metric more and read fewer outputs after each change. Improve the eval as you go: When the metric disagrees with your judgment, such as when you are sure a change helped but the score did not move, treat that as a bug in the eval. Add examples or change how outputs are graded. Add examples from real failures, edge cases, and inputs where the system falls short of an expert. For tasks that people already do, places where the system is worse than a skilled human are the best guide to what to improve. Keep a held-out set. If you tune prompts against the same 20 examples for weeks, you will overfit to them, just as with training data in machine learning. Check the final configuration on examples you did not tune on. 10.2.5 How much should you trust a score? An eval score is an estimate from a sample, so it has sampling error. For an accuracy \(\hat p\) measured on \(n\) independent examples, the standard error is \(\sqrt{\hat p (1 - \hat p) / n}\). At \(\hat p = 0.8\): Examples (\(n\)) Standard error Approximate 95% interval 20 8.9 points 80% ± 17.5 points 100 4.0 points 80% ± 7.8 points 400 2.0 points 80% ± 3.9 points A 20-example eval is good for catching large regressions and for guiding early work. It cannot distinguish 80% from 85%. Miller (2024) sets out a statistical approach to model evals that applies directly here: Report standard errors with every score. Use clustered standard errors when examples come in related groups, such as several questions about the same campaign. Analyze paired differences when comparing two systems on the same examples. The question-level comparison is far more precise than comparing two overall accuracies (McNemar’s test is the binary case). Reduce variance by resampling. Run each example several times when outputs are non-deterministic and average the results. For agents that users run repeatedly, also report how often all of \(k\) runs succeed (pass^k, Section 22.5.5). Do a power analysis before concluding that a change made no difference. The eval may simply be too small to detect it. In short. End-to-end evals have two axes: code or LLM judge, per-example reference or shared criterion. Use code whenever the criterion is objective. Trust a judge only after checking it against human labels, with kappa, not just raw agreement. Start with 10–20 examples, grow from real failures, keep a held-out set, and report error bars. 10.3 Traces and spans End-to-end evals tell you that something is wrong, not where. For that, you need the trace: the record of everything the system did for one input. The terms come from software observability. In OpenTelemetry, a trace is the path of one request through an application, and a span is one unit of work within it, with its own timing and attributes (OpenTelemetry Authors 2024). In an agentic system, each LLM call, tool call, or retrieval step is a span. For each span, log at least: its inputs and outputs (the full prompt and completion for LLM calls); the model, prompt version, and parameters; tool names, arguments, results, and errors; tokens, latency, and cost. A trace for one run of the campaign-insights agent might look like this (simplified): trace q-0117 "Why did CPA rise on Search last week?" total 27.4 s $0.07 ├─ span interpret_question llm 2.1 s in 1,200 tok out 150 tok │ output: {"channel": "Search", "metric": "CPA", "period": "2026-10-12..18"} ├─ span write_sql llm 3.8 s in 2,900 tok out 240 tok │ output: SELECT ... WHERE order_date BETWEEN '2026-10-12' AND '2026-10-18' ├─ span run_query tool 9.3 s rows 14 └─ span write_narrative llm 12.2 s in 6,400 tok out 610 tok output: "CPA on Search rose 18%, driven by ..." Reading it, an analyst would spot that the SQL filters on order_date when the metric needs the conversion date. Nothing in the final narrative reveals that; only the trace does. The habit that matters most is simple: read traces regularly, not only when something breaks. Many tools exist to collect and browse traces. On Databricks, for example, MLflow Tracing records agent runs and connects to MLflow’s evaluation tooling (Chapter 22). In short. A trace is the record of one run; a span is one step in it. Log inputs, outputs, versions, tool calls, tokens, latency, and cost for every span. Read traces regularly; they show failures the final output hides. 10.4 Error analysis Error analysis is the systematic reading of traces for examples where the system failed, in order to find which component is responsible. Consider a campaign-insights agent with four steps: interpret the question, write SQL, run the query on the warehouse, and write the narrative. The end-to-end eval shows that summaries often miss key points. Any step could be the cause. The question might be misread, the SQL might filter the wrong dates, the warehouse might hold stale data, or the writer might ignore a number it was given. Picking a component by gut feeling sometimes works. It also sometimes leads to months of work on a part that was never the problem. 10.4.1 The procedure Collect failures. Set aside the examples the system got right. Gather 10 to 100 examples where the final output was unsatisfactory. Walk each trace step by step. For each component, ask: given the input this component received, is its output clearly worse than what a skilled person would produce? Blame a component only for its own work. If the query returned stale data, the writer cannot be faulted for reporting it. The writer did as well as anyone could with what it was given. Record the judgment in a spreadsheet, one row per failed example and one column per component, with a short note. Count. For each component, compute the share of failed examples in which it erred. An illustrative result for 20 failed examples: Example Interpret question Write SQL Warehouse data Write narrative Note 1 ✗ Filtered on order date instead of conversion date 2 ✗ ✗ Wrong join; summary also buried the main result 3 ✗ Yesterday’s spend not loaded … Share of failures 10% 60% 10% 35% The shares add up to more than 100% because one example can have errors in several components. 10.4.2 From counts to priorities The counts are evidence, not a decision. Prioritize a component when: it causes a large share of failures; you have concrete ideas for improving it; and those ideas are affordable in time and cost. Here, SQL generation is the clear first target, and the narrative step comes second. Remember that the shares are fractions of failures. If 30% of outputs fail overall and SQL errors appear in 60% of those, eliminating SQL errors entirely would cut the failure rate by at most 18 percentage points. That is an upper bound, because some of those examples also have other errors. A related check from classic machine learning practice is ceiling analysis: substitute a correct output for one component (for example, hand-written SQL) and measure how much the end-to-end score rises. That tells you how much fixing the component could ever be worth. The same procedure applies to simpler workflows. For the invoice workflow, the question is whether the PDF-to-text step garbled the dates (so that even a person could not read them from its output) or whether the LLM picked the wrong date from clean text. If the LLM step accounts for most errors, weeks spent tuning the PDF converter would be wasted. In a research agent, the usual culprit is search: when the sources are poor, the writing step cannot recover, and a component eval on search (Section 10.5) is the right next step. Starting the categories. If you do not yet know which failure types to count, write a free-text note for each failed example first. Then group the notes into categories and count those. The categories usually map onto components or onto specific behaviors, such as “ignored date filter” or “invented a metric”, that can each become an eval. In short. Read the traces of failed examples and blame each component only for its own output, given its input. Count the share of failures per component; the shares can sum past 100%. Prioritize components that cause many failures and that you know how to improve. Ceiling analysis bounds the gain. 10.5 Component-level evals Once error analysis has pointed to a component, improving it by rerunning the full system after every change is slow and expensive. It is also noisy: randomness in the other components can hide a small real improvement. A component-level eval measures that one component directly. It also lets work split cleanly: the team that owns search can iterate against its own metric without waiting for, or being confused by, changes elsewhere in the pipeline. Example: retrieval or web search. For a set of queries, have an expert list the sources a good search should find. Then score each configuration on how well its results match: Precision: the fraction of returned results that are relevant. Recall: the fraction of relevant results that were returned. F1: the harmonic mean of the two, \(2PR/(P+R)\). For one query, suppose the expert lists 5 sources and the search returns 8 results, 3 of which are on the expert’s list. Precision is \(3/8 = 0.375\), recall is \(3/5 = 0.6\), and F1 is \(2 \times 0.375 \times 0.6 / 0.975 \approx 0.46\). Average these over the query set to score a configuration. Ranked variants such as precision@k and recall@k are standard in information retrieval (Manning et al. 2008). With this eval you can quickly compare search providers, the number of results, date ranges, or chunking strategies. Example: SQL generation. Compare the result of the generated query with the result of a reference query, not the SQL text. Many different queries are correct. Example: tool use. Measure tool-selection and argument accuracy on labeled requests (Section 9.7). Component evals have one danger: a component metric can improve while the end-to-end result does not, because the metric does not capture what downstream steps need. Always confirm with the end-to-end eval before declaring a component improvement done. In short. A component eval measures one step directly: faster, cheaper, and less noisy than rerunning the whole system. Retrieval: precision, recall, F1 against expert-chosen sources. SQL: compare query results, not query text. Confirm every component gain end to end. 10.6 Improving a component Non-LLM components (search engines, retrievers, OCR, classifiers) usually have settings to tune or alternatives to swap: web search: the provider, number of results, date range, domain filters; retrieval (Section 5.3): chunk size, embedding model, similarity threshold, number of chunks; a detector or classifier: the decision threshold, which trades false positives against false negatives. LLM components have a standard ladder of options, roughly from cheapest to most expensive: Improve the prompt. Add explicit instructions, context, and a few input–output examples (Chapter 6). Try a different model. Use your evals to choose. A multi-provider interface makes this cheap to test. Decompose the step. A prompt with many instructions may be too much for one call. Split it into two or three simpler calls (Chapter 7), or add a reflection step (Chapter 8). Fine-tune. Fine-tuning can add the last few points on a mature system with enough labeled data, but it costs the most development time (Chapter 3). Try the cheaper options first. 10.6.1 Building intuition about models Choosing models well is faster when you have a feel for what each one is good at. Models differ: some are stronger at coding, some at following long instructions, some at particular domains, and they differ in price and speed. Smaller models often answer simple factual questions well but follow complex, multi-part instructions less reliably. Benchmarks of verifiable instructions, such as IFEval’s “write more than 400 words” or “mention a keyword at least three times”, measure this ability with code (J. Zhou et al. 2023). Consider redacting personal information from customer-call summaries before analysis. A capable model removes every name, address, and account number, and returns exactly the requested format. A weaker model may miss a name, redact an address only partly, or add a list nobody asked for. You can catch this with a component eval: label the personal-information spans in 50 summaries and check, in code, that none survive. Ways to build this intuition: Try new models when they are released, on a small personal set of prompts that you reuse across models. Read other people’s prompts, including those in respected open-source projects, to learn what instructions models follow well. Swap models within your own workflows and compare them with traces and evals, noting quality, price, and speed. In short. Non-LLM components: tune settings or swap providers. LLM components, cheapest first: better prompt, different model, decompose or add reflection, fine-tune last. Build model intuition by testing new models on your own small prompt set. 10.7 Cost and latency Get output quality right first. It is usually the hardest part, and a fast, cheap system that gives wrong answers has no value. Once quality is acceptable, and especially once usage grows, cost and latency start to matter. The method mirrors error analysis: measure each step, then optimize the steps that dominate. Steps are billed in different ways: LLM calls are billed per token, input and output priced separately. External APIs (search, data providers, PDF conversion) are usually billed per call or per page. Compute (a warehouse query, a code sandbox, a self-hosted model) is billed by capacity used, such as seconds of compute or server hours. An illustrative breakdown for one run of the campaign-insights agent, with one extra step that pulls competitor benchmarks from a paid data API. The dollar figures are made up for the example, not real prices: Step Billing basis Latency Cost per run Interpret question (small LLM) Per token 2 s $0.001 Write SQL (mid-size LLM, schema in prompt) Per token 4 s $0.010 Run query (warehouse) Compute time 9 s $0.015 Pull competitor benchmarks (paid data API) Per call 3 s $0.080 Write narrative (strong LLM, long context) Per token 12 s $0.060 Total 30 s $0.166 Two lessons. For latency, speeding up the interpretation step barely matters; the narrative and the query are the targets. As Amdahl’s law says, the overall speed-up is limited by the share of time spent in the part you improve. For cost, the single API call costs more than all three LLM steps together ($0.071). Switching to a cheaper model would barely help; caching benchmark results, or calling the API only when the question needs it, would. Only measuring each step shows this. Levers for latency: run independent steps in parallel, such as several searches or fetches; use a smaller or faster model for a step, if its eval still passes; try a faster serving provider for the same model; stream the final output so users see progress; and trim context, because long prompts take longer to process. Levers for cost: a cheaper model for steps that do not need the strongest one; prompt caching for long, repeated prefixes such as instructions and tool definitions; batch APIs for work that does not need an immediate answer; fewer tokens: shorter prompts, concise tool results, capped loops; and cheaper tools or plans where per-call API fees dominate. Measuring often shows that some steps are not worth optimizing at all. In short. Quality first; then measure latency and cost per step and work on the steps that dominate. LLMs bill per token, APIs per call, compute by capacity. A non-LLM step can be the most expensive one. Latency: parallelize, smaller models, faster providers, trimmed context, streaming. Cost: cheaper models, caching, batching, fewer tokens. 10.8 The build–analyze loop Developing an agentic system alternates between two activities: building (writing code, prompts, and tools) and analyzing (reading outputs and traces, running evals and error analysis). Analysis can feel like it is not progress, but it is what makes the building effective. Less experienced teams tend to spend too much time building and too little analyzing. The analysis becomes more rigorous as the system matures: Stage Analysis Prototype Read final outputs and a few traces; fix obvious problems Early Small end-to-end evals (10–20 examples) on the problems you found Maturing Systematic error analysis: count which components cause failures Mature Component-level evals for the parts you are actively improving; larger, held-out end-to-end evals with error bars The process is not linear. You will move back and forth between tuning the whole system, analyzing errors, and improving single components. Current practice (October 2026). Many platforms record traces, run evals, and track cost: open-source and commercial LLM observability tools, MLflow on Databricks, and the providers’ own consoles. They save engineering time. However, most agentic workflows are custom, so the most useful evals are usually the ones you write for the specific failures you found in your own error analysis. In short. Development alternates between building and analyzing; most teams under-invest in analysis. The analysis grows with the system: read outputs, small evals, error analysis, then component evals and larger held-out sets. Hands-on. Appendix B walks through the course lab for this chapter: a component-level eval that scores the search step of a research agent by the domains of its sources. 10.9 Key takeaways The section summaries above hold the details. The chapter in five lines: Look first: build a safe prototype and read outputs; failures tell you what to evaluate. Measure the whole: end-to-end evals graded by code where possible, by validated LLM judges otherwise, with error bars. Find the cause: read traces of failures and count which component is to blame. Fix the part: component evals to iterate fast, the cheapest fix first, then confirm end to end. Then optimize: cost and latency per step, after quality is good. 10.10 Interview checkpoints You built an agent and it is not good enough. What do you do first? Run it on realistic inputs, read the outputs and traces, and note the recurring failures. Fix the obvious ones; build evals for the rest. Describe the two axes of end-to-end evals, with an example in each quadrant. Code vs. LLM judge, and per-example reference vs. shared criterion. Examples: extracted date vs. label (code, reference); length limit (code, shared); key points covered (judge, reference); chart rubric (judge, shared). When would you use an LLM judge instead of code? When the criterion requires understanding language, such as whether a point was made in different words, or tone. Use code for anything objective. How do you know an LLM judge is reliable? Compare it with human labels on a sample. Report agreement and Cohen’s kappa, and re-check after changing the judge prompt or model. What is a trace? What is a span? A trace is the full record of one run through the system. A span is one step within it, such as an LLM call or a tool call, with its inputs, outputs, and timing. Walk through error analysis. Collect failed examples, step through each trace, mark the components whose output was clearly worse than an expert’s given the same input, and count the share of failures per component. Why don’t the error-analysis percentages sum to 100%? One failed example can have errors in more than one component. The search step returned poor sources, and the selection step picked the best of them. Is selection at fault? No. It did as well as possible with its input. The fault lies with search. What is a component-level eval, and why use one? It measures one component directly, for example retrieval precision and recall against expert-chosen sources. It is faster, cheaper, and less noisy than rerunning the whole system. Confirm the gains end to end. Your eval has 20 examples, and a change moved accuracy from 80% to 85%. Did it help? You cannot tell. The 95% interval at \(n = 20\) is about ±17 points. Look at paired differences on the same examples, add examples, and run repeated trials if outputs vary. Your metric says no improvement, but you are sure the new version is better. What now? Treat it as a problem with the eval. Inspect the examples, add cases that capture the difference, or change the grading. What options do you have to improve an LLM component? Better prompts and examples, a different model, decomposition or reflection, and fine-tuning as the last resort. How do you reduce latency in an agentic workflow? Time each step, then parallelize independent steps, use smaller or faster models where evals allow, choose faster providers, trim context, and stream the output. When should you optimize cost? After quality is acceptable. Measure the cost of each step and target the dominant ones with cheaper models, caching, batching, and fewer tokens. References

Chapter 11 Planning and Multi-Agent Systems In the workflows so far, the developer decided the sequence of steps. Even with tools, the model chose only which tool to call next, inside a loop the developer wrote. This chapter covers two patterns that hand more of the design to the model: Planning: the model decides the sequence of steps for each request, then the system carries it out. Multi-agent collaboration: several role-specialized agents work on parts of a task and communicate with each other. Both extend what a system can do without the developer anticipating every case. Both also make it harder to predict and control what the system will do. That trade-off runs through the whole chapter. 11.1 Planning 11.1.1 Why let the model plan? Consider a customer-service agent for a sporting-goods store with these tools: Tool Purpose search_products(description) Find products matching a description check_inventory(sku, size) Stock level for one product and size get_price(sku) Current price get_order_history(customer_id) Past purchases process_return(order_id, sku) Start a return process_sale(sku, size, customer_id) Place an order “Do you have waterproof trail-running shoes in size 10 under $120?” needs three tools in a particular order: search for waterproof trail shoes, check which are in stock in size 10, then check prices. “I want to return the blue jacket from my last order, but keep the gloves” needs a different sequence: order history, product details to identify the blue jacket, then a return. Hard-coding a workflow for every kind of request is impossible. With planning, the model writes the sequence for each request at run time. 11.1.2 Plan, then execute The simplest planning design has two phases: Plan. Give the model the tools’ descriptions and the user’s request. Ask it to return a step-by-step plan. Execute. Carry out the plan one step at a time. For each step, call the model with the step’s instructions, the original request, the tools, and the outputs of earlier steps. The model makes the tool call for that step. Answer. After the last step, the model writes the response from the accumulated results. request ──► planner LLM ──► [step 1, step 2, step 3] │ step 1 + context ──► LLM ──► tool ──► result 1 step 2 + context + result 1 ──► LLM ──► tool ──► result 2 step 3 + context + results ──► LLM ──► tool ──► result 3 │ all results ──► LLM ──► final answer For reasoning without tools, Plan-and-Solve prompting (L. Wang et al. 2023) showed the same idea in a single prompt: asking the model to first devise a plan and then carry it out reduced missed steps compared with plain “think step by step” prompting. HuggingGPT (Shen et al. 2023) applied planning to tool selection, having an LLM plan which specialist models to call for a multi-part request (Chapter 7). 11.1.3 Plan up front or step by step? ReAct (Section 5.4.3) interleaves the two phases: think, act, observe, and decide the next step only after seeing the last result. The choice matters. In the shoe example, an up-front plan assumes step 1 finds candidates. If no waterproof trail shoe is in stock in size 10, the remaining steps are pointless; an interleaved agent would notice and suggest the nearest alternative, and a replanning agent would rewrite the rest of the plan. Approach How it works Strengths Weaknesses Plan up front Write the whole plan, then execute it The plan can be inspected, validated, or approved before anything runs; independent steps can run in parallel; fewer planning calls Breaks when an early result changes what is needed Interleaved (ReAct-style) Decide each step after seeing the previous result Adapts naturally to surprises Harder to review in advance; the trajectory can wander Plan with replanning Plan up front, but revise the plan when a step fails or returns something unexpected Combines inspectability with adaptation More logic to build and test; needs a limit on replans Plan-up-front designs also help against prompt injection. If the plan is fixed before the agent reads any untrusted content, such as emails or web pages, text in that content cannot add new actions. Beurer-Kellner et al. list plan-then-execute among their design patterns for securing agents (Beurer-Kellner et al. 2025). They note its limit: injected text can still change the arguments of planned steps, for example the recipient of an email. 11.1.4 Structured plans: JSON or XML A plan written as free text (“first, look up the shoes…”) is hard for code to execute reliably. A common practice is to ask for the plan in JSON (or with XML tags) according to a described format: { "plan": [ {"step": 1, "description": "Find waterproof trail-running shoes", "tool": "search_products", "args": {"description": "waterproof trail running shoes"}}, {"step": 2, "description": "Keep products in stock in size 10", "tool": "check_inventory", "args": {"sku": "<each sku from step 1>", "size": "10"}, "depends_on": [1]}, {"step": 3, "description": "Keep products under $120", "tool": "get_price", "args": {"sku": "<each sku from step 2>"}, "depends_on": [2]} ] } The placeholders such as "<each sku from step 1>" tell the executor to fill an argument from an earlier step’s result. Many teams make this explicit with a reference syntax, for example "sku": "$step1.results[*].sku", so that code, not the model, does the substitution. A structured plan lets code: validate it before execution: every tool exists, the arguments match the tool’s schema, and dependencies refer to earlier steps; show it to a person for approval when the actions matter; run independent steps in parallel, because the dependencies form a graph; and log it for error analysis (Chapter 10), so that “bad plan” and “good plan, bad execution” can be told apart. Practitioners generally find JSON or XML plans more reliable to parse than Markdown lists, and Markdown lists more reliable than prose. Validation is a few lines of code, run before any step executes: def validate_plan(plan, tools): errors, seen = [], set() for step in plan["plan"]: if step["tool"] not in tools: errors.append(f"Step {step['step']}: unknown tool {step['tool']}") else: missing = set(tools[step["tool"]].required) - set(step["args"]) if missing: errors.append(f"Step {step['step']}: missing args {missing}") for dep in step.get("depends_on", []): if dep not in seen: errors.append(f"Step {step['step']}: depends on later step {dep}") seen.add(step["step"]) return errors # empty list = safe to execute; otherwise send back to the planner Returning the errors to the planner and asking for a corrected plan is reflection with external feedback, applied to plans. 11.1.5 Code as the plan For many tasks there is a more expressive plan format: code. Suppose an analyst wants an assistant that answers questions about a campaign-performance table. One approach provides tools such as get_column_max, get_column_mean, filter_rows, and sum_rows. Then the questions start arriving: “Which week had the highest cost per conversion for paid social?” This needs filtering, grouping by week, a ratio, and a maximum. The tools can do it, but only through a long, error-prone chain of calls. “How many distinct customers converted in the last seven days?” There is no tool for distinct counts, so someone writes count_unique. “Show the last five conversions.” Another new tool. Teams that follow this path end up adding tools indefinitely and still missing cases. The alternative is to let the model write code against a data library and run it in a sandbox: import pandas as pd df = pd.read_csv("campaign_daily.csv", parse_dates=["date"]) # Step 1: keep paid social only social = df[df["channel"] == "paid_social"] # Step 2: aggregate spend and conversions by week weekly = social.resample("W", on="date")[["spend", "conversions"]].sum() # Step 3: compute cost per conversion, ignoring weeks with no conversions weekly = weekly[weekly["conversions"] > 0] weekly["cpa"] = weekly["spend"] / weekly["conversions"] # Step 4: report the worst week print(weekly["cpa"].idxmax().date(), round(weekly["cpa"].max(), 2)) The comments are the plan, and the code executes it. This works because a library such as pandas offers hundreds of functions that the model has seen used many times in its training data. It can compose them with variables, loops, and conditions, which no fixed set of tools can match. CodeAct (X. Wang et al. 2024) studied this systematically, using executable Python as the agent’s action format instead of JSON or text tool calls. Across 17 LLMs on API-Bank and a new multi-turn benchmark, code actions achieved up to 20% higher success rates than the alternatives. On API-Bank the advantage was larger for open models than for closed ones. The authors’ explanation is that open models had seen far more code in training than any special tool-call format, while closed models had been fine-tuned for JSON calls. On the harder multi-turn benchmark, open models of that time did poorly in every format. The models tested (2023 releases) are now outdated, so read this as evidence for the direction, not for the size of today’s gap. Code execution as a single general tool appeared in the tool-use chapter (Section 9.4), and PAL’s program-based reasoning in Section 5.4.2. CodeAct extends the same idea from single calculations to whole multi-step plans. Two caveats: Run generated code in a sandbox (Section 9.4.1). Code is not right for every action. When actions must pass through governed interfaces, such as payments, emails, or writes to production tables, keep them as narrowly scoped tools with permissions and audit logs. Some platforms let generated code call such tools as functions, which combines the flexibility of code with the control of tools. 11.1.6 Where planning works today Planning is most mature in agentic coding. Asked to build a feature, a coding agent writes a plan, often an explicit checklist (“add the schema, write the endpoint, add tests, update the docs”), then works through it, running tests along the way. Execution feedback at every step keeps the plan honest. In most other domains, planning is still maturing. The reason is control: the developer does not know at design time what plan the model will produce, which makes testing and guarantees harder. Practical safeguards: Restrict the tool set to what the application needs. Validate every plan in code before execution. Require approval for steps with consequences. Cap steps, replans, and spending. Evaluate the planner separately: is the plan valid, does it use the right tools in a sensible order, and does it lead to a correct final answer? In short. Planning lets the model write the sequence of steps for each request. Plan up front (inspectable, parallel, resists injection), step by step (adaptive), or up front with replanning. Ask for JSON or XML plans and validate them in code; code itself is often the most expressive plan, run in a sandbox. Planning is mature in coding, where tests give feedback; elsewhere, restrict tools, validate, cap, and gate. 11.2 Multi-agent systems 11.2.1 Why use several agents when it is the same model? A multi-agent system often uses one underlying LLM, prompted differently for each role. So why call it several agents? The value is mostly in decomposition, not in separate “minds”: A design tool. A programmer splits work on one CPU into processes and threads because the structure makes the program easier to write and reason about. Asking “what team of people, with which roles, would I hire for this?” is a similar way to split a complex task into pieces you can build and test one at a time. Focused context. Each agent sees only what its role needs. This is the isolate technique of context engineering (Section 22.4.3). Role-specific tools and permissions. A researcher gets web search; a writer gets no tools; only one agent may write to the database. Parallelism. Independent agents can work at the same time. Reuse and ownership. A well-built designer agent can serve several applications, and different team members can own different agents. Each agent is an LLM call (or loop) with a role prompt, a tool set, and possibly its own model choice. 11.2.2 Example: a campaign-launch team Producing launch materials for a new product might involve three roles: Agent Task Tools Researcher Summarize category trends and competitors’ offers Web search, page fetch Designer Produce charts and visual concepts Image generation, code execution for charts Copywriter Write the brochure and ad copy from the research and visuals None beyond the LLM A role prompt might read: “You are a market researcher. Research current trends in trail-running footwear and summarize what the three largest competitors are offering this season. Cite every source.” The simplest arrangement is a pipeline: the brief goes to the researcher, the research report goes to the designer, and both outputs go to the copywriter, who produces the brochure. Alternatively, a manager agent receives the brief along with descriptions of the team members, exactly as a planner receives tool descriptions. It plans (“research, then visuals, then copy, then I review”), delegates each step, collects the results, and reviews the final draft. The team members are now the manager’s tools. Anthropic describes the same idea as the orchestrator–workers workflow (Schluntz and Zhang 2024). In code, each worker is wrapped as a tool the manager can call, with its own prompt and tool set. An illustrative sketch: def make_agent(role_prompt, tools, model): def run(task: str) -> str: return agent_loop(model=model, system=role_prompt, tools=tools, user=task) return run researcher = make_agent(RESEARCHER_PROMPT, [web_search, fetch_page], model="mid") designer = make_agent(DESIGNER_PROMPT, [run_python, generate_image], model="mid") copywriter = make_agent(COPYWRITER_PROMPT, [], model="strong") TEAM = { "researcher": tool(researcher, "Research trends and competitors. Returns a cited report."), "designer": tool(designer, "Create charts and visual concepts from a report."), "copywriter": tool(copywriter, "Write brochure and ad copy from research and visuals."), } brochure = agent_loop(model="strong", system=MANAGER_PROMPT, tools=TEAM, user=brief) The manager’s loop is the ordinary tool loop from Chapter 9. Only the tools have changed: they are agents. 11.2.3 Communication patterns How agents talk to each other is a central design decision, much like designing an organization chart. Pattern How it works Predictability Typical use Linear (pipeline) Each agent passes its output to the next High Repeatable processes with a known order Hierarchical A manager delegates to workers; workers report back to the manager Medium–high Tasks that need routing and synthesis; the most common dynamic design Deep hierarchy Some workers are managers of their own sub-agents (a researcher with a web searcher and a fact-checker) Medium Large tasks with distinct sub-teams All-to-all Any agent can message any other; a message is added to the recipient’s context; the run ends when the agents declare they are done Low Experimental and creative tasks where variation is acceptable The four shapes, drawn for the campaign-launch team (R = researcher, D = designer, C = copywriter, M = manager): Linear Hierarchical Deep hierarchy All-to-all R ──► D ──► C M M R ◄──► D ┌──┼──┐ ┌──┼──┐ ▲ ╲ ╱ ▲ R D C R D C │ ╳ │ ┌┴┐ ▼ ╱ ╲ ▼ search fact-check C ◄──► M In the hierarchical shapes, results flow back up to the manager along the same lines. Linear and single-level hierarchical patterns account for most systems in practice. In a hierarchy, it is usually simpler for workers to report back to the manager than to pass results directly to each other. All-to-all systems are hard to predict. They suit applications where a bad run can simply be repeated. A structured relative of all-to-all is multi-agent debate (Du et al. 2024). Several instances of a model each propose an answer, read each other’s answers, and revise over several rounds until they converge. This improved factual accuracy and reasoning in the original study, at a cost that grows with the number of agents and rounds. 11.2.4 When multi-agent systems help, and when they hurt The evidence is mixed, and the reasons are instructive. A case where it helped. Anthropic built a research system in which a lead agent plans and launches several subagents that search in parallel, each in its own context window (Hadfield et al. 2025). On the company’s internal research evaluation, the multi-agent system outperformed a single-agent system by 90.2%. It also used about 15 times as many tokens as a chat interaction. On the BrowseComp benchmark, token usage alone explained 80% of the variance in performance. Much of the gain, in other words, comes from spending more computation in parallel across separate contexts. The authors judged the design a good fit for broad, parallelizable research. It is a poor fit for tasks in which all agents need the same context or depend heavily on each other, which includes most coding. These are vendor-reported results on an internal evaluation. A counterargument from practice. Cognition, which builds a coding agent, argued against multi-agent designs for most work (Yan 2025). Its two principles: agents should share full context, not just messages, and every action embeds implicit decisions. Parallel subagents that cannot see each other’s work make conflicting assumptions, and the combined result is fragile. Systematic failure analysis. Cemri et al. (2025) annotated over 1,600 traces from seven popular multi-agent frameworks. They identified 14 failure modes in three categories: system design issues, such as poor role definitions or ignoring termination conditions; inter-agent misalignment, such as withholding information, ignoring another agent’s input, or drifting from the task; and task verification, such as stopping too early or failing to check the result. They also found that multi-agent systems often show minimal gains over simpler baselines on popular benchmarks. Reading the evidence together. Multi-agent systems help when a task splits into independent, context-heavy subtasks that benefit from parallel work, such as reading many sources. They hurt when the task needs one coherent understanding, when subtasks depend tightly on each other, or when cost and latency matter. Start with one well-scoped agent. Add agents only when evaluation shows that a single agent’s context or sequential speed is the bottleneck. Chapter 25 applies the same rule to supervisor agents on Databricks. In short. Multi-agent systems are mainly a decomposition tool: focused context, role-specific tools, parallelism, reuse. Linear and hierarchical patterns are the most common and predictable; all-to-all is experimental. They help on independent, context-heavy, parallel work such as broad research, largely by spending more tokens. They hurt when the task needs one shared understanding; start with one agent. 11.2.5 Designing and evaluating a multi-agent system Write role and handoff descriptions carefully. A worker needs the objective, the boundaries of its task, the expected output format, and which tools to use. Vague delegation causes duplicated or missing work. Use structured handoffs. Agree on the format each agent returns, such as a JSON report with sources, so the next agent can rely on it. Define termination. Who decides the task is done, and what is the maximum number of rounds or messages? Add verification. Task verification is one of the three main failure categories, so make checking the result someone’s explicit job, ideally with external feedback (Chapter 8). Trace every message. Error analysis works as in Section 10.4, with agents in place of components. Evaluate the whole system end to end, then each agent’s output given its input. Compare with a single-agent baseline at the same budget. A multi-agent design must beat it to justify the extra cost and complexity. Current practice (October 2026). Many frameworks support multi-agent systems, including AutoGen (Q. Wu et al. 2023), LangGraph, CrewAI, and the agent SDKs from model providers. They make it easy to implement the patterns above. Agentic coding tools commonly use a lead agent with subagents for parallel exploration, each subagent returning a condensed summary so the lead’s context stays small. Managed platforms offer supervisor agents over governed data (Chapter 25). 11.3 Choosing the level of autonomy This part has described a ladder of designs, each giving the model more control: Design Who decides the steps Choose it when Single prompt Nobody; one pass The prompt has everything and one pass is good enough Fixed workflow The developer The steps are known in advance + Reflection The developer, with a check-and-revise loop Outputs can be checked, ideally with external feedback + Tool use The model chooses tools within developer-written steps The task needs information or actions outside the model Planning The model writes the sequence Requests vary too much to hard-code the steps Multi-agent Several models divide the work Independent, context-heavy subtasks; parallel work pays off Climb only as far as your evaluations show you need to. Each step up adds flexibility, and with it cost, latency, and unpredictability. In short. The designs form a ladder: single prompt, fixed workflow, reflection, tool use, planning, multi-agent. Climb only as far as your evaluations require. Hands-on. Appendix B walks through the course labs for this chapter: a customer service agent that plans in code, and a four-agent market research pipeline. 11.4 Key takeaways The section summaries above hold the details. The chapter in five lines: Planning: the model writes the steps; structured plans let code validate, approve, parallelize, and log them. Code as plan: often the most expressive format, sandboxed, with consequential actions kept behind governed tools. Multi-agent: a decomposition tool; agents become the manager’s tools. When it pays: independent, parallel, context-heavy work; not tasks that need one shared understanding. Discipline: validate, cap, gate, trace, and beat a single-agent baseline before adding autonomy. 11.5 Interview checkpoints What is the planning pattern? The model produces a sequence of steps or tool calls for a request, and the system executes them. The developer does not fix the sequence in advance. Plan up front vs. ReAct? Up-front plans can be inspected, approved, and parallelized but break when early results change the task. ReAct adapts step by step but is harder to review in advance. Replanning combines the two. Why ask for a plan in JSON? So code can parse it unambiguously, validate tools and arguments, run independent steps in parallel, and log it for error analysis. Why can code be a better plan format than JSON tool calls? Code composes a huge library of functions the model already knows, with variables, loops, and conditions. CodeAct reported up to 20% higher success rates than JSON or text actions. When should you not let the agent act through code? When actions need permissions, audit trails, or strict validation, such as payments, emails, and production writes. Expose those as narrow tools. How does plan-then-execute help against prompt injection? The actions are fixed before untrusted content is read, so injected text cannot add actions. It can still alter the arguments of planned actions. Why build several agents from the same LLM? Decomposition: each agent has a focused context, its own tools and permissions, can run in parallel, and can be built, tested, and reused independently. Name four multi-agent communication patterns. Linear, hierarchical (manager–workers), deep hierarchy, and all-to-all. When does a multi-agent system beat a single agent? When the task splits into independent, context-heavy subtasks that can run in parallel, such as broad research. Much of the gain comes from spending more tokens across separate contexts. Why might a multi-agent system fail? Poor role and termination design, agents ignoring or withholding information from each other, conflicting implicit decisions, and missing verification. Cemri et al. group 14 failure modes into system design, inter-agent misalignment, and task verification. How would you evaluate a multi-agent system? End to end against a single-agent baseline at the same budget, then trace-based error analysis per agent, as for components. Which level of autonomy should you choose? The lowest that meets your quality bar on evaluations. Each step up adds cost, latency, and unpredictability. References
