Chapter 12 Claude Fundamentals and Product Context 12.1 Claude is a model family, not one fixed interface Claude is a family of language models developed by Anthropic. The capabilities available in a session depend on both the selected model and the product that hosts it. Claude.ai, Claude Code, an API integration, and a third-party product can expose different tools, permissions, context, and data-retention policies. Claude can work with text, code, and images. When a host provides tools, it may also search the web, read and edit files, execute commands or code, and connect to external systems. Do not infer available capabilities from the model name alone; inspect the current product, tool list, and permission settings. Primary references: Claude documentation Claude Code overview Claude tool-use overview 12.2 A practical mental model For most tasks, treat the system as four layers: Model — generates and interprets language, code, and structured content. Context — the instructions, conversation, files, and tool results visible during the current request. Tools — capabilities supplied by the host, such as file editing, Bash, web search, or code execution. Permissions and environment — boundaries controlling what tools can read, change, or communicate externally. This distinction prevents common mistakes. For example, a chat session without a code tool cannot execute a program, while Claude Code can run project commands when its environment and permissions allow it. 12.3 Useful strengths Claude is often useful for: explaining unfamiliar code and technical concepts; drafting, refactoring, and documenting code; proposing tests, edge cases, and alternative designs; synthesizing information supplied in the current context; exploring a repository and carrying out multi-step work when tools are available; and translating ambiguous goals into a concrete plan for human review. These are capabilities, not guarantees. Output quality depends on the task, context, model, tools, and verification process. 12.4 Important limitations 12.4.1 Outputs can be wrong Claude can produce plausible but incorrect facts, citations, assumptions, code, or calculations. Verify consequential claims against primary sources and verify code with tests, builds, static analysis, or direct inspection. 12.4.2 Product capabilities vary Web access, code execution, file access, memory, and integrations are not universal. A feature may be unavailable, disabled, permission-gated, or supplied by a third-party host. State the environment when documenting a workflow. 12.4.3 Context is finite Long conversations, large files, and verbose tool output consume context. As context fills, earlier detail may be summarized or receive less attention. Provide focused evidence, keep durable project rules in repository instructions, and begin a fresh session when the task changes substantially. 12.4.4 Current information requires retrieval Model training knowledge is not a substitute for current documentation. For changing APIs, models, prices, regulations, or library behavior, use an enabled retrieval tool and cite an authoritative source. If retrieval is unavailable, label the information as unverified rather than guessing. 12.4.5 Tool use creates real risk An agent with file, shell, browser, or external-service access can change state. Use least privilege, protect secrets, review destructive commands, preserve unrelated work, and require explicit approval for publishing or external actions. 12.5 A verification-centered partnership Divide responsibilities deliberately: Human responsibility Agent contribution Define goals, risk tolerance, and factual constraints Explore, draft, compare, and implement Supply domain and organizational context Surface assumptions and missing information Approve consequential or external actions Run authorized checks and report evidence Judge whether the result is useful and correct Iterate in response to test results and review The agent should show evidence rather than merely announce success. Appropriate evidence might include a passing test, a clean build, a rendered screenshot, a query result, or a primary-source link. 12.6 Exercise: compare environments Choose one task and try it in two Claude environments, such as a chat interface and Claude Code. Record which model and tools are visible. Ask each environment to explain a small local function. Ask whether it can run the function and verify the answer. Compare what each environment can actually inspect or execute. Write down which claims were generated and which were verified. 12.7 Key takeaways Separate the model from the host product, tools, and permissions. Never assume web, file, memory, or execution capabilities are present. Treat fluent output as a candidate result until evidence validates it. Use current primary documentation for changing product behavior. Keep humans responsible for goals, risk, and consequential decisions.

Chapter 13 Prompting Strategies: Ask Better Questions 13.1 The Principle: Clarity Improves Controllability Clear goals, relevant context, examples, constraints, and verification criteria usually make an answer easier to evaluate and refine. Detail is useful only when it is relevant; a longer prompt does not guarantee a better result. Vague request → many plausible interpretations Scoped request → fewer interpretations Scoped request + checks → an answer you can verify 13.2 Structure of a Good Question Many strong requests include these elements: 13.2.1 1. What (What do you want?) Be specific. “Write a function” is vague. “Write a Python function that validates email addresses” is clear. 13.2.2 2. Why (Why do you need it?) Context helps Claude understand intent. “I need to validate emails for a signup form” helps Claude suggest better solutions. 13.2.3 3. How (How should it work?) Constraints and requirements. “It should accept common email formats but reject obvious spam patterns” guides the implementation. 13.2.4 4. Constraints (What are the limits?) Languages, frameworks, performance needs. “Use Python 3.11, must be under 50 lines, no external libraries” keeps answers practical. 13.3 A CLEAR Working Mnemonic The following mnemonic is used in this guide; it is not an Anthropic product feature or an empirical guarantee: Context - What’s the background? Level - What’s your skill level? Example - Can you show an example? Action - What exactly do you want? Result - What’s the expected outcome? 13.4 Comparison: Bad vs. Good Questions 13.4.1 ❌ Bad Question How do I write a function? Problem: Too vague. What kind of function? What language? What should it do? 13.4.2 ✅ Good Question I need a Python function that: - Takes a list of dictionaries with 'date' and 'amount' fields - Groups transactions by month - Returns a dictionary with month as key and total amount as value - Should handle dates in YYYY-MM-DD format - Performance isn't critical, clarity matters more Can you write this with clear variable names? Why it’s better: - Specific about input/output - Clear requirements - Shows format expectations - States preferences (clarity over performance) 13.5 Question Templates You’ll Use Often 13.5.1 Template 1: Code Generation I need to [action] in [language]. Requirements: - [Requirement 1] - [Requirement 2] - [Requirement 3] Input: [example input] Output: [example output] Constraints: [any limits or preferences] 13.5.2 Template 2: Code Explanation I have this code: [paste code] Explain: 1. What does it do? 2. What's the time complexity? 3. What could break? 4. How would you improve it? 13.5.3 Template 3: Debugging I'm trying to [what you're doing]. My code: [paste relevant code] The error: [paste full error message] What I've tried: [what you already attempted] Expected behavior: [what should happen instead] 13.5.4 Template 4: Learning I'm trying to understand [concept]. Context: [what you know already] Can you explain: 1. How it works simply 2. When to use it 3. A practical example 13.6 Prompting Tips & Tricks 13.6.1 ✅ DO: Provide Context I'm building a data pipeline for marketing data. I need to [...] Better than: “I need a function” 13.6.2 ✅ DO: Show Your Attempt I tried this approach: [code] But it's slow. Can you optimize it? Better than: “Make this faster” 13.6.3 ✅ DO: Be Specific About Format Return the result as JSON with keys: 'status', 'data', 'timestamp' Better than: “Return the result” 13.6.4 ✅ DO: Mention Constraints Use only built-in Python libraries (no pandas or numpy) Better than: No constraints 13.6.5 ✅ DO: Ask Follow-up Questions Why is that approach better? Can you show an alternative? How would this scale to 1M rows? Better than: Single question only 13.7 ❌ DON’T: Common Mistakes 13.7.1 ❌ DON’T: Provide Indiscriminate Context Here is a large dump from several unrelated files. What's wrong? Better: In chat, provide the smallest relevant excerpt and enough surrounding context to interpret it. Good variable names? # GOOD def calculate_customer_ltv(transactions): valid = [t for t in transactions if 0 <= t <= 10000] return sum(valid) * 12 # BAD def f(x): y = [a for a in x if a > 0 and a < 10000] return sum(y) * 12 Clear logic? # GOOD - steps are obvious transactions = read_transactions() valid_transactions = filter_outliers(transactions) ltv = calculate_ltv(valid_transactions) return ltv # BAD - what's happening? return sum([t for t in read_transactions() if 0<t<10000])*12 14.3.3 ✅ Does It Handle Edge Cases? Example: # WORSE - no error handling def calculate_ltv(transactions): return sum(transactions) * 12 # BETTER - handles edge cases def calculate_ltv(transactions): """Calculate customer lifetime value.""" if not transactions: return None if not isinstance(transactions, (list, tuple)): raise TypeError("transactions must be list or tuple") valid = [ t for t in transactions if isinstance(t, (int, float)) and 0 <= t <= 10000 ] return sum(valid) * 12 if valid else None 14.3.4 ✅ Is It Efficient? Chapter 17 Claude Code Hooks: Deterministic Automation 17.1 What hooks are Claude Code hooks are user-defined commands or evaluations that run at specific points in the agent lifecycle. They can format files after edits, block unsafe operations, run checks, send notifications, or add context. Unlike a prompt that asks the model to remember a rule, a command hook provides deterministic control whenever its configured event fires. This chapter is about Claude Code hooks, not React hooks. Product behavior changes over time; consult Anthropic’s current hooks guide and hooks reference before adopting an example. 17.2 When a hook is appropriate Use a hook when all three conditions hold: A lifecycle event can identify when the check should run. A command or structured evaluation can decide the result reliably. Running automatically is safer or more consistent than relying on memory. Good candidates include formatting edited files, rejecting writes to protected paths, checking generated output, or notifying the user that input is required. Do not use a hook for subjective decisions that need rich context unless a prompt- or agent-based hook is explicitly appropriate and its uncertainty is acceptable. 17.3 Core lifecycle pattern Common events include: SessionStart — when a session begins or resumes; UserPromptSubmit — before Claude processes a submitted prompt; PreToolUse — before a matching tool call executes; PostToolUse — after a matching tool call succeeds; Stop — when Claude is preparing to finish; and Notification — when Claude needs attention or permission. The exact event set and schemas are versioned product behavior. Verify event names in the current reference rather than copying an old list into production. Command hooks normally receive JSON on standard input. Their standard output, standard error, exit code, and—in some cases—structured JSON tell Claude Code what happened. An exit code of zero does not automatically grant permission to a tool; the normal permission flow still applies unless the event supports and receives an explicit decision. 17.4 Example: format edited Python files The following project setting illustrates a narrowly scoped post-edit hook: { "hooks": { "PostToolUse": [ { "matcher": "Edit|Write", "hooks": [ { "type": "command", "command": "python .claude/hooks/format_python.py" } ] } ] } } The script should read the event JSON from standard input, validate the supplied path, do nothing for non-Python files, and invoke the project’s pinned formatter. Avoid interpolating untrusted paths directly into a shell command. Prefer a small script that parses JSON and passes arguments to a subprocess without a shell. 17.5 Example: protect sensitive paths A PreToolUse hook can inspect an impending edit and block access to paths such as .env, credential stores, or .git/. A robust implementation should: parse the documented JSON field rather than scrape text; canonicalize and validate the path; compare against a small explicit denylist or allowlist; return the documented blocking result; and explain the reason without printing secret contents. Hooks supplement permissions and repository policy; they are not a complete security boundary. A configuration mistake, unmatched tool, indirect command, or future schema change can bypass an incomplete rule. 17.6 Safe design checklist Before enabling a hook: Pin or verify every external command it invokes. Quote paths safely and avoid eval or shell construction from event input. Keep matchers narrow so unrelated tools do not trigger side effects. Make repeated execution idempotent where possible. Bound runtime and output volume. Do not print tokens, environment secrets, or private file contents. Test allow, deny, malformed-input, and missing-dependency cases. Document whether failure blocks work or only reports a warning. Review project-level hooks before running an unfamiliar repository. 17.7 Choosing between instructions, skills, and hooks Mechanism Best use CLAUDE.md or project instructions Durable facts, conventions, and commands Claude should know Skill Reusable, on-demand procedure with instructions and supporting resources Command hook Deterministic action tied to a lifecycle event Prompt/agent hook Judgment-based event evaluation where model uncertainty is acceptable Start with the least complex mechanism that solves the problem. A short project instruction is easier to inspect than a hook; a hook is valuable when reliable automatic enforcement justifies its operational risk. 17.8 Exercise: design before enabling Design a hook on paper for one repeated task: Name the exact lifecycle event and matcher. Specify the JSON fields the handler needs. Define success, warning, and blocking outcomes. List side effects and secrets the handler must not expose. Write test cases before enabling the hook. Compare the configuration with the current official reference. 17.9 Key takeaways Claude Code hooks are lifecycle automation, not React state-management hooks. Use command hooks for narrow, deterministic checks and actions. Treat hook input as untrusted and keep permissions least-privileged. Test failure behavior and idempotency before relying on a hook. Recheck official documentation because event schemas and capabilities evolve.

Chapter 18 Claude Code Skills: Reusable Procedures 18.1 What a skill is A Claude Code skill is a directory whose required SKILL.md file describes a reusable procedure. Claude can load a skill when its description matches the task, or the user can invoke it directly. Skills are useful when the same instructions, checklist, or multi-step workflow would otherwise be pasted into many conversations. Claude Code skills follow the Agent Skills open standard and add product-specific features. Review the current Claude Code skills documentation before depending on invocation or frontmatter behavior. 18.2 Where skills live Common locations are: Scope Location Intended use Personal ~/.claude/skills/<skill-name>/SKILL.md Available across the user’s projects Project .claude/skills/<skill-name>/SKILL.md Shared rules for one repository Plugin <plugin>/skills/<skill-name>/SKILL.md Distributed as part of a plugin Use project scope for procedures that depend on repository-specific commands, paths, or standards. Do not put personal credentials or machine-specific secrets inside a shared skill. 18.3 Minimal structure .claude/ └── skills/ └── summarize-changes/ └── SKILL.md A minimal SKILL.md contains YAML frontmatter and instructions: --- description: Summarize uncommitted changes and flag security, privacy, testing, or deployment risks. Use when reviewing a diff before a commit. --- # Review procedure 1. Inspect repository instructions and Git status. 2. Review source and generated-output diffs separately. 3. Identify secrets, personal data, large files, and unrelated changes. 4. Run the smallest relevant validation. 5. Report evidence, uncertainty, and remaining risks. The directory name normally supplies the command name. The description should state both what the skill does and when it applies; vague descriptions lead to missed or inappropriate activation. 18.4 Progressive disclosure Keep the main skill focused on routing and procedure. Put long examples, schemas, or domain references in supporting files and tell the skill exactly when to read them. model-review/ ├── SKILL.md ├── references/ │ ├── classification.md │ └── regression.md └── scripts/ └── validate_metrics.R This design reduces unnecessary context while keeping important detail available. Supporting scripts should be deterministic, reviewed, and narrowly scoped. 18.5 Methodologically sound data-science skills A skill should encode decisions that remain valid across the intended tasks and surface decisions that depend on context. Avoid hard-coding one universal model, split ratio, imputation rule, or metric. For a model-development skill, require the agent to: Define the prediction target, observation unit, decision use, and costs of errors. Inspect data provenance, sampling, missingness, and temporal structure. Choose a split strategy before fitting transformations; use temporal or grouped splitting when random splitting would leak information. Fit preprocessing only on training data, preferably inside a pipeline. Establish a simple baseline before tuning complex models. Select metrics that match the use case and class distribution. Preserve a held-out test set for final evaluation. Report uncertainty, subgroup behavior, assumptions, and limitations. Save reproducibility information such as seeds, package versions, and data snapshot identifiers. The skill should request missing context instead of silently inventing it. 18.6 Example skill: notebook review --- description: Review a data-science notebook for reproducibility, leakage, methodological validity, privacy, and clear communication. --- # Procedure 1. Read the notebook from top to bottom and identify its analytical objective. 2. Check whether a clean kernel can run all cells in order. 3. Trace data splits and ensure preprocessing is learned from training data only. 4. Check metrics against the decision problem and baseline. 5. Identify secrets, personal data, absolute paths, or uncontrolled downloads. 6. Separate exploratory conclusions from validated findings. 7. Run the notebook only when execution is authorized and dependencies are safe. 8. Report findings by severity with file or cell references. 18.7 Evaluation and maintenance Test a skill with representative prompts, borderline prompts, and prompts where it should not activate. Review whether it: loads at the right time; requests necessary information; follows project safety rules; produces a consistent, useful artifact; runs only authorized tools; and remains understandable to another maintainer. Version skills in Git when they are part of a project. Review them after tool, workflow, or product changes, and remove instructions that duplicate higher priority repository policy. 18.8 Skills are not enforcement A skill supplies instructions and optional resources; it is not a security boundary. Use permissions, protected branches, CI checks, secrets management, and narrowly scoped hooks for controls that must be enforced independently of model behavior. 18.9 Exercise: create one project skill Choose a repeated, bounded procedure such as validating a book build: Define the trigger in one sentence. Write a minimal SKILL.md with expected evidence and stop conditions. Add only the references or scripts the procedure genuinely needs. Test correct activation, non-activation, and a failure case. Ask another reviewer to follow the skill without additional explanation. 18.10 Key takeaways A skill is a scoped directory with a required SKILL.md, not an arbitrary saved-prompt folder. Put repository-specific procedures in project scope and keep secrets out. Encode invariant safeguards; ask for context-dependent methodological choices. Evaluate activation, output quality, safety, and failure behavior. Use permissions, CI, and hooks when instructions alone are insufficient.

Chapter 19 Verification Loops for Agent-Assisted Work 19.1 What Are Quality Loops? Loops are systematic processes that improve work quality over time. First Pass → Review → Feedback → Improvement → Next Pass Three useful levels are: 1. Execution loop — make the smallest checkable unit run. 2. Quality loop — review robustness, clarity, tests, security, and maintainability. 3. Outcome-validation loop — determine whether the result works for the real use case. These levels are conceptual, not fixed schedules. The time and evidence required depend on risk, complexity, reversibility, and the cost of error. 19.2 Loop 1: Execution Loop Purpose: Produce the smallest runnable increment and obtain direct evidence. Cycle: Generate → Test → Refine 19.2.1 The execution-loop process 1. Ask Claude for code ↓ 2. Run it (test immediately) ↓ 3. Does it work? ├─ YES → keep it └─ NO → tell Claude the error ↓ 4. Claude fixes it ↓ 5. Test again (repeat until working) 19.2.2 Execution-loop checklist Generation Phase: - ✓ Provide clear requirements - ✓ Include examples if possible - ✓ Specify constraints (language, libraries) Testing Phase: - ✓ Run the code immediately - ✓ Test with actual data - ✓ Check edge cases Refinement Phase: - ✓ Share exact error messages - ✓ Explain what’s wrong - ✓ Ask for specific fixes 19.2.3 Example: execution loop in action You: "Write a function that validates email addresses" Claude: [Response with regex function] You: [Run function] "Error: It rejects valid emails like test+tag@gmail.com" Claude: [Updates regex to handle plus sign] You: [Run again] "The examples now pass. Add a docstring and property-based tests for edge cases." Claude: [Adds documentation] You: [Final test] "Great, this works!" 19.3 Loop 2: Quality Loop Purpose: Make code production-ready Cycle: Working → Review → Improve → Test 19.3.1 Quality Loop Process Working code ↓ Code review checklist ↓ Ask Claude for improvements ↓ Error handling added ↓ Edge cases handled ↓ Documentation complete ↓ Performance acceptable ↓ Production-ready code 19.3.2 Quality Loop Checklist Error Handling: - ✓ What if input is wrong type? - ✓ What if input is missing? - ✓ What if data is empty? - ✓ Graceful error messages Robustness: - ✓ Edge cases (boundaries, empty input) - ✓ Large inputs (performance) - ✓ Unusual inputs (null, negative, etc) Code Quality: - ✓ Readable variable names - ✓ Clear logic, simple flow - ✓ DRY (Don’t Repeat Yourself) - ✓ Follows team standards Documentation: - ✓ Function docstring - ✓ Parameters explained - ✓ Return values explained - ✓ Example usage Testing: - ✓ Unit tests included - ✓ Tests cover edge cases - ✓ Tests pass 19.3.3 Example: Quality Loop Working function: def calculate_roi(investment, return_value): profit = return_value - investment roi = (profit / investment) * 100 return roi You ask Claude: "Make this production-ready. Add: 1. Error handling for invalid inputs 2. Docstring 3. Unit tests 4. Handle edge cases (zero investment, negative values)" Claude improves it with: - Input validation - Clear docstring with examples - Type hints - Unit tests - Edge case handling 19.4 Loop 3: Outcome-Validation Loop Purpose: Verify solution solves real problem Cycle: Deploy → Monitor → Collect feedback → Improve 19.4.1 Validation Loop Process Deploy to staging ↓ Collect real usage data ↓ Measure performance/quality ↓ Gather user feedback ↓ Identify issues ↓ Ask Claude to fix ↓ Re-test ↓ Deploy to production 19.4.2 Validation Loop Checklist Pre-Deployment: - ✓ Works in staging environment - ✓ Performance acceptable - ✓ Data looks correct - ✓ Team has reviewed During Testing: - ✓ Monitor for errors - ✓ Track performance metrics - ✓ Get user feedback - ✓ Watch for edge cases Post-Feedback: - ✓ Document issues found - ✓ Prioritize fixes - ✓ Ask Claude to improve - ✓ Re-test improvements Validation Questions: - ✓ Does it solve the original problem? - ✓ Do real users find it useful? - ✓ Does it handle real data well? - ✓ Are there unexpected issues? 19.4.3 Example: Validation Loop Deployed customer segmentation model... Initial real-data validation - Result: Model works but misses 15% of high-value customers - Action: Tell Claude "The model misses high-value customers with unusual purchase patterns" Claude improves feature engineering... Next validation cycle: Re-test - Result: Better, but still has issues - Action: Gather feedback from domain experts Final pre-release cycle - Claude tunes model based on expert feedback - Record remaining limitations and obtain the required release approval - Deploy through the normal controlled process 19.5 Combining All Three Loops EXECUTION LOOP QUALITY LOOP OUTCOME-VALIDATION LOOP Get it working → Make it robust → Verify it solves problem Test immediately Review comprehensively Monitor real world Iterate fast Test edge cases Collect feedback Fix errors quickly Add docs/tests Improve based on use 19.6 Tips for Effective Loops 19.6.1 ✅ Execution-loop tips Run code immediately after Claude generates it Share exact error messages (copy-paste full traceback) Test with real data, not just examples 19.6.2 ✅ Quality Loop Tips Use checklists (helps catch issues) Ask Claude: “What could go wrong here?” Write tests while code is fresh Have Claude add docstrings 19.6.3 ✅ Validation Loop Tips Start with staging/test environment Monitor real usage, not test data Collect specific feedback (“when X happens…”) Document issues for Claude to fix 19.7 Common Mistakes 19.7.1 ❌ Skipping execution-loop testing You: "Write me a function" Claude: [Response] You: Never run it, just use it immediately Problem: Hidden bugs appear in production 19.7.2 ❌ Skipping Quality Loop You: Code works, ship it! Problem: Missing error handling, no docs, fails on edge cases 19.7.3 ❌ Skipping Validation Loop You: Model looks good, deploy to production Problem: Real data behaves differently than test data 19.8 Exercise: Practice Loops Take a small project: 1. Execution Loop: Generate → Test → Fix 2. Quality Loop: Add error handling, documentation, review, and tests 3. Validation Loop: Test with real data, get feedback Record the evidence from each loop. Notice how: - Code loop catches syntax/logic errors fast - Quality review reduces avoidable production risk - Validation loop catches real-world issues 19.9 Key Takeaways ✅ Execution loop = direct evidence that the increment runs ✅ Quality loop = evidence about robustness and maintainability ✅ Outcome-validation loop = evidence about usefulness under realistic conditions ✅ Use all three for best results ✅ Follow the checklists ✅ Test at every stage

Chapter 21 Model Context Protocol (MCP): Connecting Agents to Data and Tools 21.1 Why this chapter exists Earlier chapters treated tools as something the host application “supplies.” The Model Context Protocol (MCP) is the most widely adopted open standard for how those tools, data sources, and reusable prompts get supplied. For a data scientist, MCP is the bridge between a foundation model and the governed tables, models, jobs, and dashboards that already exist. Chapter 9 explains how tool calling itself works; this chapter builds on it. MCP is evolving quickly. This chapter separates stable concepts from version-specific details. Check the MCP documentation and the specification before relying on any wire-level behavior. When this chapter was reviewed (October 2026), the latest protocol version was 2026-07-28. 21.2 The problem MCP solves Without a standard, every pairing of an AI application and a data system needs its own integration. With M AI applications (Claude Code, a Streamlit assistant, a Databricks agent, an IDE) and N systems (Unity Catalog, Jira, Google Drive, an internal API), you face roughly M × N custom connectors. MCP turns this into M + N: each system exposes one MCP server, and each AI application implements one MCP client. Any compliant client can then use any compliant server. A common analogy is USB-C for AI applications: one connector shape, many devices. Interview framing: MCP is a protocol, not a model, framework, or agent. It standardizes how context and capabilities are discovered and invoked. It does not decide which model you use or how the model reasons. 21.3 Core architecture Role What it is Example Host The AI application the user interacts with; it coordinates the model and one or more clients Claude Code, Claude Desktop, VS Code, your own Streamlit app Client A connector inside the host that holds one connection to one server The object Claude Code creates for each configured server Server A program that exposes tools, resources, and prompts Databricks managed SQL server, GitHub server, your own audience-tools server A host creates one client per server. The model never talks to a server directly: the model proposes a tool call, the host routes it through the right client, the server executes it, and the result returns to the model as context. User ──► Host (app + LLM) ├── MCP client ──► MCP server: Databricks SQL ──► SQL warehouse ├── MCP client ──► MCP server: UC functions ──► governed functions └── MCP client ──► MCP server: custom (Apps) ──► Jobs API, models 21.3.1 Two layers Data layer — JSON-RPC 2.0 messages that define discovery, the primitives below, and notifications. Transport layer — how the messages travel: stdio: the host launches the server as a local subprocess and talks over standard input and output. Best for personal, local tools. Streamable HTTP: the server runs remotely and is reached over HTTP, with standard authentication (OAuth is recommended). Best for shared, governed, team-wide servers. An older SSE transport is deprecated. A practical stdio pitfall: never write to stdout from a stdio server (for example with print()), because stdout carries the protocol messages. Log to stderr instead. 21.4 The primitives The primitives are the most important concept to learn. Servers expose three: Primitive Who controls it Purpose Marketing-analytics example Tools The model decides when to call (with host approval) Executable actions with a JSON Schema for inputs audience_overlap(segment_a, segment_b), submit_lookalike_job(seed_table) Resources The application or user decides what to attach Read-only context identified by a URI A table schema, a metric glossary, a campaign brief Prompts The user chooses, often as a slash command Reusable, parameterized templates “Explain this basket-analysis output to a client” Each primitive has list and get or call methods (for example tools/list and tools/call), so a client can discover capabilities at run time instead of having them hard-coded. Clients can also offer capabilities to servers. The main one is elicitation: a server can ask the user for missing input or confirmation through the host. Sampling (a server requesting an LLM completion from the client) is deprecated as of protocol version 2026-07-28. 21.4.1 What a tool definition looks like A server advertises each tool with a name, a description, and an input schema. Simplified: { "name": "audience_overlap", "description": "Count users in two audience segments and their Jaccard overlap. Use when the user asks how much two audiences overlap.", "inputSchema": { "type": "object", "properties": { "segment_a": {"type": "string", "description": "First segment ID"}, "segment_b": {"type": "string", "description": "Second segment ID"} }, "required": ["segment_a", "segment_b"] } } The description is effectively a prompt. The model chooses tools based on it, so a clear statement of what the tool does and when to use it matters as much as the code. 21.5 MCP compared with related ideas Concept What it is Relationship to MCP Function or tool calling A model API feature: the model emits a structured call MCP standardizes where tool definitions come from and how calls are executed REST API A service interface for programs An MCP server often wraps a REST API with model-friendly names, descriptions, and narrower inputs Skills (Chapter 18) Instructions and procedures loaded into context A skill tells the agent how to do a task; MCP gives it access to systems. They work well together RAG Retrieving documents into context A vector-search MCP server is one way to deliver RAG Agent frameworks Orchestration code (LangGraph, the Agent SDK, Mosaic AI Agent Framework) Frameworks can act as MCP hosts or clients A useful rule: skills encode know-how, MCP servers expose capabilities, and permissions or hooks enforce boundaries. 21.6 Common examples Typical servers you will meet: Developer tools: GitHub (issues, pull requests), Sentry (errors), the local filesystem. Knowledge and collaboration: Notion, Google Drive, Slack, Atlassian. Data platforms: Databricks, BigQuery, Snowflake, Postgres, often with schema browsing and query tools. Documentation: vendor documentation servers that let an agent search current docs instead of relying on training data. In Claude Code, adding servers looks like this (see the Claude Code MCP documentation): # Remote server over HTTP claude mcp add --transport http notion https://mcp.notion.com/mcp # Local stdio server; everything after -- is the server command claude mcp add --transport stdio audience-tools -- uv run server.py # Share a server with the team through .mcp.json in the repo claude mcp add --transport http shared-sql --scope project https://example.com/mcp claude mcp list # inspect configured servers Project scope writes to .mcp.json, which can reference environment variables such as ${DATABRICKS_TOKEN} so that secrets never enter version control. 21.7 MCP in a Databricks marketing-analytics stack This section maps MCP onto a typical agency setup: Streamlit analytical apps, reusable Databricks jobs (lookalike modeling, audience overlap, basket analysis), and assistants built on Databricks-hosted foundation models. 21.7.1 Three ways Databricks supports MCP Based on the Databricks MCP documentation (reviewed October 2026; most features were in Public Preview): Managed MCP servers: Databricks hosts the server, and Unity Catalog permissions apply automatically. Server URL pattern Use Databricks SQL https://<workspace-hostname>/api/2.0/mcp/sql Ad hoc SQL against warehouses Unity Catalog functions https://<workspace-hostname>/api/2.0/mcp/functions/{catalog}/{schema}/{function_name} Governed, predefined logic as tools Genie https://<workspace-hostname>/api/2.0/mcp/genie/{genie_space_id} Natural-language analytics over a curated Genie space AI Search (vector search) https://<workspace-hostname>/api/2.0/mcp/ai-search/{catalog}/{schema}/{index_name} Retrieval over documents such as briefs and reports External MCP servers registered in Unity Catalog (for example Slack, GitHub, or Google Drive), so access is governed centrally. Custom MCP servers hosted as Databricks Apps, reachable at https://<app-url>/mcp over Streamable HTTP, with access controlled by Databricks Apps permissions. See custom MCP servers. Exact URLs, scopes, and preview status change. Confirm them in your workspace’s documentation before building on them. 21.7.2 Pattern 1: Governed analytics as Unity Catalog functions The lowest-effort, best-governed option is to package your reusable, validated logic as Unity Catalog SQL functions and expose them through the managed functions server. The agent can only run what you defined, under the caller’s permissions. An illustrative audience-overlap function (table and column names are hypothetical): CREATE OR REPLACE FUNCTION marketing.analytics.audience_overlap( segment_a STRING COMMENT 'First segment ID', segment_b STRING COMMENT 'Second segment ID' ) RETURNS TABLE (size_a BIGINT, size_b BIGINT, overlap BIGINT, jaccard DOUBLE) COMMENT 'Sizes of two audience segments, their shared users, and Jaccard overlap. Use for audience-overlap questions.' RETURN WITH a AS ( SELECT DISTINCT user_id FROM marketing.analytics.segment_members WHERE segment_id = segment_a ), b AS ( SELECT DISTINCT user_id FROM marketing.analytics.segment_members WHERE segment_id = segment_b ), counts AS ( SELECT (SELECT COUNT(*) FROM a) AS size_a, (SELECT COUNT(*) FROM b) AS size_b, (SELECT COUNT(*) FROM a JOIN b USING (user_id)) AS overlap ) SELECT size_a, size_b, overlap, try_divide(overlap, size_a + size_b - overlap) AS jaccard FROM counts; The function and parameter comments become the tool description that the model reads. The same pattern fits basket analysis, for example top_associations(category, min_support) returning precomputed support, confidence, and lift from a table that a scheduled job refreshes. Why this is a strong default: The logic is reviewed once and reused by every app and agent. Unity Catalog lineage, permissions, and auditing apply. The model cannot invent a different overlap definition from one run to the next. 21.7.3 Pattern 2: A custom server for long-running jobs Lookalike modeling is not a quick query. It trains or scores a model over large data and can run for minutes or hours. Do not make the model wait on a synchronous tool call. Instead, expose a small custom server with job-shaped tools: submit_lookalike_job(seed_audience_id, expansion_pct) triggers an existing, parameterized Databricks Job and returns a run_id; get_job_status(run_id) reports state and, when finished, output table names and validation metrics; describe_lookalike_output(run_id) summarizes the audience size, score distribution, and holdout performance recorded by the job. A minimal local sketch using the official Python SDK (install with uv add "mcp[cli]"). This is an instructional example, not tested production code. In practice the tools would call the Databricks Jobs API through the Databricks SDK: import logging from mcp.server import MCPServer logging.basicConfig(level=logging.INFO) # stderr; never print() in stdio servers logger = logging.getLogger(__name__) mcp = MCPServer("audience-tools") ALLOWED_EXPANSION = {1, 3, 5, 10} # percentages the job was validated for @mcp.tool() def submit_lookalike_job(seed_audience_id: str, expansion_pct: int) -> str: """Start the validated lookalike-modeling Databricks Job for a seed audience. Use only when the user explicitly asks to build a lookalike audience. Returns a run ID; call get_job_status to follow progress. Args: seed_audience_id: Registered seed audience ID, for example "aud_123". expansion_pct: Target audience size as a percent of the reference population. One of 1, 3, 5, or 10. """ if expansion_pct not in ALLOWED_EXPANSION: return f"expansion_pct must be one of {sorted(ALLOWED_EXPANSION)}." logger.info("Submitting lookalike job for %s", seed_audience_id) run_id = trigger_databricks_job(seed_audience_id, expansion_pct) # your wrapper return f"Submitted. run_id={run_id}" @mcp.tool() def get_job_status(run_id: str) -> str: """Return the state of a lookalike job run and, if finished, its outputs.""" return fetch_run_summary(run_id) # your wrapper around the Jobs API if __name__ == "__main__": mcp.run(transport="stdio") # use Streamable HTTP when hosting on Databricks Apps Design choices worth noting: The server calls an existing, versioned job. It does not let the model write modeling code at run time. Inputs are narrow and validated (an allow-list of expansion sizes) rather than free-form. The tool description says when not to call it, because submitting a job costs money. Outputs include validation evidence recorded by the job, so the assistant reports holdout metrics instead of guessing quality. 21.7.4 Pattern 3: An AI-assisted Streamlit app as an MCP host Your Streamlit app can be the host. Its loop is: The user asks a question, for example “How much do our sports-fans and new-parents segments overlap, and what do they buy together?” The app sends the conversation and the MCP tool list to a Databricks foundation-model serving endpoint. The model returns tool calls (audience_overlap, top_associations). The app’s MCP client executes them against the managed or custom servers, using the signed-in user’s identity where possible (on-behalf-of-user authentication) so Unity Catalog permissions apply per user. Results go back to the model, which writes the explanation, while the app renders the actual numbers in tables and charts from the tool output. Rendering numbers from tool results, not from the model’s prose, is a simple and important guard against hallucinated metrics. Databricks also provides client helpers for connecting agent code to its MCP servers. Follow Use MCP servers in agents for the currently supported library and authentication pattern rather than copying older snippets. 21.7.5 Pattern 4: Coding agents connected to the workspace Connecting Claude Code to the managed Databricks SQL server lets a coding agent inspect schemas and run read-only exploratory queries while you build a job or app. Point it at a development catalog, prefer a role with read-only access, and treat its query results as exploration, not validated analysis. 21.8 Choosing the right integration Need Prefer Stable, reusable metric or analysis Unity Catalog function via the managed server Business users asking questions of curated tables Genie space via the managed server Search over briefs, decks, or research Vector (AI) Search via the managed server Long-running or multi-step workflows (lookalike, scoring) Custom server on Databricks Apps wrapping existing Jobs One-off personal automation on a laptop Local stdio server A fixed pipeline with no model in the loop No MCP; a scheduled Databricks Job is simpler MCP adds value when a model must choose among capabilities at run time. If the sequence of steps is fixed, ordinary code or orchestration is simpler, cheaper, and easier to test. 21.9 Security, governance, and failure modes MCP servers give a model real access, so treat them as production integrations. Least privilege. Use dedicated service principals or on-behalf-of-user authentication, restrict servers to the catalogs and schemas they need, and prefer read-only access for exploration. Prompt injection. Content returned by a tool (documents, web pages, free-text table fields) can contain instructions. Treat tool output as data, and keep humans approving actions that write, spend, or send. Trust in third-party servers. A server runs code and sees your data. Install only from trusted publishers, pin versions, and review what each tool can do. Secrets. Keep tokens in environment variables or secret scopes, never in .mcp.json, notebooks, or prompts. Too many tools. Dozens of overlapping tools confuse tool selection and consume context. Expose a small set of well-described, task-shaped tools. Privacy. Audience data can be personal data. Return aggregates, enforce minimum cell sizes, and avoid passing user-level identifiers to a model unless that use is approved. Cost. Tools that trigger clusters or jobs should require confirmation and report expected cost or runtime. Version drift. The protocol, SDKs, and vendor servers change. Pin versions and recheck documentation when something breaks. As with skills, MCP is not itself a security boundary. Enforcement belongs in Unity Catalog permissions, Apps permissions, host approval settings, and hooks. 21.10 Exercise: expose one analysis as a governed tool Pick one analysis you repeat often, such as audience overlap. Write it as a Unity Catalog SQL function with clear function and parameter comments. Test it directly in SQL with known segments, including empty and identical segments. Connect a host (Claude Code or a small Streamlit prototype) to the managed functions server for that function. Ask questions that should trigger the tool, questions that should not, and an ambiguous question. Record whether tool selection and answers were correct. Check that numbers in the final answer match the tool output exactly. 21.11 Key takeaways MCP is an open protocol that lets any compliant AI application use any compliant data source or tool, turning M × N integrations into M + N. Hosts contain clients; each client connects to one server; servers expose tools, resources, and prompts. Use stdio for local, personal servers and Streamable HTTP for shared, remote, governed servers. On Databricks, start with managed servers and Unity Catalog functions for reusable logic, and add a custom server on Databricks Apps for job-shaped workflows such as lookalike modeling. Tool descriptions are prompts: say what a tool does, when to use it, and when not to. Apply least privilege, guard against prompt injection, protect personal data, and render reported numbers from tool output. 21.12 References MCP architecture overview MCP specification Build an MCP server (official quickstart) Claude Code: connect tools via MCP Databricks: MCP on Databricks Databricks: managed MCP servers Databricks: custom MCP servers on Databricks Apps

Chapter 22 Context Engineering and Harness Engineering 22.1 Why these two terms matter Earlier chapters covered prompting, verification loops, hooks, skills, and MCP as separate techniques. Two newer terms give those techniques a common frame: Context engineering asks: which tokens should the model see at this step? It covers instructions, retrieved data, tool definitions, tool outputs, conversation history, and memory. Harness engineering asks: what system around the model makes it reliable over many steps? It covers the agent loop, tools, sandbox, state files, hooks, permissions, tests, and evaluation. Both terms are young, and their boundaries are still debated. This chapter separates three kinds of claim: concepts that are likely to last, vendor practices and features that change quickly, and evidence. The evidence is labeled by strength throughout. Source labels used in this chapter [Vendor]: an organization reporting on its own product or results. [Secondary]: the original could not be read; the claim comes from a mirror, summary, or aggregator. [Unverified]: no primary source was found. Product names, API identifiers, and preview status are as of October 2026. 22.2 Where the terms came from 22.2.1 Context engineering (mid-2025) The term spread through a cluster of posts in June and July 2025. No single person has a verified claim to coining it, so “popularized by” is the accurate phrasing. Shopify CEO Tobi Lütke described it as “the art of providing all the context for the task to be plausibly solvable by the LLM” (June 2025, quoted by Simon Willison). Harrison Chase of LangChain defined it as building dynamic systems that give the model “the right information and tools in the right format,” and credited earlier practitioners (LangChain). Andrej Karpathy called it “the delicate art and science of filling the context window with just the right information for the next step.” He compared the model to a CPU and the context window to its RAM (June 2025, quoted by Simon Willison). Drew Breunig named common ways long contexts fail (How contexts fail; How to fix your context). Manus published lessons from running a production agent (Manus, July 2025). Anthropic’s engineering guide (29 September 2025) gave the most-cited definition: strategies for curating and maintaining the optimal set of tokens during LLM inference (Anthropic). 22.2.2 Harness engineering (early 2026) “Harness” and “scaffold” already meant the code around a model. The phrase harness engineering became common in early 2026. Phil Schmid (January 2026) described the agent harness as the infrastructure that wraps a model to manage long-running tasks, and said it is not the agent itself. He extended Karpathy’s analogy: model = CPU, context = RAM, harness = operating system, agent = application (philschmid.de). Mitchell Hashimoto (February 2026) gave the most practical definition: whenever an agent makes a mistake, engineer a fix so it never makes that mistake again. His fixes were updates to AGENTS.md plus small, purpose-built scripts (mitchellh.com). OpenAI published “Harness engineering: leveraging Codex in an agent-first world” (February 2026). It describes a team that designs the environment while agents write the code (OpenAI). [Secondary]: the page could not be read for this chapter. Its widely repeated figures (code volume, team size, number of pull requests) are therefore not reproduced here. LangChain summarized the idea as “Agent = Model + Harness” (LangChain, March 2026). Birgitta Böckeler’s article on martinfowler.com (April 2026) reframed harness engineering for teams that use coding agents (martinfowler.com). Anthropic documented harness patterns for long-running agents (November 2025; March 2026) [Vendor]. These definitions emphasize different things. Hashimoto’s is incremental, OpenAI’s is organizational, Schmid’s and LangChain’s are architectural, and Böckeler’s treats the harness as a control system. 22.3 How prompt, context, and harness relate Layer Question it answers Typical artifacts Prompt engineering How should the instruction be worded? System prompt, few-shot examples Context engineering Which tokens should the model see at this step? Retrieval, tool selection, compaction, memory files, sub-agent summaries Harness engineering What system makes the model reliable over many steps? Agent loop, sandbox, hooks, tests and linters, evaluator agents, state logs, permissions LangChain calls prompt engineering “a subset of context engineering,” and Anthropic calls context engineering its “natural progression.” Treat the chain prompt ⊂ context ⊂ harness as a teaching heuristic, not a settled taxonomy: it appears mostly in explainers, not in primary lab writing. The more precise statement is that the harness contains context management, but it also includes deterministic machinery, such as linters, sandboxes, and permission checks. That machinery affects the model only when its output is fed back into the context. Is it just a rebrand? In part. Retrieval, summarization, and RAG all predate the label, and some experienced developers dismiss the term as rebranded prompt engineering (Addy Osmani). What is new is treating these techniques as one budgeted design problem for multi-step agents, which a prompt-only view hides. 22.4 Context engineering 22.4.1 Context is a finite attention budget The founding premise is that more context can make results worse. Anthropic describes a finite “attention budget” and names context rot: recall falls as the token count grows. The goal it sets is “the smallest set of high-signal tokens” that makes the desired outcome likely. Evidence: Lost in the middle. Accuracy was highest when the relevant information sat at the beginning or end of a long input, and worse in the middle (Liu et al., arXiv 2307.03172). Context rot. Across 18 models, performance degraded as input length grew, often unevenly (Chroma, July 2025). [Vendor]: Chroma sells retrieval infrastructure, and the study is not peer reviewed. A practical consequence: a larger advertised context window is a capacity limit, not a promise that the model will use every token equally well. 22.4.2 Four ways context fails Breunig’s taxonomy pairs each failure with a fix. The examples he cites are secondhand and were not checked against the original papers for this chapter. Failure What happens Typical fix Poisoning A hallucination or error enters context and is reused as if true Validate before writing to memory; prune; quarantine Distraction A long history crowds out the task; the agent repeats past actions Summarize or compact; start fresh with a handoff note Confusion Irrelevant tools or documents degrade choices Load fewer tools; retrieve selectively Clash New information contradicts earlier context Remove stale content; keep one source of truth 22.4.3 Four families of technique: write, select, compress, isolate LangChain groups the techniques into four families (LangChain). Write: persist state outside the window. Scratchpads, progress notes, and to-do files let an agent recover after its history is trimmed. Manus has the agent rewrite a todo.md so its goals stay at the end of the context, a direct counter to lost-in-the-middle. Select: retrieve just in time. Keep lightweight identifiers (file paths, table names, saved queries) and load content only when needed. Claude Code combines an up-front CLAUDE.md with on-demand file search. Selection applies to tools too: a smaller, relevant toolset reduces confusion. Compress: summarize or prune. Compaction replaces old history with a summary that keeps decisions, open issues, and key details, and drops redundant tool output. Isolate: give sub-tasks clean windows. A sub-agent explores in its own context and returns a short summary (Anthropic suggests roughly 1,000 to 2,000 tokens). Isolation costs extra tokens, and some practitioners argue that splitting work across agents fragments shared understanding. Choose it for parallel, separable work, not by default. Supporting guidance from the Anthropic guide: Write system prompts at the “right altitude”: specific enough to guide behavior, but heuristic rather than a brittle list of rules (Section 6.6 compares the three levels). Use a few diverse, canonical examples rather than every edge case. Make tools self-contained, robust to errors, and clearly distinct from one another. Return compact tool outputs, not raw dumps. 22.4.4 Cost: the overlooked dimension Agents read far more tokens than they write. Manus reports a ratio of roughly 100 input tokens per output token and calls the KV-cache hit rate the most important production metric [Vendor]. Cached input tokens are much cheaper than uncached ones, which leads to rules such as: keep the prompt prefix stable (a timestamp at the top breaks the cache); append to the context rather than editing earlier turns; serialize JSON deterministically; and disable tools by masking them rather than removing their definitions. These rules conflict with compaction and dynamic tool removal, which invalidate the cache. Good designs compress rarely and in large steps rather than continuously. Manus also advises leaving failed attempts in context so the model avoids repeating them, which seems to contradict “poisoning.” One reasonable reconciliation (the author’s judgment): observed error messages are useful feedback, while unverified claims stored as facts are harmful. 22.4.5 Context features are becoming platform features Vendors now ship these techniques as features, for example Anthropic’s context editing, memory tool, server-side compaction, and the progressive disclosure built into Agent Skills (Chapter 18). Learn the four families. The API names will change, but the families will still apply. 22.5 Harness engineering 22.5.1 What is in a harness A short working definition: the harness is everything except the model weights. LangChain’s list includes system prompts; tools, skills, and MCP servers (Chapter 21); infrastructure such as a filesystem, sandbox, or browser; orchestration such as sub-agents and model routing; and hooks or middleware for deterministic steps (LangChain). It helps to separate: the builder harness: the product runtime (Claude Code, the Claude Agent SDK, Codex, LangChain Deep Agents, a custom agent); and the user harness: what your team adds on top, such as AGENTS.md, specs, tests, linters, hooks, permissions, and CI. Most data scientists work mainly on the user harness, or build a small builder harness inside an application. 22.5.2 Guides and sensors Böckeler classifies harness controls on two axes (martinfowler.com): Computational (deterministic, cheap, reliable) Inferential (model-based, slower, non-deterministic) Guides (before the agent acts) Templates, schemas, scaffolding scripts, type definitions AGENTS.md, specs, feature lists, skills Sensors (after the agent acts) Tests, linters, type checks, schema validation, data-quality checks AI code review, LLM judges, evaluator agents Prefer computational sensors wherever they can answer the question, and use inferential ones for judgments that code cannot make. Böckeler also notes the limits: tests do not catch a misdiagnosed problem, over-engineering, or a misunderstood instruction. 22.5.3 Each pattern fixes a named failure Recurring failure Harness response Source Declares success too early Feature list where every item starts “failing”; checklist before exit; stop hooks that require evidence Anthropic (Nov 2025), LangChain [Vendor] Tries to do everything at once Work on one feature per session; commit after each Anthropic (Nov 2025) [Vendor] Edits tests to pass Explicit rule against changing tests; protected test files; CI Anthropic (Nov 2025) [Vendor] Loses track over long runs Progress log, setup script, descriptive commits, handoff notes Anthropic (Nov 2025) [Vendor] Praises its own mediocre work A separate evaluator agent that exercises the result Anthropic (Mar 2026) [Vendor] Repeats the same failing edit Loop detection that interrupts the agent LangChain (Feb 2026) [Vendor] Repeats a known mistake Add a rule to AGENTS.md or a deterministic check Hashimoto (Feb 2026) Documentation is part of the harness, and long documents rot. Several practitioners, OpenAI reportedly among them [Secondary], replaced one large instruction file with a short index that points to focused documents. This is the same idea as progressive disclosure in skills and just-in-time retrieval. Security gaps. The primary harness posts reviewed say little about permissions, sandboxing, secret handling, or prompt injection through tool outputs. Treat these as first-class harness components anyway: apply least privilege, require human approval for actions that write, spend, or send, and keep secrets out of context (see Chapters 17 and 21). 22.5.4 The thin-harness debate Rich Sutton’s “Bitter Lesson” argues that general methods that scale with compute eventually beat hand-built cleverness. Applied to agents, it raises the question of whether harness logic is a temporary crutch. Thin-harness view. Anthropic writes that every harness component “encodes an assumption about what the model can’t do on its own.” When a stronger model arrived, it removed parts of its own harness (Anthropic, March 2026) [Vendor]. Schmid recommends harnesses that make yesterday’s clever logic easy to delete. Harness-matters view. With the model held fixed, LangChain changed only its harness and raised its Terminal-Bench 2.0 score from 52.8% to 66.5% (LangChain) [Vendor]. A May 2026 position paper argues that harness-induced variance can exceed model-induced variance and can reverse model rankings (arXiv 2605.23950); it is an argument, not a controlled meta-analysis. The two views are compatible. Specific components (elaborate prompts, rigid step structures, large tool collections) are absorbed as models improve. The need for an environment, verification, persistent state, and permissions remains. Practical implication: a leaderboard score measures a model–harness pair. When you compare models for your own application, hold the harness constant, and when you change the harness, hold the model constant. 22.5.5 Evaluation is a harness too Anthropic’s guide to agent evaluation distinguishes the evaluation harness from the agent harness and defines tasks, trials, graders, transcripts, and outcomes (Anthropic, January 2026): Graders can be code-based (tests, exact match, schema checks), model-based (rubrics, pairwise comparison), or human (expert review). Grade outcomes, not paths. Judge what the agent produced, but keep transcripts for debugging and for spotting reward hacking, such as an agent editing the tests it is graded on. pass@k versus pass^k. pass@k is the chance that at least one of k attempts succeeds; pass^k is the chance that all k succeed. For a production tool that users run repeatedly, pass^k is the more honest reliability measure. For a statistician, this is familiar ground: define the estimand (task success), use repeated trials to estimate variance, and avoid grading on the training set (tasks the harness was tuned on). Chapter 10 covers the vendor-neutral method: end-to-end and component evals, error analysis, and error bars. 22.6 Applying both to Databricks analytics apps The design principle that follows from the evidence is: The model chooses and explains; governed engines compute; sensors verify. This is the author’s synthesis rather than an official Databricks rule, but each part has support in the sources above. 22.6.1 Metadata is the highest-return context Text-to-SQL research suggests that semantic context often matters more than which frontier model you pick: Adding a 4 KB semantic-layer document raised accuracy on 100 retail questions from about 46–51% to about 68–69% across three frontier models, and the differences between models were not statistically significant in either condition (arXiv 2604.25149). This is a single study on one domain. On the BIRD benchmark, better column descriptions improved accuracy, although ambiguous columns still needed expert input (arXiv 2408.04691). Automatically profiled metadata helped one team reach the top of the BIRD leaderboard (arXiv 2505.19988). Databricks’ own Genie guidance is a context-engineering playbook (Genie best practices): Rely on clear Unity Catalog table and column names and descriptions. Start with a small number of tables (the docs suggest five or fewer). Prefer SQL expressions for metrics, filters, and dimensions, then example SQL for complex questions, and use plain-text instructions only as a last resort. Unity Catalog metric views define each measure once (reach, overlap rate, lift, support, confidence) so that every app and agent computes it the same way. For an analytics team, this is good news: the highest-return work is data governance work you may already own. Column comments, metric definitions, and verified example queries now have a new consumer. 22.6.2 Mapping to the three workloads Workload Context engineering Harness engineering Evaluation Streamlit analytical apps on Databricks Apps Send aggregates (top-N, group-bys, summary statistics), not audience-level rows. Keep few tables in scope. Keep a stable system-prompt prefix On-behalf-of-user auth so Unity Catalog row filters and column masks apply per user. The model proposes SQL or tool parameters; tables and charts render from the result DataFrame, not from model text A code check that every number in the narrative appears in the result table; an LLM judge for groundedness Reusable jobs (lookalike, audience overlap, basket analysis) Unity Catalog comments on seed, segment, and transaction tables; metric views for overlap, lift, support, and confidence; a few verified example queries for tricky logic such as fiscal calendars Expose validated logic as Unity Catalog functions or job-triggering tools via MCP. For coding agents that maintain the job code, a short AGENTS.md map plus tests act as guides and sensors Compare results with known gold outputs; measure pass^k across repeated runs; protect unit tests from agent edits AI-assisted apps on Databricks foundation models (Genie, Agent Bricks, custom agents) Follow the Genie order of instruction types; retrieve methodology documents just in time with AI Search rather than preloading them Gateway quotas and budgets; guardrails; durable memory only for state that must persist. Inference logging stores whatever enters context, so keep personal data out Genie benchmarks; MLflow GenAI evaluation with code scorers and judges; labeled cases where the app should ask for clarification or refuse Relevant Databricks references: Databricks Apps authorization, managed MCP servers (Public Preview), and the Foundation Model APIs supported models page. Product names change often: Genie spaces are now called Genie Agents, Vector Search is now AI Search, and AI Gateway is now Unity Gateway. Check each docs page’s preview banner before relying on a feature. 22.6.3 Three cautions for marketing data Schema confusion is tool confusion. Too many tables in scope degrade text-to-SQL the same way too many tools degrade tool choice. Curate. Client data in prompts is both a privacy risk and a cost. Aggregate first, enforce minimum cell sizes, and use per-user authorization. Do not let the assistant grade its own narrative. A deterministic check against the result table is cheaper and more reliable than asking a model whether its lift or overlap summary is correct. 22.7 A minimal sketch: the number-check sensor This illustrative check implements the third caution. It is an instructional example, not tested production code, and the regular expression handles only simple number formats. import re import pandas as pd def numbers_in_text(text: str) -> set[float]: """Extract plain numbers such as 12, 3.5, 1,200 or 45% from narrative text.""" tokens = re.findall(r"-?\d[\d,]*\.?\d*", text) return {round(float(t.replace(",", "")), 2) for t in tokens} def unsupported_numbers(narrative: str, result: pd.DataFrame) -> set[float]: """Return numbers in the narrative that do not appear in the result table.""" numeric = result.select_dtypes("number").to_numpy().ravel() allowed = {round(float(x), 2) for x in numeric} allowed |= {round(float(x) * 100, 2) for x in numeric} # shares shown as % return numbers_in_text(narrative) - allowed result = pd.DataFrame({"segment": ["A", "B"], "overlap_rate": [0.18, 0.07]}) narrative = "Segment A overlaps 18% with the seed audience, versus 9% for B." print(unsupported_numbers(narrative, result)) # {9.0} -> flag for review In a harness, this check runs after the model writes its summary. If it finds unsupported numbers, the app either asks the model to revise using only the table or shows the table without the narrative. 22.8 Exercise: audit one AI-assisted app Choose an existing assistant or prototype and answer: Context inventory. List everything in the context window on a typical request: system prompt, tool definitions, retrieved text, history. Estimate tokens for each. What could be removed or loaded just in time? Failure mapping. Find one real failure and classify it as poisoning, distraction, confusion, or clash, or as a harness failure such as premature success or missing verification. One guide, one sensor. Add one guide (a metric definition, example query, or AGENTS.md rule) and one computational sensor (a schema check, number check, or test). Measure. Build 20 to 30 representative questions with known answers. Run each several times and report pass^k before and after your change, holding the model constant. 22.9 Key takeaways Context engineering decides what the model sees at each step; harness engineering builds the system that makes many steps reliable. Treat prompt ⊂ context ⊂ harness as a useful heuristic, not an official taxonomy; the harness also includes deterministic parts that never enter the context. Context is a finite attention budget: more tokens can reduce quality. Use the four families—write, select, compress, isolate—and watch the cost trade-off with caching. Organize harness controls as guides and sensors, and prefer deterministic sensors where possible. Each harness component should fix a named failure. Benchmarks measure a model–harness pair. Hold one fixed when you evaluate the other, and report pass^k for reliability. On Databricks, governed metadata is the best context, deterministic functions and jobs are the best tools, and numbers should come from query results. Expect specific techniques and API names to expire; the separation of concerns is the durable lesson. 22.10 References Context engineering Anthropic: Effective context engineering for AI agents (Sep 2025) LangChain: The rise of context engineering (Jun 2025) LangChain: Context engineering for agents (Jul 2025) Simon Willison: Context engineering (Jun 2025) Phil Schmid: The new skill in AI is not prompting, it’s context engineering (Jun 2025) Drew Breunig: How long contexts fail (Jun 2025) Drew Breunig: How to fix your context (Jun 2025) Manus: Context engineering for AI agents (Jul 2025) Chroma: Context rot (Jul 2025) Liu et al.: Lost in the middle (2023) Harness engineering Phil Schmid: The importance of agent harness in 2026 (Jan 2026) Mitchell Hashimoto: My AI adoption journey (Feb 2026) OpenAI: Harness engineering (Feb 2026) LangChain: Improving deep agents with harness engineering (Feb 2026) LangChain: The anatomy of an agent harness (Mar 2026) Birgitta Böckeler: Harness engineering (martinfowler.com, Apr 2026) Anthropic: Effective harnesses for long-running agents (Nov 2025) Anthropic: Harness design for long-running application development (Mar 2026) Anthropic: Demystifying evals for AI agents (Jan 2026) arXiv 2605.23950: position paper on harness-induced variance (May 2026) Databricks and text-to-SQL Databricks: Genie best practices Databricks: Unity Catalog metric views Databricks: MLflow GenAI evaluation Databricks: Apps authorization arXiv 2604.25149: semantic layer and text-to-SQL accuracy (Apr 2026) arXiv 2408.04691: column descriptions on BIRD arXiv 2505.19988: automatic metadata for text-to-SQL

Chapter 23 AI Models in Marketing Analytics 23.1 Introduction Marketing analytics has used statistical and machine-learning models for decades. Response models, customer segmentation, propensity scores, and marketing mix models were standard well before large language models existed. What has changed is the range of tasks that models can now take on. Predictive models score audiences. Causal models estimate what spend actually caused. Generative models write copy, summarize research, and turn questions into SQL. Agents chain these steps together and call governed tools. This chapter maps where each kind of model fits in day-to-day marketing analytics work, especially in an agency setting that serves many clients, markets, and data sources. It ties the earlier chapters to the domain: prompting and verification (Chapters 13 and 19), MCP (Chapter 21), and context and harness engineering (Chapter 22). Two principles run through the chapter: Use the right model family for the question. A language model is not a substitute for a causal design, and a propensity model does not estimate incrementality. Many costly mistakes in marketing analytics come from answering a causal question with a predictive tool. The model chooses and explains; governed engines compute. Generative AI is most useful as an interface to validated analyses, not as the source of the numbers. Measurement theory (marketing mix modeling, attribution, experimentation, and segmentation) is covered in depth in the companion Marketing Analytics book. This chapter focuses on how AI models are used across that work. 23.2 A map of AI model families in marketing Four families of models solve different kinds of problems: predictive (classification, regression, ranking), causal (experiments, quasi-experiments, econometric models), generative (language, image, and multimodal models), and agentic systems that combine models with tools. For each, this section will cover the typical marketing questions it answers, the data it needs, and the question it cannot answer on its own. 23.3 Audience and customer modeling This section covers segmentation, lookalike and propensity modeling, customer lifetime value, and churn. It will also discuss where foundation models and embeddings add value, for example by turning unstructured behavioral or text data into features. The recurring risks are leakage from post-outcome features, seed-audience bias, and treating a high propensity score as proof of incrementality. Chapter 24 treats lookalike modeling as positive-unlabeled learning and covers two-tower embeddings and typed decision models in depth. 23.4 Measurement, attribution, and incrementality This section explains how AI fits around measurement without replacing causal identification. Topics include marketing mix models (for example the open-source Meridian and Robyn projects), multi-touch attribution and its limits, geo and holdout experiments, and how language models can help explain results to clients while the estimates themselves come from validated models. 23.5 Media planning, reach, and audience overlap This section covers budget allocation and scenario planning, reach and frequency estimation, and audience overlap across platforms and segments. It discusses optimization on top of response curves and how an assistant can expose these analyses as governed tools rather than ad hoc calculations. 23.6 Basket analysis and recommendations This section covers market basket analysis (support, confidence, and lift), product affinity, and recommendation systems. It also covers embedding-based approaches and how to explain affinity results in plain language without overstating causality. 23.7 Generative AI for content and creative This section covers copy and creative variation, localization across markets, brief generation, and creative pre-testing. It addresses brand safety, factual claims in ads, intellectual-property and disclosure considerations, and why creative variants still need a proper experiment to show which one works. 23.8 Voice of the customer: text, reviews, and social This section covers using language models to classify, summarize, and extract themes from reviews, survey open-ends, call transcripts, and social posts. It compares zero-shot LLM labeling with traditional supervised classifiers and explains how to validate LLM labels against a human-coded sample before reporting the results. 23.9 AI-assisted analytics workflows This section covers analytics copilots and text-to-SQL assistants (such as Databricks Genie), automated reporting and insight narration, and Streamlit apps built on foundation models. It applies the metadata-first, numbers-from- the-engine design from Chapter 22. 23.10 Agents in marketing operations This section covers multi-step agents that monitor campaign performance, detect anomalies, prepare client reports, or trigger reusable jobs such as lookalike builds. It addresses permissions, human approval for actions that spend or publish, and auditability. 23.11 Data foundations and privacy This section covers first-party data, identity resolution, data clean rooms, consent, and regional privacy regulation. It explains why aggregation, minimum cell sizes, and per-user authorization matter more once client data can flow into model context and logs. 23.12 Evaluation and governance This section covers how to evaluate each model family: offline metrics for predictive models, validity checks for causal estimates, human-validated benchmarks for generative tasks, and repeated-run reliability (pass^k) for assistants and agents. It also covers fairness in targeting, monitoring for drift, and documenting model limits for clients. 23.13 Interview takeaways This section will summarize how to explain these choices in an interview: which model family fits a stated business question, how to defend a measurement approach, and how to describe the safe use of generative AI on client data. 23.14 Key takeaways Marketing analytics uses four model families: predictive, causal, generative, and agentic. Match the family to the question. Predictive accuracy is not incrementality; causal questions need causal designs. Generative AI is strongest as an interface to validated analyses and as a tool for unstructured text and creative work. Governed metadata, deterministic tools, privacy controls, and evaluation turn AI prototypes into dependable client-facing products.
