Chapter 24 Classification and Lookalike Modeling: PU Learning, Two-Tower Networks, and Typed Decision Models 24.1 Introduction Marketing data science classifies constantly. It scores leads, routes inquiries, labels reviews, and finds new customers who resemble existing ones. Three developments have changed how this work can be done: Positive-unlabeled (PU) learning gives lookalike modeling a principled footing when advertisers know their positives (the seed audience) but have no confirmed negatives. Two-tower neural networks embed users and items in a shared vector space so that similarity search scales to hundreds of millions of users. Typed decision models, such as TypeSafe AI’s Jev (released in September 2026), return probabilities for predefined choices instead of generating text. They target fast, cheap, structured classification that generative LLMs handle awkwardly. This chapter explains when each approach fits, what it assumes, and how to validate it before it touches live campaigns. The interactive Classification Lab lets you experiment with the confidence formulas, calibration, and PU audience sizing used in this chapter. It builds on the transformer background in Chapter 1 and the workflow chapters on notebooks (Chapter 20), verification loops (Chapter 19), and MCP (Chapter 21). Provenance note. This chapter began as an AI-generated research summary. Its claims were checked against primary sources. Several were corrected or removed because they could not be verified, or because they confused a vendor’s marketing claims with established results. Vendor claims that remain are labeled [Vendor]. 24.2 Choosing a model family Approach Core mechanism Typical marketing use Main assumption or risk Classical supervised ML (logistic regression, gradient boosting) Learns a decision boundary from labeled features Propensity, churn, lead scoring with reliable labels Labels represent the target; no leakage PU learning Learns from positives plus unlabeled records Lookalike audiences, account expansion How positives were selected into the seed (often assumed random) Two-tower networks Separate user and item encoders, compared by dot product Large-scale retrieval, recommendations, embedding-based lookalikes Enough interaction data; well-designed negative sampling Generative LLMs Generate text token by token Labeling ambiguous text, explanations, content Cost, latency, output-format errors, ungrounded claims Typed decision models (e.g., Jev) Return probabilities over a predefined schema High-volume routing, triage, text-to-feature labeling, guardrails Vendor-reported accuracy and calibration must be checked on your data None of these is a causal method. A high lookalike score or propensity score says who resembles converters, not who would convert because of the campaign. Incrementality needs an experiment or a credible quasi-experimental design. 24.3 Lookalike modeling as positive-unlabeled learning 24.3.1 The problem: no true negatives A lookalike model starts from a seed audience, such as repeat purchasers or high-value accounts, and searches a wider population for similar people. The wider population is not negative. It is unlabeled: it contains future customers, customers of competitors, and people who simply were never observed. Treating all unlabeled records as negatives is the common shortcut. It biases probability estimates downward because the “negatives” contain hidden positives. 24.3.2 The key assumption and a useful result Most PU methods assume that labeled positives are a random sample of all positives, often called selected completely at random (SCAR). Under SCAR, Elkan and Noto (2008) showed that: \[ P(y = 1 \mid x) = \frac{P(s = 1 \mid x)}{c}, \qquad c = P(s = 1 \mid y = 1), \] where \(s = 1\) means “in the seed” and \(y = 1\) means “truly positive.” Two practical consequences follow: Ranking is unchanged. Dividing by a constant does not change the order of scores. If you only need the top-k users, the naive seed-versus-rest classifier already produces the same ranking as the PU-corrected one under SCAR. Probabilities and audience sizes change. If you need calibrated probabilities, expected conversions, or an estimate of how many positives exist in the population, you must estimate \(c\). The SCAR assumption is often doubtful in marketing. Seed audiences come from past campaigns, specific channels, or loyalty programs, so they are rarely a random sample of all potential customers. When selection depends on features, the naive ranking inherits that selection bias. More recent methods relax SCAR; see the survey by Bekker and Davis (2020). 24.3.3 Common strategies Two-step methods first identify reliable negatives in the unlabeled data and then train an ordinary classifier. Spy technique: hide a random subset of seed members (“spies”) in the unlabeled set, train seed versus unlabeled, and treat unlabeled records that score below most spies as reliable negatives (Liu et al., 2002). Initial-classifier approach: train seed versus unlabeled, then take the lowest-scoring unlabeled records as reliable negatives. Bagging PU trains many classifiers, each on the positives against a random subsample of unlabeled records, and averages their scores (Mordelet and Vert, 2014). Class-prior methods estimate \(c\) (or the positive share) and correct the classifier’s output, as in Elkan and Noto. 24.3.4 Worked example: a retailer’s lookalike audience The numbers are invented and kept round so the logic is easy to follow. Setup. A retailer’s addressable population has 1,000,000 people. Suppose (unknown to the analyst) 200,000 of them would become high-value customers. The seed audience is 60,000 known high-value customers. So the seed captures \(c = 60{,}000 / 200{,}000 = 0.30\) of all true positives. Step 1: the naive model. The analyst trains “seed versus everyone else.” The model outputs \(P(s = 1 \mid x)\): the probability that a person is in the seed, not the probability that they are high value. Person Naive score \(P(s=1 \mid x)\) Corrected \(P(y=1 \mid x) = \text{score} / 0.30\) Ana 0.15 0.50 Ben 0.06 0.20 Cem 0.01 0.03 What changes and what does not. Ranking is the same. Ana > Ben > Cem under both columns. If the media plan says “target the top 100,000 people,” the naive model already picks the right people (under SCAR). Probabilities and sizes change. The naive scores sum to roughly the seed size (about 60,000) across the population, so the naive model implies “about 60,000 people like our customers exist.” The corrected scores sum to about 200,000. If a client asks “how big is the opportunity?” or “how many conversions should we expect?”, the naive answer is too low by a factor of about three. Step 2: the spy technique in numbers. To find reliable negatives, hide 6,000 seed members (10%) as “spies” inside the unlabeled population and train seed versus unlabeled. Suppose 95% of spies score above 0.08. Unlabeled people scoring below 0.08 look less like customers than almost every real customer does, so they are treated as reliable negatives. A second model is then trained on seed versus those reliable negatives. Step 3: when the assumption fails. Suppose the seed came only from the email loyalty program. Mobile-app-only customers are high value but rarely in the program, so they are under-represented in the seed. The model learns “looks like an email subscriber” rather than “looks like a high-value customer.” It ranks valuable mobile-only prospects low, and no PU correction fixes that, because the correction assumes the seed is a random sample of all positives. The remedies are a better seed (combine sources), features that describe selection, or methods that relax SCAR. To see how class overlap distorts audience sizing while leaving the ranking unchanged, open tab 3 of the Classification Lab. 24.3.5 A runnable illustration The simulation below knows the true labels, so it can show both what the Elkan–Noto correction does and when it fails. Results were produced with scikit-learn 1.5; other versions may differ slightly. import numpy as np from sklearn.datasets import make_classification from sklearn.linear_model import LogisticRegression from sklearn.metrics import roc_auc_score from sklearn.model_selection import train_test_split def pu_demo(class_sep: float, label_freq: float = 0.3, seed: int = 42) -> None: rng = np.random.default_rng(seed) X, y = make_classification(n_samples=20_000, n_features=10, n_informative=5, weights=[0.8, 0.2], class_sep=class_sep, random_state=seed) # Seed audience: a random 30% of true positives (the SCAR assumption) s = ((y == 1) & (rng.random(len(y)) < label_freq)).astype(int) X_fit, X_rest, s_fit, s_rest, _, y_rest = train_test_split( X, s, y, test_size=0.4, random_state=seed, stratify=s) X_hold, X_te, s_hold, _, _, y_te = train_test_split( X_rest, s_rest, y_rest, test_size=0.5, random_state=seed, stratify=s_rest) # Naive model: seed (s=1) vs everyone else treated as negative clf = LogisticRegression(max_iter=1000).fit(X_fit, s_fit) # Elkan-Noto: c = P(s=1 | y=1), estimated on held-out seed members c_hat = clf.predict_proba(X_hold[s_hold == 1])[:, 1].mean() p_pos = np.clip(clf.predict_proba(X_te)[:, 1] / c_hat, 0, 1) print(f"class_sep={class_sep}: c_hat={c_hat:.2f} (true {label_freq}), " f"AUC={roc_auc_score(y_te, p_pos):.3f}, " f"est. positive share={p_pos.mean():.3f} (true {y_te.mean():.3f})") for sep in [1.0, 3.0]: pu_demo(sep) class_sep=1.0: c_hat=0.11 (true 0.3), AUC=0.832, est. positive share=0.465 (true 0.207) class_sep=3.0: c_hat=0.24 (true 0.3), AUC=0.981, est. positive share=0.209 (true 0.207) Interpretation. When positives and negatives are well separated (class_sep=3.0), the estimate of \(c\) is close to the truth and the estimated positive share is accurate. When the classes overlap (class_sep=1.0), which is typical of behavioral marketing data, the estimator of \(c\) is badly biased downward. The positive share is then overstated by more than a factor of two. This estimator assumes the classifier gives true positives a score near \(c\), which fails when classes overlap. The ranking (AUC) is identical to the naive classifier in both cases, illustrating consequence 1 above. Takeaway: use PU corrections for audience sizing only after checking their assumptions. For audience ranking, the larger risks are selection bias in the seed and leakage, not the missing negatives. 24.3.6 An enterprise example IBM has described using PU learning in its account-based marketing to find lookalike accounts. It reported identifying nurturable lower-engagement accounts “93% of the time” and lookalike accounts converting at twice the average rate (Content Marketing Institute). [Vendor]: this is a company-reported case study without a published methodology. The meaning of “93% of the time,” the baseline, and the evaluation design are not stated. 24.4 Two-tower networks for retrieval and lookalikes 24.4.1 Architecture A two-tower model has two independent neural networks: the user tower encodes user features (demographics, context, recent behavior, engagement history) into an embedding vector \(u\); and the item tower encodes item features (category, text description, images, popularity) into an embedding \(v\) of the same dimension. The model scores a user–item pair by their similarity: \[ \text{score}(u, v) = u \cdot v = \sum_{i=1}^{d} u_i v_i \quad \text{or} \quad \cos(u, v) = \frac{u \cdot v}{\lVert u \rVert \, \lVert v \rVert}. \] The dot product rewards both direction and magnitude. Cosine similarity uses only direction, which removes the effect of vector length, often a proxy for popularity. The idea goes back to the deep structured semantic model for search (Huang et al., 2013). YouTube’s candidate-generation network (Covington et al., 2016) and its sampling-bias-corrected two-tower model (Yi et al., 2019) made it standard for large-scale recommendation. 24.4.2 Why it scales: late interaction and approximate search The towers interact only at the final similarity step (“late fusion”). That separation enables a two-stage system: Offline: compute embeddings for every item (or every user) and store them in a vector index. Online: compute the query embedding and run an approximate nearest neighbor (ANN) search to retrieve the top candidates quickly, even across very large catalogs. Because the towers never see each other’s features before the final step, they cannot model detailed user–item feature crosses. Production systems therefore add a ranking stage. A heavier model, such as Wide & Deep (Cheng et al., 2016) or DeepFM (Guo et al., 2017), re-scores the few hundred retrieved candidates and applies business rules such as diversity, frequency caps, and brand safety. 24.4.3 Using embeddings for lookalike audiences Once user embeddings exist, lookalike modeling becomes a search problem: Centroid search: average the seed users’ embeddings and retrieve the nearest non-seed users. This is simple but assumes a single, compact seed cluster. Multi-anchor search: cluster the seed first, then search around each cluster center. This works better when the seed contains distinct personas. Classifier in embedding space: train a PU or ordinary classifier on the embeddings, combining the two approaches in this chapter. 24.4.4 Worked example: dot product versus cosine Real embeddings have dozens to hundreds of dimensions that have no names. For intuition, imagine three dimensions: sport, tech, and family. A user who mostly buys sports gear, sometimes family items, and rarely tech has the embedding \(u = (0.9, 0.1, 0.4)\). Three candidate items: Item Embedding \(v\) Length \(\lVert v \rVert\) Dot product \(u \cdot v\) Cosine Running shoes (0.8, 0.0, 0.3) 0.85 0.84 0.99 Phone case (very popular) (1.5, 1.2, 1.0) 2.17 1.87 0.87 Kids’ bike (0.2, 0.1, 0.9) 0.93 0.55 0.60 How to read it: The running shoes point in almost exactly the user’s direction (cosine 0.99): they are the best match in taste. The phone case has a long vector. In many trained models, popular items end up with larger embeddings because they appear in many interactions. The dot product rewards that length, so the phone case wins on dot product even though it matches the user’s taste less well. Neither metric is “right.” Dot product mixes relevance with popularity, which can raise click-through but narrows exposure. Cosine focuses on taste, which helps niche items and new products. Choose deliberately and evaluate both. 24.4.5 Worked example: why a single centroid can fail Suppose the seed has two personas in a two-dimensional embedding: bargain hunters near (1, 0) and premium buyers near (0, 1). Their centroid is (0.5, 0.5). Prospect Distance to centroid Distance to nearest persona Bargain-hunter-like (0.9, 0.1) 0.57 0.14 Premium-like (0.1, 0.9) 0.57 0.14 In-between (0.5, 0.5) 0.00 0.71 A centroid search ranks the in-between prospect first even though that person resembles neither real persona. Clustering the seed first and searching around each cluster center (multi-anchor search) ranks the two persona-like prospects first, which is what the client wants. 24.4.6 Training choices that matter Negative sampling. Interaction logs contain mostly positives (clicks, purchases). Negatives usually come from in-batch sampling or random sampling. In-batch sampling over-represents popular items, which Yi et al. correct for. The ratio of negatives to positives is a tuning choice, not a fixed rule. Popularity bias. Without correction, retrieval favors already-popular items and users who resemble the majority. Common responses are sampling corrections, re-weighting rare items, and diversity rules at the ranking stage. Cold start. Because the towers use content and context features, new users and items get embeddings from their metadata. Their quality still needs separate evaluation. Privacy. User embeddings derived from behavior are personal data in many jurisdictions. Govern them like the raw data. On Databricks, embeddings are typically stored in Delta tables and served through AI Search (formerly Vector Search) for ANN retrieval. Check the current documentation for supported index types and limits. 24.5 Typed decision models: Jev and “System One” classification 24.5.1 Why a different model type Generative LLMs can classify text, but for high-volume pipelines they bring three costs: latency and token cost, because they generate output token by token; format errors when asked to return JSON; and free-text output that downstream code must parse and validate. Teams already address these with structured-output features, small fine-tuned encoders (BERT-style classifiers), or embedding-plus-classifier pipelines. A newer option is a model built only for typed decisions. 24.5.2 What Jev is TypeSafe AI describes Jev as the first “System One model,” a name borrowed from Kahneman’s distinction between fast, intuitive thinking and slow, deliberate thinking (TypeSafe announcement, Sep 2026). Jev takes a piece of state (text or JSON) and one or more typed questions, and returns only structured answers. It never generates prose, explanations, or code. According to the TypeSafe documentation, it supports three question primitives: Primitive Question form Returns Marketing example Choice Pick one option from a list The chosen option, a probability for each option, confidence Route an inquiry to billing, support, or sales Score Place the state on an ordered rubric A score, probabilities over levels, confidence Rate lead urgency or customer frustration Noul Is this statement true? A single probability that the answer is yes “Does this email request a refund?” TypeSafe says it trains Jev with a method it calls Reinforcement Learning for Calibrated Decisions (RLCD), which it contrasts with the RLHF used for chat models. It has not published the method’s details. 24.5.3 Confidence is not calibration TypeSafe’s documentation defines confidence as a summary of how concentrated the probability distribution is (TypeSafe: Confidence): Choice, with \(n\) options and top probability \(p_{\max}\): \[\text{confidence} = \frac{p_{\max} - 1/n}{1 - 1/n},\] which is 0 for an even split and 1 for certainty. Noul, with probability \(p\): the suggested summary is \(\text{confidence} = |2p - 1|\). Score, with level probabilities \(p_i\) and most likely level \(m\): \[\text{confidence} = \max\left(0,\; 1 - \frac{\sum_i p_i \lvert i - m \rvert}{\text{MAD}_{\text{unif}}}\right),\] where \(\text{MAD}_{\text{unif}}\) is the same average distance for an even spread across all levels, measured from the middle level. Uncertainty between adjacent levels lowers confidence less than uncertainty between distant levels. 24.5.4 Worked examples: computing confidence by hand Choice: routing a customer email to one of four teams (\(n = 4\), so an even split gives each team \(1/n = 0.25\)). Returned probabilities (Billing, Support, Sales, Cancel) \(p_{\max}\) Confidence 0.70, 0.15, 0.10, 0.05 0.70 \((0.70 - 0.25)/(1 - 0.25) = 0.60\) 0.40, 0.30, 0.20, 0.10 0.40 \((0.40 - 0.25)/(0.75) = 0.20\) 0.25, 0.25, 0.25, 0.25 0.25 0.00 Read confidence as “how far the top answer stands above a coin-toss among the options,” rescaled to run from 0 to 1. Score: rating complaint urgency on five levels numbered 0 (calm) to 4 (furious). For five levels, an even spread has an average distance of 1.2 levels from the middle level, so \(\text{MAD}_{\text{unif}} = 1.2\). Case Probabilities on levels 0–4 Most likely level Average distance \(\sum p_i \lvert i - m \rvert\) Confidence A: torn between angry and furious 0, 0, 0, 0.6, 0.4 3 \(0.4 \times 1 = 0.4\) \(1 - 0.4/1.2 = 0.67\) B: torn between angry and calm 0.4, 0, 0, 0.6, 0 3 \(0.4 \times 3 = 1.2\) \(1 - 1.2/1.2 = 0.00\) Both cases put 60% on level 3, yet A has useful confidence and B has none. In A the model only hesitates about how angry the customer is. In B it cannot tell whether the customer is angry or calm, which is useless for prioritizing. Noul: “Does this email request a refund?” Returned \(p\) Confidence \(\lvert 2p - 1 \rvert\) Reading 0.94 0.88 Confident yes 0.55 0.10 Close to a coin toss 0.06 0.88 Confident no Confidently wrong. In the first Choice row, suppose the email actually came from a customer about to cancel. The model said Billing with confidence 0.60, and it was wrong. Nothing in the formula can reveal that; only comparing predictions with true labels across many emails can. That comparison is calibration, described next. Try your own distributions in tab 1 of the Classification Lab. These formulas describe the shape of the distribution, not whether it is right. A model can be confidently wrong. Calibration means that among cases predicted at 90%, about 90% are actually positive. Calibration is an empirical property that you must measure on your own labeled data. TypeSafe says Jev is trained for calibrated probabilities, but no calibration evaluation (such as reliability diagrams or expected calibration error) was found in its published materials as of October 2026. 24.5.5 Vendor-reported performance TypeSafe reports [Vendor]: end-to-end latency of roughly 70 to 500 milliseconds, against seconds for frontier LLMs; input pricing of $0.042 per million tokens, with output not billed; and that answers always match the declared schema, so type errors are impossible by construction. TypeSafe notes that its published evaluations were run from its own machines and that its workflow benchmarks were built by its own team. Schema conformance by construction is credible. Accuracy, calibration, and real-world latency still need independent testing. As of October 2026 the model was proprietary and served through TypeSafe’s hosted API; access terms may change. 24.5.6 Where a typed decision model fits Routing and triage: a Choice question picks the destination while a Score question rates urgency, evaluated on the same input. Text-to-feature labeling: turn reviews, survey open-ends, or call notes into categorical features for downstream models. Guardrails for agents: ask a Noul question such as “Is this proposed action read-only?” before an agent runs a tool. This complements deterministic permissions and hooks; it does not replace them. Design questions atomically: ask one factor per question, and let ordinary code combine the answers into the final action. This keeps each probability interpretable and testable. 24.6 Validating classifiers before automation Whatever the model, decide thresholds from evidence, not from reported confidence. Build a labeled sample that represents production traffic, including rare and ambiguous cases. Have humans label it, and measure agreement between labelers. Run in shadow mode. Score live traffic in parallel with the current process without affecting decisions. Measure discrimination and calibration separately. Discrimination (AUC, precision at the chosen threshold) says whether the model ranks well. Calibration says whether its probabilities can be taken at face value. Set thresholds from costs. Choose automation thresholds from the cost of each error type, and route the uncertain middle band to people or to a slower model. Monitor drift. Re-check calibration when products, campaigns, or language change. A minimal calibration check: import numpy as np import pandas as pd from sklearn.calibration import calibration_curve from sklearn.metrics import brier_score_loss def calibration_report(y_true, p_pred, n_bins: int = 10) -> pd.DataFrame: """Compare predicted probabilities with observed frequencies on labeled data.""" frac_pos, mean_pred = calibration_curve(y_true, p_pred, n_bins=n_bins, strategy="quantile") print(f"Brier score: {brier_score_loss(y_true, p_pred):.3f}") return pd.DataFrame({"mean_predicted": mean_pred.round(2), "observed_rate": frac_pos.round(2)}) # Simulated shadow-mode log: an overconfident classifier rng = np.random.default_rng(7) true_p = rng.uniform(0, 1, 2_000) y = rng.binomial(1, true_p) p_reported = np.clip(0.5 + 1.6 * (true_p - 0.5), 0.01, 0.99) # pushed toward 0/1 print(calibration_report(y, p_reported, n_bins=5)) Brier score: 0.180 mean_predicted observed_rate 0 0.01 0.10 1 0.18 0.30 2 0.49 0.51 3 0.82 0.68 4 0.99 0.91 The simulated model reports 0.99 when the observed rate is 0.91, and 0.01 when it is 0.10. A threshold of “automate above 0.95” would therefore be much less safe than it appears. If calibration is poor but ranking is good, recalibrate with Platt scaling or isotonic regression on held-out data. Do not tune the threshold on the same sample you use to report performance. 24.6.1 Worked example: from calibration to an automation threshold Checking calibration in plain terms. In shadow mode, a classifier flags 1,000 emails as “refund request” with probability around 0.90. Human reviewers check them and find that 760 really are refund requests. The observed rate is 0.76, not 0.90, so the model is overconfident in that range. Repeat the check for other probability bands (0.1, 0.3, 0.5, …) to draw the full calibration curve. Choosing a threshold from costs. Suppose the app escalates likely churn emails to a retention specialist: escalating an email that was not churn risk (false positive) wastes about $1 of specialist time; missing a real churn-risk email (false negative) loses about $9 in expected customer value. With calibrated probability \(p\), escalating costs \((1 - p) \times 1\) in expectation and not escalating costs \(p \times 9\). Escalation is worth it when \(p \times 9 > (1 - p) \times 1\), that is, when \[ p > \frac{C_{FP}}{C_{FP} + C_{FN}} = \frac{1}{1 + 9} = 0.10. \] Two lessons follow: The threshold comes from the business costs, not from the model. Here escalating at only 10% probability is rational because misses are nine times as costly as false alarms. A default threshold of 0.5 would miss many saveable customers. The rule only works with calibrated probabilities. If the model’s “0.10” really means 0.03, the threshold is wrong. Calibrate first, then apply the cost rule. Tab 2 of the Classification Lab simulates an overconfident model, draws its calibration curve, and converts business costs into a threshold. For lookalike audiences, the final test is an outcome experiment: compare conversion or incremental lift for the new audience against a control or the current method. Offline metrics show the model learned the seed; only an experiment shows business value. 24.7 Putting the pieces together A practical marketing stack might combine these approaches: Two-tower embeddings for large-scale audience retrieval and recommendations. PU-aware classifiers to rank and size lookalike audiences, with explicit checks on seed selection. A typed decision model or small fine-tuned classifier for high-volume routing and text-to-feature labeling. Generative LLMs for explanation, ambiguous cases, and content, connected to governed tools through MCP (Chapter 21). Verification loops around all of them: execution checks, quality checks against labeled data, and outcome experiments (Chapter 19). Develop these models in reproducible notebooks with a clear setup, analysis, and outputs structure, deterministic seeds, and held-out evaluation, as described in Chapter 20. 24.8 Implementing this in a Databricks marketing practice This section turns the chapter into four concrete projects for an agency data science team that runs reusable Databricks jobs and Streamlit apps. Each project lists the steps, the deliverable, and how to prove it works. Product names follow the Databricks documentation as of October 2026; check current docs before building. 24.8.1 Project 1: upgrade the lookalike job to be PU-aware Goal: keep the existing lookalike ranking, but add honest audience sizing and a check on seed bias. Document the seed. Record where each seed member came from (CRM, loyalty program, campaign responders) as a column in the seed table in Unity Catalog. Compare seed with population. Before modeling, compare the seed’s distribution on key features (region, channel, device, age band) with the population’s. Large gaps warn that SCAR is doubtful. Report them to the client. Train the ranking model as usual (seed versus unlabeled, for example with gradient boosting), logged with MLflow. Add a sizing step. Estimate \(c\) on held-out seed members, as in the runnable example. Report the estimated audience size with a range. Flag the estimate as unreliable when the classes overlap heavily, which shows up as a low held-out AUC. Make the job reusable. Parameterize seed table, population table, and audience size; write scores and a run summary (size estimate, AUC, seed-gap report) to Delta tables. Validate with an experiment. For important clients, run a holdout or geo test comparing the new audience with the current method. Deliverable: a ranked audience table plus a one-page run summary that a client lead can read. 24.8.2 Project 2: embedding-based lookalikes and recommendations Goal: find similar users or products at scale, and explain why they are similar. Start simple. Before training a two-tower model, build user embeddings from existing features or from purchase sequences (for example, embeddings of product IDs averaged per user). This gives a baseline. Train a two-tower model when interaction data is large enough (clicks, purchases, views). Use in-batch negatives and a popularity correction. Index embeddings with Databricks AI Search (formerly Vector Search) for nearest-neighbor retrieval. Use multi-anchor search for lookalikes: cluster the seed embeddings and retrieve around each cluster center. Evaluate offline, then online. Offline: recall@K of held-out purchases, plus coverage and diversity of retrieved items. Online: an A/B test on conversion. Expose as a tool. Wrap “find lookalikes for seed X” as a Unity Catalog function or a job-triggering tool, so a Streamlit assistant can call it through MCP (Chapter 21). Deliverable: an embedding table, a search index, and a retrieval tool with documented evaluation. 24.8.3 Project 3: high-volume text classification for voice of the customer Goal: turn reviews, survey open-ends, or support emails into categorical features (topic, sentiment, urgency, refund request) cheaply and reliably. Define atomic questions. For example: topic (Choice), urgency (Score 0–4), refund request (yes or no). Write clear definitions and two or three examples for each label. Create a labeled sample. Have two people label 300 to 500 records and measure agreement. Low agreement means the label definitions need work before any model can do better. Compare candidate classifiers on the same sample: a generative LLM from Databricks Foundation Model APIs with structured output, a small fine-tuned encoder, and, if you have access, a typed decision model such as Jev. Compare accuracy, calibration, latency, and cost per 1,000 records. Calibrate and set thresholds with the cost rule above. Route the uncertain middle band to people. Run as a scheduled job that writes labels and probabilities to a Delta table, then feed those columns into dashboards or downstream models (churn, satisfaction drivers). Monitor monthly. Re-label a small random sample and re-check accuracy and calibration. Deliverable: a labeled feature table, a model comparison report, and a monitoring check. 24.8.4 Project 4: a calibration check as a reusable tool Goal: make “is this model’s probability trustworthy?” a standard step for every classifier the team ships. Package the calibration_report function from this chapter, plus AUC and the cost-based threshold, as a shared Python module. Add it to the team’s notebook template (Chapter 20) and to the evaluation step of every job, logging results to MLflow. Add a rule to the team’s AGENTS.md or skill: an agent may not recommend an automation threshold without a calibration report (Chapter 18). Deliverable: one shared function and one team rule. This is the smallest project and a good first step. 24.8.5 Where to start Start with Project 4, because it is small and improves every other project. Then do Project 1, which adds value to a job you already run. Projects 2 and 3 depend on data volume and access to labeled text, so scope them with a specific client use case. 24.9 Interview takeaways “How would you build a lookalike model?” Frame it as PU learning. State the SCAR assumption, explain why ranking is unaffected by the missing negatives but sizing is not, and propose an experiment to validate lift. “Why use a two-tower model?” It separates user and item encoders so that embeddings can be precomputed and searched with approximate nearest neighbors. The trade-off is weaker feature interactions, which a ranking stage recovers. “Can I trust a model’s confidence score?” Only after measuring calibration on representative labeled data. Concentration of probability is not accuracy. “LLM or classifier for ticket routing?” For stable categories at high volume, use a classifier or typed decision model with measured calibration. Reserve generative models for ambiguous cases and explanations. 24.10 Key takeaways Lookalike modeling is a positive-unlabeled problem. The SCAR assumption determines what corrections are valid, and seed selection bias is often the bigger risk. Two-tower networks make embedding-based retrieval and lookalikes scale; negative sampling and popularity bias need deliberate design. Typed decision models such as Jev return structured probabilities instead of text. Their schema guarantees are credible by design, but accuracy and calibration claims require your own validation. Confidence measures how concentrated a distribution is; calibration measures whether probabilities match reality. Automate only on measured calibration. Validate in shadow mode first, then prove business value with experiments. 24.11 References Positive-unlabeled learning Elkan, C., and Noto, K. (2008). Chapter 25 Supervisor Agents and Multi-Agent Systems on Databricks 25.1 Introduction A single agent with a few tools can answer many questions. Real analytics questions often cross domains, though: “Why did conversions drop for the spring campaign, and which audience should we test next?” needs campaign metrics, audience overlap, research reports, and perhaps a modeling job. A supervisor agent handles this by coordinating specialized agents and tools. It decides who should answer each part, delegates, and combines the results. This chapter covers: the supervisor pattern and when multiple agents help or hurt; Databricks Supervisor Agent: how it works and how to build one; what Databricks recommends for new work as of October 2026; and a marketing-analytics example with descriptions, test questions, and evaluation. It builds on MCP (Chapter 21), context and harness engineering (Chapter 22), and the analytics tools in Chapter 24. Status check (October 2026). On 6 October 2026 the Databricks documentation labeled Supervisor Agent a legacy offering. For new low-code agents it recommends Genie Agents. To coordinate multiple agents in code it recommends the Agent Bricks CLI, which was in Beta at the time of writing. The related Supervisor API (Beta) was deprecated, with end of life on 30 September 2026. The supervisor pattern in this chapter remains current; the specific product is likely to change. Check the Supervisor Agent page and What is Agent Bricks? before building. 25.2 The supervisor pattern 25.2.1 What a supervisor does A supervisor is an agent whose tools are other agents (and ordinary tools). For each request it: interprets the question and breaks it into parts; routes each part to the subagent or tool whose description fits best; delegates and collects the answers; and synthesizes one response, or asks the user to clarify. Anthropic describes the same idea as the orchestrator–workers workflow: a central model breaks down a task, delegates subtasks to workers, and synthesizes their results (Building effective agents). 25.2.2 Common multi-agent shapes Pattern How it works Good for Router Sends the whole request to one specialist Clearly separable domains (billing vs. analytics) Supervisor Splits the request, calls several specialists, combines results Cross-domain questions Hierarchical A supervisor calls other supervisors Large organizations with domain teams Pipeline Fixed sequence of steps Repeatable workflows; often better as ordinary code 25.2.3 When multiple agents help, and when they hurt They help when: domains have different data, permissions, and owners (each team curates its own Genie Agent); a specialist needs a focused context, which is the isolate technique from Chapter 22; and subtasks can run independently and be combined. They hurt when: the task needs one shared, detailed understanding that gets lost in handoffs; latency and cost matter, because every delegation adds model calls; and a fixed workflow would do. A scheduled job is simpler, cheaper, and easier to test than an agent deciding the steps each time. A good rule: start with one well-scoped agent, and add a supervisor only when routing between distinct, well-defined specialists is the actual problem. Chapter 11 covers the vendor-neutral theory: communication patterns, the evidence on when multi-agent systems help, and their common failure modes. 25.3 Databricks Supervisor Agent The facts in this section come from the Supervisor Agent documentation as of 6 October 2026. 25.3.1 What it provides Supervisor Agent builds a supervisor system that coordinates Genie Agents, agent endpoints, Unity Catalog functions, MCP servers, and custom agents. It produces a serving endpoint that you can query from AI Playground, the API, or a Databricks App. Domain experts can improve its routing with natural-language feedback. Databricks lists use cases such as market analysis across research reports and usage data, internal-process questions, and customer-service answers. 25.3.2 Requirements Serverless compute and Unity Catalog enabled, in a supported region. Access to Model Serving and to a serverless usage policy with a nonzero budget. At least one subagent ready to use. End users need explicit access to each subagent (next table). 25.3.3 Supported subagents and required end-user permissions Subagent or tool Required end-user permission Genie Agent Access to the Genie Agent and its underlying Unity Catalog objects Published dashboard CAN VIEW on the dashboard Knowledge Assistant endpoint CAN QUERY on the endpoint Model serving endpoint CAN QUERY on the endpoint Unity Catalog function EXECUTE on the function Unity Catalog table SELECT, plus USE CATALOG and USE SCHEMA Unity Catalog volume READ VOLUME, plus USE CATALOG and USE SCHEMA AI Search index (Delta Sync only) SELECT, plus USE CATALOG and USE SCHEMA Another Supervisor Agent CAN QUERY on it Unity Catalog MCP Service EXECUTE, plus USE CATALOG and USE SCHEMA Custom MCP server or custom agent on Databricks Apps CAN_USE on the app Web search (built in) No extra permission; the user approves each search A supervisor can use up to 50 agents and tools. Access control is per user. End users reach only the subagents and data they are allowed to use. If a user can access none of the subagents, the supervisor ends the conversation. If they can access only some, it steers away from the others. This is the behavior an agency needs when different teams may see different clients’ data. 25.3.4 Built-in code execution Every supervisor includes a code execution tool. It runs model-generated Python (default), SQL, or shell commands in a sandboxed serverless session with no internet access. Its only data access is read-only access to the Unity Catalog tables and volumes added as tools, subject to the end user’s permissions. Databricks warns that running arbitrary code can expose data the agent can reach, so permissions and guardrails remain the customer’s responsibility. 25.3.5 Web search Web search uses the databricks-gpt-5 Foundation Model API regardless of the model that powers the supervisor. The workspace must allow that model, and web search is unavailable in some regions and in workspaces with the Enhanced Security and Compliance add-on. The supervisor asks the user to approve each search before sending the query to the public web. Never let client data appear in a web query. 25.3.6 Building one: five steps Configure. Go to Agents → Create Agent → Supervisor Agent. Add tools and subagents, and write a description for each one; the supervisor routes based on these descriptions. Optionally add supervisor-level Instructions and a user-facing Description. Test. Chat in the right pane, or open the endpoint in AI Playground, where AI Judge and synthetic task generation may be available. Check that each question reaches the right subagent. Improve. In the Examples tab, add representative questions. Share the configuration page with subject-matter experts (they need Can Manage on the agent and access to the subagents). Experts attach natural-language Guidelines to questions, and guidelines take effect when saved. Manage permissions. Grant Can Manage (edit and improve) or Can Query (use the endpoint only) to users, groups, or service principals. Query the endpoint. From AI Playground, Get code provides curl and Python examples for applications such as a Streamlit app on Databricks Apps. 25.3.7 Managing supervisors with the SDK (Beta) The Databricks SDK for Python can create supervisors and manage their tools. From the documentation: from databricks.sdk import WorkspaceClient from databricks.sdk.service.supervisoragents import SupervisorAgent w = WorkspaceClient() supervisor_agent = SupervisorAgent( display_name="<display-name>", description="<description>", instructions="<instructions>", ) created = w.supervisor_agents.create_supervisor_agent(supervisor_agent=supervisor_agent) print(created) Tools (subagents) are added with w.supervisor_agents.create_tool(...), and their descriptions can be updated with update_tool. This lets a team keep supervisor configurations in version control and recreate them across workspaces. See the documentation for the tool types and fields. 25.3.8 Limitations At most 50 agents and tools per supervisor. AI Search subagents support only Delta Sync indexes. Web search has the regional and compliance restrictions above. It is a legacy offering, so plan for migration. 25.4 What to use for new work (October 2026) Need Databricks recommendation Notes Low-code agent over tables and documents Genie Agents Curated with Unity Catalog metadata, example SQL, instructions, and trusted assets Business users exploring data, dashboards, apps Genie One Can also be called as a tool by custom agents Custom agent in code, including multi-agent coordination Agent Bricks CLI (Beta) deploying to Agent Runtime Scaffolds a project, runs locally, deploys with managed memory, sessions, tools, and MLflow tracing Composing several agents, such as coding agents Omnigent Described by Databricks as a meta-harness Existing Supervisor Agent Keep running, plan migration Legacy; no new investment Sources: What is Agent Bricks?, September 2026 release notes. In code, the pattern stays the same. Databricks’ multi-agent app template builds an orchestrator that treats each subagent as a tool: Genie Agents reached through their MCP server, other agents on Databricks Apps, and serving endpoints. Each subagent has a name, an endpoint, and a detailed description to improve routing (multi-agent apps). That page uses the legacy agent server; follow the Agent Bricks CLI documentation for new deployments. What carries over regardless of product: clear subagent descriptions, per-user permissions, a labeled set of test questions, and expert guidelines. Building these now is not wasted if the product changes. 25.5 Worked example: a campaign insights supervisor An agency team wants one assistant for account leads that answers cross-domain questions about a client’s campaigns. 25.5.1 The specialists Subagent or tool Type What it covers campaign_performance Genie Agent over campaign metric views Spend, impressions, reach, conversions, CPA by channel, market, and week audience_overlap Unity Catalog function Size and overlap of two audience segments basket_affinity Unity Catalog function Precomputed support, confidence, and lift for product pairs lookalike_jobs Custom MCP server on Databricks Apps Start the validated lookalike job; check status and results research_library Document Q&A (Knowledge Assistant or AI Search index) Client briefs, research reports, past campaign learnings 25.5.2 Write descriptions that route well The supervisor routes on descriptions, so treat them as prompts. Compare: Weak: “Campaign data.” Strong: “Answers quantitative questions about this client’s paid-media campaigns: spend, impressions, reach, clicks, conversions, CPA, and ROAS by channel, market, campaign, and week, from 2024 onward. Use for ‘how much’, ‘how did it change’, and ‘which channel’ questions. Does not contain audience membership, product purchases, or research documents.” A strong description says what the tool covers, when to use it, and what it does not cover. The “does not” part prevents many routing errors. 25.5.3 Test questions and expected routing Question Expected route “What was CPA by channel last month in Germany?” campaign_performance “How much do our sports-fans and new-parents segments overlap?” audience_overlap “Which products are most often bought with running shoes?” basket_affinity “Why did spring conversions drop, and what did last year’s brief say about seasonality?” campaign_performance + research_library “Build a 3% lookalike from the loyalty seed.” lookalike_jobs, after confirmation “What’s the weather in Paris?” Politely decline (out of scope) “Show me individual customer emails in the seed.” Decline (personal data) 25.5.4 Expert guidelines Account leads and analysts add guidelines to example questions, such as: “When reporting CPA, always state the date range and currency.” “Do not compare markets with different currencies without converting.” “For lookalike requests, confirm the seed, size, and client before starting a job.” “Overlap results come from the function; never estimate overlap from memory.” “If a question mixes two clients, ask which client is meant.” 25.5.5 Agency-specific design choices Client separation. Use one supervisor per client, or Unity Catalog row filters and per-user permissions, so that no conversation can mix clients’ data. Test this explicitly with users who lack access. Numbers from tools. Display numeric results from tool outputs, not from the model’s prose. Apply the number-check sensor from Chapter 22. Actions need confirmation. Starting a job costs money; require explicit user confirmation and log who approved it. Web search off or tightly scoped. Client names or results must not appear in public web queries. 25.6 Evaluating a supervisor Evaluate two things separately: Routing accuracy. For each labeled question, did the supervisor call the expected subagents, and avoid the wrong ones? Trace data in MLflow shows which tools were called. Answer quality. Are the numbers correct (they should match the tool output exactly), is the answer grounded, and did the supervisor clarify or decline when it should? Practical steps: Build 30 to 50 labeled questions covering every subagent, multi-domain questions, out-of-scope requests, and permission edge cases. Run each question several times and report pass^k (all runs correct), not just one lucky run. Re-run the set after every change to descriptions, guidelines, or subagents. A better description for one tool can steal traffic from another. Use MLflow GenAI evaluation with code-based checks for routing and number matching, and LLM judges or expert review for answer quality. 25.7 Common pitfalls Pitfall Symptom Fix Overlapping descriptions Questions bounce between two subagents Make scopes exclusive; add “does not cover” lines Too many subagents Slow, inconsistent routing Merge narrow tools; add a supervisor only where domains truly differ Missing user permissions “I can’t help with that” for some users Grant access to each subagent, or explain the restriction Synthesized numbers The answer contains figures not in any tool output Render numbers from tool outputs; add a number check Silent actions Jobs started without approval Require confirmation for writing or spending actions Untested changes Quality drops after an edit Re-run the labeled question set after every change 25.8 Exercise: design a supervisor on paper List three to five specialists you already have or could build (a Genie Agent, two Unity Catalog functions, a document index). Write a strong description for each, including what it does not cover. Write 15 test questions with expected routes, including two multi-domain questions, two out-of-scope requests, and one permission edge case. Write five expert guidelines. Decide whether you need a supervisor at all, or whether one Genie Agent or a scheduled job would do. 25.9 Key takeaways A supervisor routes, delegates, and synthesizes across specialists; it is the orchestrator–workers pattern. Use multiple agents only when distinct domains, permissions, or contexts justify them; otherwise one agent or a fixed workflow is simpler. Databricks Supervisor Agent coordinates up to 50 agents and tools, enforces per-user access, includes sandboxed code execution, and improves through expert guidelines. As of October 2026, Supervisor Agent is legacy. Use Genie Agents for low-code work and the Agent Bricks CLI for custom multi-agent code. Descriptions, permissions, labeled test questions, and guidelines are durable assets that survive product changes. Evaluate routing and answer quality separately, repeatedly, and after every change. 25.10 References Databricks: Use Supervisor Agent to create a coordinated multi-agent system Databricks: What is Agent Bricks? A Course Labs: Walkthroughs A.1 Common setup A.2 Lab 1: Summarization with prompting and generation settings A.3 Lab 2: Full fine-tuning vs. LoRA A.4 Lab 3: Detoxifying with RLHF (PPO) A.5 What the three labs show together

A Course Labs: Walkthroughs The course Generative AI with Large Language Models (DeepLearning.AI / AWS, Coursera) had three hands-on labs. All three used one task: summarizing dialogues with Flan-T5. Each lab applied one stage of the lifecycle (Section 1.7) to that task: prompting, then fine-tuning, then alignment. This appendix records what each lab did and what it teaches. It is written in my own words, and the course notebooks are not reproduced. About the numbers. Results below are as reported in the course labs, not reproduced here. They came from small samples and short training runs on 2023-era library versions. Read them as directional evidence. The libraries used (Hugging Face transformers, peft, trl, and evaluate) have changed their APIs since then, so check current documentation before rebuilding any of these workflows. A.1 Common setup Item Choice Model google/flan-t5-base: an instruction-tuned encoder–decoder model of about 250M parameters (Chapter 3) Data DialogSum (Y. Chen et al. 2021): about 13,000 everyday and service dialogues, each with a human-written summary. Not part of Flan-T5’s training mixture. Task Generate a one- or two-sentence summary of a dialogue Reference The human summary, used for side-by-side reading and as the ROUGE reference Limits Flan-T5’s 512-token input limit; long dialogues get truncated A.2 Lab 1: Summarization with prompting and generation settings Goal. Find out how far prompting alone can take a small model, before any training. This is the first step with any new model and dataset. Steps: No instruction. Pass the raw dialogue to the model. The output was a continuation or fragment, not a summary. The model could not tell what task was wanted. Zero-shot instruction. Wrap the dialogue as “Summarize the following conversation. … Summary:”. The output became summary-like but missed nuance. Model-native template. Use one of the phrasings from Flan-T5’s own training templates (“Dialogue: … What was going on?”). This gave a modest improvement. Prompts that match the model’s instruction-tuning format tend to work better. One-shot and few-shot. Prepend one, then three, complete examples (dialogue plus human summary) before the target dialogue. One-shot helped; few-shot did not clearly beat one-shot on the example shown. Some few-shot prompts also exceeded the 512-token limit. Generation settings. Vary max_new_tokens, sampling on or off, and temperature (Section 1.6). Low temperature gave conservative, repeatable summaries. High temperature gave varied and sometimes incoherent ones. Lessons: With a small model, the instruction wording and format matter, and in-context examples give a limited lift. The course team’s rule of thumb was that more than five or six examples rarely help. Examples consume the context window. For a 512-token model this is a hard constraint. When prompting plateaus below the quality you need, fine-tune (Lab 2). A.3 Lab 2: Full fine-tuning vs. LoRA Goal. Improve zero-shot summarization by fine-tuning on DialogSum, and compare full fine-tuning with parameter-efficient LoRA (Section 3.5). Steps: Format the data as instructions. Map each record to the prompt “Summarize the following conversation. {dialogue} Summary:”, with the human summary as the target. Tokenize, and split into training, validation, and test sets. Full instruction fine-tuning. Train all ~250M parameters with the Hugging Face Trainer. The in-lab run used a small subsample and very few steps to save time. A checkpoint trained longer offline was then loaded for evaluation. That checkpoint was about 945 MB, a full copy of the model. LoRA fine-tuning. Wrap the same base model with a LoRA configuration of rank \(r = 32\), a relatively high rank. That left about 1.4% of parameters trainable. Train the same way, then load an offline-trained adapter of about 14 MB. Inference. Load the adapter on top of the frozen base model with training disabled. That reported 0% trainable parameters and avoids allocating training state. Evaluate. Compare human, base-model, fully fine-tuned, and LoRA-tuned summaries, first by reading them and then with ROUGE (Section 3.6) on a larger held-out set. Reported results: Full fine-tuning clearly beat the base model on every ROUGE variant. The walkthrough quoted about 18 (ROUGE-1), 10 (ROUGE-2), 13 (ROUGE-L), and 13.7 (ROUGE-Lsum) “percent” higher. It did not say whether these are relative changes or absolute ROUGE points. The lecture summarized the same comparison as absolute ROUGE-1 gains of +0.19 (full) and +0.17 (LoRA), which suggests absolute points. LoRA scored about 1–2 points below full fine-tuning across the ROUGE metrics. It trained about 1.4% of the parameters and stored about 14 MB instead of about 945 MB. Lessons: A small amount of task-specific instruction data can lift a general instruct model substantially on a narrow task. LoRA gives up a little quality for large savings in training memory and storage. The base model can be shared, with one small adapter per task. Read outputs as well as metrics. A ROUGE gain says nothing directly about invented details or missing actions. A.4 Lab 3: Detoxifying with RLHF (PPO) Goal. Make the Lab 2 summarizer less likely to produce hateful or toxic language, using reinforcement learning against a reward model (Chapter 4). Components: Role What was used Policy The LoRA-tuned Flan-T5 from Lab 2, plus a value head. The head is a single linear layer from the 768-dimensional hidden state to a scalar: 768 weights plus 1 bias. Only the LoRA adapter and the value head were trained. Reference policy A frozen copy of the Lab 2 model, used for the KL penalty Reward model An off-the-shelf RoBERTa hate-speech classifier with two classes, not hate and hate. The logit of the “not hate” class was the reward. Algorithm PPO from the trl library, with batch size 16 and few PPO epochs to keep the run short Evaluation Mean and standard deviation of the classifier’s hate probability over generated summaries, before and after training Steps: Build prompts from DialogSum dialogues, sampling input lengths to fit the model’s context. Measure the baseline toxicity of the Lab 2 model’s summaries. For each batch: generate summaries, score each (prompt, summary) pair with the classifier, and pass the prompts, responses, and rewards to a PPO step. The KL divergence to the reference model was monitored so that the policy could not drift into reward hacking. Re-measure toxicity, and compare summaries and rewards before and after. Reported results. After a short run, rewards rose on many examples and mean toxicity fell “by a decent amount”. The KL divergence stayed roughly stable during training. The course noted that the effect was modest because DialogSum is not a toxic dataset to begin with. Training longer, on more toxic prompts, would show a larger difference. Lessons: Check the reward’s class index. The classifier put “not hate” at index Optimizing the wrong index would actively increase toxicity. Reward definitions deserve tests of their own. A classifier is a narrow reward. The policy is optimized towards whatever this one model measures, which is why the KL penalty and human review of samples matter (Section 4.4). PEFT makes RLHF affordable. Training only the adapter and the value head kept memory low. The reference policy could share the frozen base weights. A.5 What the three labs show together Lab Lifecycle stage Lever What changes Main cost 1 Adapt (prompting) Instructions, examples, generation settings Only the input Context tokens; limited ceiling 2 Adapt (fine-tuning) Supervised training, full or LoRA Weights or adapter Labelled data and compute 3 Align PPO against a reward model, with a KL penalty Adapter and value head Reward design, run stability, evaluation The progression is the one recommended throughout this part of the book: start with prompting, fine-tune when prompting plateaus, align when outputs must follow preferences that labels alone do not capture, and evaluate at every step.
